If the claim is not true, then there is a surgery at some time \( \widetilde{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) such that some point \( \widetilde{y} \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},\rho }\right) \) lies in the instant gluing cap. We can choose sufficiently small \( {\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) such that \( 2{\rho }_{0} < {\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\widetilde{h} \) , where \( \widetilde{h} \geq  {D}^{-1}{20}^{-\frac{1}{2}}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) is the cutoff radius of the rescaled solutions at \( \widetilde{t} \) . By applying Assertion 3 with \( \left( {\widetilde{y},0}\right)  = \left( {{y}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , we see that there is a \( k\left( {{\rho }_{0}, M\left( \rho \right) }\right)  > 0 \) such that when \( k \geq  k\left( {{\rho }_{0}, M\left( \rho \right) }\right) \) ,

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  2{D}^{\prime \prime }
\]

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},\rho }\right) \) . This is a contradiction as \( \rho  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} \) .

Since for each fixed \( 0 < \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) with \( \rho \) near \( {\rho }_{0} \) , the rescaled solutions are defined on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},\rho }\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) for all large \( k \) , by Step 1 and Shi’s derivative estimate, we know that the covariant derivatives and higher order derivatives of the curvatures on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},\rho  - \frac{\left( {\rho }_{0} - \rho \right) }{2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{32}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) are also uniformly bounded.

By the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}},\bar{x}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },\bar{x}}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( \gamma \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( \bar{x} \) .

Clearly, the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption. Consider a tubular neighborhood along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) defined by

\[
V = \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{{q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty }}}{B}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,
\]

where \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty } \) denotes the scalar curvature of the limit and

\[
{B}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)
\]

is the ball centered at \( {q}_{0} \in  {B}_{\infty } \) with the radius \( {4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . Let \( {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) denote the completion of \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) \) , and \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) the limit point of \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . Exactly as in the second step of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1, it follows from the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty } \) is cylindrical at any point \( {q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) which is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) and then the metric space \( \bar{V} = V \cup  \left\{  {y}_{\infty }\right\} \) by adding the point \( {y}_{\infty } \) has nonnegative curvature in the Alexandrov sense. Consequently we have a three-dimensional non-flat tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) at \( {y}_{\infty } \) which is a metric cone with aperture \( \leq  {20\varepsilon } \) .

On the other hand, note that by the canonical neighborhood assumption, the canonical \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck neighborhoods are strong. Thus at each point \( q \in  V \) near \( {y}_{\infty } \) , the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty } \) actually exists on the whole parabolic neighborhood

\[
V\bigcap P\left( {q,0,\frac{1}{3}{\eta }^{-1}{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( q\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( q\right) \right) }^{-1}}\right) ,
\]

and is a smooth solution of the Ricci flow there. Pick \( z \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) with distance one from the vertex \( {y}_{\infty } \) and it is nonflat around \( z \) . By definition the ball \( B\left( {z,\frac{1}{2}}\right)  \subset \; {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) is the Gromov-Hausdorff convergent limit of the scalings of a sequence of balls \( {B}_{\infty }\left( {{z}_{\ell },{\sigma }_{\ell }}\right) \left( { \subset  \left( {V,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) }\right) \) where \( {\sigma }_{\ell } \rightarrow  0 \) . Since the estimate (7.4.14) survives on \( \left( {V,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) \) for all \( A <  + \infty \) , and the tangent cone is three-dimensional and nonflat around \( z \) , we see that this convergence is actually in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology and over some ancient time interval. Since the limiting \( {B}_{\infty }\left( {z,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \left( { \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V}}\right) \) is a piece of nonnegatively curved nonflat metric cone, we get a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum principle (Theorem 2.2.1) as before. So we have proved \( {\rho }_{0} = \infty \) . This proves (i).

By the same proof of Assertion 1 in Step 2, we can further show that for any \( L \) , the rescaled solutions on the balls \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, L}\right) \) are defined at least on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( L\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) . This proves (ii).

Step 4. For any subsequence \( \left( {{\alpha }_{k},{\beta }_{k}}\right) \) of \( \left( {\alpha ,\beta }\right) \) with \( {r}^{{\alpha }_{k}} \rightarrow  0 \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \rightarrow  0 \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) , by Step 3, the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property and Hamilton’s compactness theorem, we can extract a \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) convergent subsequence of \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) over some space-time open subsets containing the slice \( \{ t = 0\} \) . We now want to show any such limit has bounded curvature at \( t = 0 \) . We prove by contradiction. Suppose not, then there is a sequence of points \( {z}_{\ell } \) divergent to infinity in the limiting metric at time zero with curvature divergent to infinity. Since the curvature at \( {z}_{\ell } \) is large (comparable to one), \( {z}_{\ell } \) has a canonical neighborhood which is a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap or strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck. Note that the boundary of \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap lies in some \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck. So we get a sequence of \( {2\varepsilon } \) -necks with radius going to zero. Note also that the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature. Without loss of generality, we may assume \( {2\varepsilon } < {\varepsilon }_{0} \) , where \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) is the positive constant in Proposition 6.1.1. Thus this arrives at a contradiction with Proposition 6.1.1.

Step 5. In this step, we will choose some subsequence \( \left( {{\alpha }_{k},{\beta }_{k}}\right) \) of \( \left( {\alpha ,\beta }\right) \) so that we can extract a complete smooth limit of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) to the Ricci flow with surgery on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some \( a > 0 \) .

Choose \( {\alpha }_{k},{\beta }_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) so that \( {r}^{{\alpha }_{k}} \rightarrow  0,{\widetilde{\delta }}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \rightarrow  0 \) , and Assertion 1,2,3 hold with \( \alpha  = {\alpha }_{k},\beta  = {\beta }_{k} \) for all \( A \in  \{ p/q \mid  p, q = 1,2,\ldots , k\} \) , and \( B, C \in  \{ 1,2,\ldots , k\} \) . By Step 3, we may assume the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) converge in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology at the time \( t = 0 \) . Since the curvature of the limit at \( t = 0 \) is bounded by Step 4, it follows from Assertion 1 in Step 2 and the choice of the sequence \( \left( {{\alpha }_{k},{\beta }_{k}}\right) \) that the limiting \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is defined at least on a backward time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some positive constant \( a \) and is a smooth solution to the Ricci flow there.

Step 6. We further want to extend the limit in Step 5 backwards in time to infinity to get an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Let \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) be the convergent sequence obtained in the above Step 5.

Denote by

\( {t}_{\max } = \sup \left\{  {{t}^{\prime } \mid  }\right. \) we can take a smooth limit on \( \left( {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) (with bounded curvature at each time slice) from a subsequence of

\[
\text{ the rescaled solutions }\left. {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\right\}  \text{ . }
\]

We first claim that there is a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) which converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) on the maximal time interval \( \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Indeed, let \( {t}_{\ell } \) be a sequence of positive numbers such that \( {t}_{\ell } \rightarrow  {t}_{\max } \) and there exist smooth limits \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\ell }^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) defined on \( \left( {-{t}_{\ell },0}\right\rbrack \) . For each \( \ell \) , the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature and has bounded curvature at each time slice. Moreover by the gradient estimate in canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) , the limit has bounded curvature on each subinterval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \subset  \left( {-{t}_{\ell },0}\right\rbrack \) . Denote by \( \widetilde{Q} \) the scalar curvature upper bound of the limit at time zero \( \left( {\widetilde{Q}\text{ is independent of }}\right. \ell ) \) . Then we can apply Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5) to get

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\ell }^{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{{t}_{\ell }}{t + {t}_{\ell }}\widetilde{Q}
\]

where \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\ell }^{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right) \) are the scalar curvatures of the limits \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\ell }^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) . Hence by the definition of convergence and the above curvature estimates, we can find a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) which converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) on the maximal time interval \( \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

We need to show \( - {t}_{\max } =  - \infty \) . Suppose \( - {t}_{\max } >  - \infty \) , there are only the following two possibilities: either

(1) The curvature of the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) becomes unbounded as \( t \searrow   - {t}_{\max } \) ; or

(2) For each small constant \( \theta  > 0 \) and each large integer \( {k}_{0} > 0 \) , there is some \( k \geq \; {k}_{0} \) such that the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) has a surgery time \( {T}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \theta ,0}\right\rbrack \) and a surgery point \( {x}_{k} \) lying in a gluing cap at the times \( {T}_{k} \) so that \( {d}_{{T}_{k}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},\bar{x}}\right) \) is uniformly bounded from above by a constant independent of \( \theta \) and \( {k}_{0} \) .

We next claim that the possibility (1) always occurs. Suppose not; then the curvature of the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is bounded on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) by some positive constant \( \widehat{C} \) . In particular, for any \( A > 0 \) , there is a sufficiently large integer \( {k}_{1} > 0 \) such that any rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) with \( k \geq  {k}_{1} \) on the geodesic ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and its scalar curvature is bounded by \( 2\widehat{C} \) there. (Here, without loss of generality, we may assume that the upper bound \( \widehat{C} \) is so large that \( - {t}_{\max } + \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1} < 0 \) .) By Assertion 1 in Step 2, for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) over \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) can be defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and has the scalar curvature \( \widetilde{R} \leq  {10}\widehat{C} \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . So we can extract a smooth limit from the sequence to get the limiting solution which is defined on a larger time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . This contradicts the definition of the maximal time \( - {t}_{\max } \) .

It remains to exclude the possibility (1).

By using Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5) again, we have

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{{t}_{\max }}{t + {t}_{\max }}\widetilde{Q}.
\]

So we only need to control the curvature near \( - {t}_{\max } \) . Exactly as in Step 4 in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1, it follows from Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality that

(7.4.16)

\[
{\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  + {30}{t}_{\max }\sqrt{\widetilde{Q}}
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Since the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time, we have some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and some time \( - {t}_{\max } < {t}_{\infty } <  - {t}_{\max } + \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1} \) such that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty }}\right)  < \; 5/4 \) . By (7.4.16), there is a constant \( {\widetilde{A}}_{0} > 0 \) such that \( {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{y}_{\infty }}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{A}}_{0}/2 \) for all \( t \in  \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Now we come back to the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) . Clearly, for arbitrarily given small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) , when \( k \) large enough, there is a point \( {y}_{k} \) in the underlying manifold of \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) at time 0 satisfying the following properties

(7.4.17)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{\infty }}\right)  < \frac{3}{2},\;{\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{A}}_{0}
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . By the definition of convergence, we know that for any fixed \( {A}_{0} \geq  2{\widetilde{A}}_{0} \) , for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solution over \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{A}_{0}}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{2{t}_{\max }}{t + {t}_{\max }}\widetilde{Q}
\]

on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{A}_{0}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) . Then by Assertion 2 of Step 2, we have proved that there is a sufficiently large integer \( {\bar{k}}_{0} \) such that when \( k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0} \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) at \( {y}_{k} \) can be defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and satisfy

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{y}_{k}, t}\right)  \leq  {15}
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) .

We now prove a statement analogous to Assertion 4 (i) of Step 3.

Assertion 5. For the above rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) and \( {\bar{k}}_{0} \) , we have that for any \( L > 0 \) , there is a positive constant \( \omega \left( L\right) \) such that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \omega \left( L\right)
\]

for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  L \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) , and for all \( k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0} \) .

Proof of Assertion 5. We slightly modify the argument in the proof of Assertion 4 (i). Let

\[
M\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  \rho }\right. \text{ and }t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
\text{ in the rescaled solutions }\left. {{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}, k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0}}\right\}
\]

and

\[
{\rho }_{0} = \sup \{ \rho  > 0 \mid  M\left( \rho \right)  <  + \infty \} .
\]

Note that the estimate (7.4.14) implies that \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) . We only need to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) .

We argue by contradiction. Suppose \( {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) . Then, after passing to a subsequence, there is a sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{y}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) in the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) with \( {t}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\widetilde{d}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\widetilde{y}}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) such that \( \widetilde{R}\left( {{\widetilde{y}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Denote by \( {\gamma }_{k} \) a minimizing geodesic segment from \( {y}_{k} \) to \( {\widetilde{y}}_{k} \) at the time \( {t}_{k} \) and denote by \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) the open geodesic ball centered at \( {y}_{k} \) of radius \( {\rho }_{0} \) on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

For any \( 0 < \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) with \( \rho \) near \( {\rho }_{0} \) , by applying Assertion 3 as before, we get that the rescaled solutions on the balls \( {B}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho }\right) \) are defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for all large \( k \) . By Step 1 and Shi’s derivative estimate, we further know that the covariant derivatives and higher order derivatives of the curvatures on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho  - \frac{\left( {\rho }_{0} - \rho \right) }{2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{32}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) are also uniformly bounded. Then by the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) ,{y}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {y}_{\infty } \) .

Clearly, the limit also has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption. Then by repeating the same argument as in the proof of Assertion 4 (i) in the rest, we derive a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum principle. This proves Assertion 5.

We then apply the second estimate of (7.4.17) and Assertion 5 to conclude that for any large constant \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) , there is a positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) such that for any small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

(7.4.18)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Then by applying Assertion 1 in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on the geodesic balls \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Furthermore, by the gradient estimates as in Step 1, we have

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right)
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) is arbitrarily small and the positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) is independent of \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) , we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfy

(7.4.19)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right) ,
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) .

Now, by taking convergent subsequences from the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) , we see that the limit solution is defined smoothly on a space-time open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times \; ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . By Step 4, we see that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , - {t}_{\max }}\right) \) at time \( - {t}_{\max } \) has bounded curvature. Then by combining with the canonical neighborhood assumption of accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) , we conclude that the curvature of the limit is uniformly bounded on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . So we have excluded the possibility (1).

Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Finally by combining with the canonical neighborhood theorem (Theorem 6.4.6), we see that \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) has a canonical neighborhood with parameter \( \varepsilon \) , which is a contradiction. Therefore we have completed the proof of the proposition. 0

Finally we try to extend the limit backwards in time to get an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Since the curvature of the limit is bounded at \( t = 0 \) , it follows from the estimate (7.5.14) that the limit is a smooth solution to the Ricci flow defined at least on a backward time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some positive constant \( a \) . Let \( \left( {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal time interval over which we can extract a smooth limiting solution. It suffices to show \( {t}_{\infty } =  - \infty \) . If \( {t}_{\infty } >  - \infty \) , there are only two possibilities: either there exist surgeries in finite distance around the time \( {t}_{\infty } \) or the curvature of the limiting solution becomes unbounded as \( t \searrow  {t}_{\infty } \) .

Let \( c > 0 \) be a positive constant much smaller than \( \frac{1}{100}{\eta }^{-1} \) . Note again that the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time. Then we can find some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and some time \( t = {t}_{\infty } + \theta \) with \( 0 < \theta  < \frac{c}{3} \) such that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right)  \leq  2 \) .

Consider the (unrescaled) scalar curvature \( R \) of \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at the point \( \bar{x} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the scalar curvature \( {R}_{\infty } \) of the limit on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{3},0}\right\rbrack \) is uniformly bounded by some positive constant \( C \) , we have the curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {\bar{x}, t}\right)  \leq  {2C}\bar{Q}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) and all sufficiently large \( m \) . For each fixed \( m \) and \( {\alpha }_{m} \) , we may require the chosen \( {\beta }_{m} \) to satisfy

\[
{\left( {\bar{\delta }}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\right) }^{-2}{\left( \widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}}}{2}\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  m\widetilde{r}{\left( {t}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}}\right) }^{-2} \geq  m\bar{Q}.
\]

When \( m \) is large enough, we observe again that Lemma 3.4.1 (ii) is applicable for \( {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},\bar{x}}\right) \) with \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . Then by repeating the argument as in the derivation of (7.2.1),(7.2.2) and (7.2.3), we deduce that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) . \)

Let \( \left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) be a sequence of associated points and times in the (unrescaled) solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) so that after rescaling, the sequence converges to \( \left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right) \) in the limit. Clearly \( \frac{\theta }{2} \leq  {\theta }_{m} \leq  {2\theta } \) for all sufficiently large \( m \) . Then by the argument as in the derivation of (7.5.13), we know that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the solution \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at \( {y}_{m} \) is defined on the whole time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m} - }\right. }\right. \; \left. {\left. {\frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies the curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {{y}_{m}, t}\right)  \leq  8\bar{Q}
\]

there; moreover the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) with \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  4\bar{Q} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) .

We now consider the rescaled sequence \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) with the marked points replaced by \( {y}_{m} \) and the times replaced by \( {s}_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) . As before the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality implies the rescaling limit around \( \left( {{y}_{m},{s}_{m}}\right) \) agrees with the original one. Then the arguments in previous paragraphs imply the limit is well-defined and smooth on a space-time open neighborhood of the maximal time slice \( \left\{  {t = {t}_{\infty }}\right\} \) . Particularly this excludes the possibility of existing surgeries in finite distance around the time \( {t}_{\infty } \) . Moreover, the limit at \( t = {t}_{\infty } \) also has bounded curvature. By using the gradient estimates in the canonical neighborhood assumption on the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) , we see that the second possibility is also impossible. Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Therefore we have proved the canonical neighborhood statement (ii).

(iii) This is analogous to Theorem 7.2.1. We also argue by contradiction. Suppose for some \( A <  + \infty \) and sequences of positive numbers \( {K}_{2}^{\alpha } \rightarrow   + \infty ,{\bar{r}}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) there exists a sequence of times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) such that for any sequences \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } > 0 \) with \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \rightarrow  0 \) for fixed \( \alpha \) , we have sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery and sequences of points \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) , of positive constants \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\sqrt{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }} \) which satisfy the assumptions, but for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) there hold

(7.5.16)

\[
R\left( {{x}^{\alpha \beta },{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\right)  > {K}_{2}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2}\text{ , for some }{x}^{\alpha \beta } \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }, A{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) .
\]

We may assume that \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) , where \( {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) is chosen so that the statements (i) and (ii) hold on \( {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta },{4A}{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) \) . Let \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions of \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) around the origins \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with factor \( {\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \) and shift the times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) to zero. Then by applying the statement (ii), we know that the regions, where the scalar curvature of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) is at least \( {K}_{1}\left( { = {K}_{1}\left( {4A}\right) }\right) \) , are canonical neighborhood regions. Note that canonical \( \varepsilon \) -neck neighborhoods are strong. Also note that the pinching assumption and the assertion

\[
{t}_{0}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \geq  {\left( {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty ,\text{ as }\alpha  \rightarrow   + \infty ,
\]

imply that any subsequent limit of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) must have nonnegative sectional curvature. Thus by the above argument in the proof of the statement (ii) (or the argument in Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1), we conclude that there exist subsequences \( \alpha  = {\alpha }_{m},\beta  = {\beta }_{m} \) such that the curvatures of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) stay uniformly bounded at distances from the origins \( {x}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) not exceeding \( {2A} \) . This contradicts (7.5.16) for \( m \) sufficiently large. This proves the statements (iii).

Clearly for fixed \( A \) , after defining the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) for each \( {t}_{0} \) , one can adjust the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) so that it is nonincreasing in \( {t}_{0} \) .

Therefore we have completed the proof of the theorem.

From now on we redefine the function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) so that it is also less than \( {\bar{\delta }}_{2\left( {t + 1}\right) }\left( {2t}\right) \) and then the above theorem always holds for \( A \in  \left\lbrack  {1,2\left( {{t}_{0} + 1}\right) }\right\rbrack \) . Particularly, we still

have

\[
\widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  \leq  \bar{\delta }\left( t\right)  = \min \left\{  {\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}\log \left( {1 + t}\right) },{\delta }_{0}}\right\}  ,
\]

which tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) . We may also require that \( \widetilde{r}\left( t\right) \) tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: (cf. G. Perelman [33, Th. 12.1]). Let \( \left( {M,{g}_{0}}\right) \) be a compact manifold with positive isotropic curvature of dimension \( n \geq  {12} \) , which does not contain any nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space forms. Let \( g\left( t\right) , t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , denote the solution to the Ricci flow with initial metric \( {g}_{0} \) . Given a small number \( \widetilde{\varepsilon } > 0 \) and a large number \( {A}_{0} \) , we can find a positive number \( \widehat{r} \) with the following property: If \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is a point in space-time with \( Q \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {\widehat{r}}^{-2} \) , then the parabolic neighborhood \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},{A}_{0}{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times \; \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {A}_{0}{Q}^{-1},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) is, after scaling by the factor \( Q,\widetilde{\varepsilon } \) -close to the corresponding subset of an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution satisfying \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC.

The proof of Theorem 7.2 is an adaptation of Perelman's work [33]. (See also [12], where the four-dimensional case is treated.) By Corollary 1.3, the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature for some function \( f \) satisfying \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{s \rightarrow  \infty }}\frac{f\left( s\right) }{s} \; = 0 \) and some constant \( \theta  > 0 \) . Let us fix a small number \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , and let \( {C}_{1} = {C}_{1}\left( {n,\theta ,\varepsilon }\right) \) and \( {C}_{2} = {C}_{2}\left( {n,\theta ,\varepsilon }\right) \) denote the constants in Corollary 6.22. It suffices to prove the assertion when \( {A}_{0} \geq  8{C}_{1} \) and \( \widetilde{\varepsilon } \) is much smaller than \( \varepsilon \) . To do that, we argue by contradiction. If the assertion is false, then we can find a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) in space-time with the following properties:

(i) \( {Q}_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {j}^{2} \) .

(ii) After dilating by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) , the parabolic neighborhood

\[
{B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{A}_{0}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{j} - {A}_{0}{Q}_{j}^{-1},{t}_{j}}\right\rbrack
\]

is not \( \widetilde{\varepsilon } \) -close to the corresponding subset of any ancient \( \kappa \) -solution satisfying \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC.

By a point-picking argument, we can arrange that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the following condition:

(iii) If \( \left( {\widetilde{x},\widetilde{t}}\right) \) is a point in space-time such that \( \widetilde{t} \leq  {t}_{j} \) and \( \widetilde{Q} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {\widetilde{x},\widetilde{t}}\right)  \geq  4{Q}_{j} \) , then the parabolic neighborhood \( {B}_{g\left( \widetilde{t}\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{A}_{0}{\widetilde{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {\widetilde{t} - {A}_{0}{\widetilde{Q}}^{-1},\widetilde{t}}\right\rbrack \) is, after dilating by the factor \( \widetilde{Q},\widetilde{\varepsilon } \) -close to the corresponding subset of an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution satisfying \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC.

Our strategy is to rescale the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) around the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . We will show that the rescaled flows converge to an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution satisfying \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. To that end, we proceed in several steps:

Step 1: We first establish a pointwise curvature derivative estimate. By Corollary 6.20, we can find a large constant \( \eta \) , depending only on \( n \) and \( \theta \) , such that \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  \eta {\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  \eta {\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) on every ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Using property (iii) above, we conclude that \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) for each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in space-time satisfying \( t \leq  {t}_{j} \) and \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  4{Q}_{j} \) .

Step 2: We next prove bounds for the higher order covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor. Suppose that \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is a point in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  + {Q}_{j} \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . The pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1 implies that \( \operatorname{scal} \leq  8{r}_{0}^{-2} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{{r}_{0}}{100\eta }, - \frac{{r}_{0}^{2}}{100\eta }}\right) \) . Using Shi’s interior derivative estimates, we conclude \( \left| {{D}^{m}R}\right|  \leq  C\left( {n, m,\eta }\right) {r}_{0}^{-m - 2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) .

Step 3: We next prove a long-range curvature estimate. Given any \( \rho  > 0 \) , we define

\[
\mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right) .
\]

Here, we allow the possibility that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  = \infty \) . The pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1 implies that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  \leq  8 \) for \( 0 < \rho  < \frac{1}{100\eta } \) .

We claim that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) for all \( \rho  > 0 \) . Suppose this is false. Let

\[
{\rho }^{ * } = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 : \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \}  < \infty .
\]

Clearly, \( {\rho }^{ * } \geq  \frac{1}{100\eta } \) . By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , we have an upper bound for the curvature in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . By Step 2, we obtain bounds for the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Moreover, Perelman’s noncollapsing estimate gives a lower bound for the volume. We rescale around \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) and pass to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) . In the limit, we obtain an incomplete manifold \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) that is weakly PIC2 (cf. [31, Th. 5.6]).

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , we can find a sequence of points \( {y}_{j} \) such that

\[
{\rho }_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {Q}_{j}^{\frac{1}{2}}{d}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{y}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }^{ * }\;\text{ and }\;{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty .
\]

For each \( j \) , we can find a unit speed geodesic \( {\gamma }_{j} : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) such that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( 0\right)  = {x}_{j} \) and \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  = {y}_{j} \) . Let \( {\gamma }_{\infty } : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }^{ * }}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) denote the limit of \( {\gamma }_{j} \) . Using the pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1, we obtain

\[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( s\right) }\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {s{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( \eta \left( {\rho }^{ * } - s\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  {100}
\]

if \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) .

Let us consider a real number \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) such that \( 8{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . We claim that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) lies at the center of a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ). Indeed, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, it follows from property (iii) and Corollary 6.22 that the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap; or a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) ; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -quotient neck. Furthermore, the Canonical Neighborhood is contained in a geodesic ball around \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) of radius \( 2{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , and the scalar curvature is at most \( 2{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) at each point in the Canonical Neighborhood. Since \( \mathbb{M}\left( \bar{s}\right)  < \infty \) , we obtain

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  = \infty ;
\]

consequently, \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  4{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {y}_{j} \) . We next observe that

\[
8{C}_{1}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}{\left( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  8{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s}.
\]

This implies \( 4{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {x}_{j} \) . In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) cannot be a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) . Moreover, if the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap, then the geodesic \( {\gamma }_{j} \) must enter and exit this \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap, but this is impossible since \( {\gamma }_{j} \) minimizes length. Finally, if the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a quotient neck, then Theorem A. 1 in [6] implies that \( M \) contains a nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space form, contrary to our assumption. To summarize, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck. In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

Passing to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) , we conclude that \( \left| {D{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}_{{q}^{\infty }}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) . Integrating this estimate along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) gives \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) }\right)  \geq \; {\left( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \left( {\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-2} \) . Moreover, since \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies at the center of a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck for \( j \) sufficiently large, the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) must lie on a \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) .

As in [33, §12.1], there is a sequence of rescalings that converges to a piece of a nonflat metric cone in the limit. Using the pointwise curvature derivative estimate established in Step 1, we can extend the metric backwards in time. This gives a locally defined solution to the Ricci flow that is weakly PIC2 and that, at the final time, is a piece of nonflat metric cone. This contradicts Proposition 6.5.

Step 4: We now rescale the manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) around the point \( {x}_{j} \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . By Step 3, we have uniform bounds for the curvature at bounded distance. Using the curvature derivative estimate in Step 1 together with Shi's interior derivative estimates, we conclude that the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor are bounded at bounded distance. Combining this with Perelman's noncollapsing estimate, we conclude that (after passing to a subsequence) the rescaled manifolds converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete smooth limit manifold \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) . Since \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature, the curvature tensor of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is weakly PIC2 and satisfies \( R - \; \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. Using property (iii) and Corollary 6.22, we conclude that every point in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with scalar curvature greater than 4 has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -quotient neck. Note that the last possibility cannot occur; indeed, if \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) contains a quotient neck, then \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) contains a quotient neck for \( j \) sufficiently large, and Theorem A.1 in [6] then implies that \( M \) contains a nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space form, contrary to our assumption.

We claim that the limit manifold \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature. Indeed, if there is a sequence of points in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with curvature going to infinity, then \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) contains a sequence of necks with radii converging to 0, contradicting Proposition 6.9. Thus, \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature.

Step 5: We now extend the limit \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time. By Step 4, the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is bounded from above by a constant \( \Lambda  > 4 \) . Using the pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1, we conclude that

\[
\mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{j} - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1},{t}_{j}}\right\rbrack  }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {2\Lambda }
\]

for each \( A > 1 \) . Hence, if we put \( {\tau }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }}  - \frac{1}{200\eta \Lambda } \) , then we can extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) of the Ricci flow that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  {2\Lambda } \) . In the next step, we put \( {\tau }_{2} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{1} - \frac{1}{{200n}{\Lambda }_{1}} \) . Using the pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1, we can extend the solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack \) , backwards in time to a solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{2},0}\right\rbrack \) . Moreover, \( {\Lambda }_{2} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \; \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{2},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{1} \) . Continuing this process, we can extend the solution backwards in time to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack \) , where \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) and \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m} \) .

Let \( {\tau }^{ * } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\tau }_{m} \leq   - \frac{1}{200\eta \Lambda } \) . Using a standard diagonal sequence argument, we obtain a complete, smooth limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined on the interval \( \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) and that has bounded curvature for each \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature, the curvature tensor of the limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is weakly PIC2 and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \) id \( \in \) PIC.

Step 6: We claim that \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . To prove this, we argue by contradiction. Suppose \( {\tau }^{ * } >  - \infty \) . Clearly, \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {\tau }_{m + 1}}\right)  = 0 \) , hence \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) .

By the Harnack inequality (cf. Theorem 6.1 above), the function \( t \mapsto \; \left( {t - {\tau }^{ * }}\right) {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( x\right) \) is monotone increasing at each point \( x \in  {M}^{\infty } \) . Since \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\left( x\right)  \leq  \Lambda \) for all \( x \in  {M}^{\infty } \) , we obtain

\[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( x\right)  \leq  \frac{-{\tau }^{ * }}{t - {\tau }^{ * }}\Lambda
\]

for all \( x \in  {M}^{\infty } \) and all \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) . Using Lemma 8.3(b) in [33], we conclude that

\[
0 \leq   - \frac{d}{dt}{d}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  C\left( n\right) \sqrt{\frac{-{\tau }^{ * }}{t - {\tau }^{ * }}\Lambda }
\]

for all \( x, y \in  {M}^{\infty } \) and all \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) . Integrating over \( t \) gives

\[
{d}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {d}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {d}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\left( {x, y}\right)  + C\left( n\right) \left( {-{\tau }^{ * }}\right) \sqrt{\Lambda }
\]

for all \( x, y \in  {M}^{\infty } \) and all \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) .

By the maximum principle,

\[
\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) } \leq  1
\]

for all \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) . Hence, we can find a point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}^{\infty } \) such that \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( {y}_{\infty }\right) \; \leq  4 \) for \( t = {\tau }^{ * } + \frac{1}{1000\eta \Lambda } \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) . Using the pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1, we obtain \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( {y}_{\infty }\right)  \leq  8 \) for all \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },{\tau }^{ * } + \frac{1}{1000\eta \Lambda }}\right\rbrack \) . In particular, \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) }\left( {y}_{\infty }\right)  \leq  8 \) if \( m \) is sufficiently large. Arguing as in Step 3, we can show that

\[
\mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) \left( {{y}_{\infty }, A}\right) }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) } < \infty
\]

for every \( A > 1 \) .

Consequently, a subsequence of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) ,{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) converges in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete, smooth limit. If this limit manifold has unbounded curvature, then (by property (iii) above) it contains a sequence of necks with radii converging to 0 , contradicting Proposition 6.9. Therefore, a subsequence of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) ,{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) converges in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete, smooth limit with bounded curvature. Consequently, we can find a constant \( {\Lambda }^{ * } > \Lambda \) (independent of \( A \) ) such that

\[
\mathop{\liminf }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) }{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) } \leq  {\Lambda }^{ * }
\]

for every \( A > 1 \) . Using the distance estimate, we obtain \( {B}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\left( {{y}_{\infty }, A}\right)  \subset \; {B}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) }\left( {{y}_{\infty }, A + C\left( n\right) \left( {-{\tau }^{ * }}\right) \sqrt{\Lambda }}\right) \) . Putting these facts together, we conclude that

\[
\mathop{\liminf }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( 0\right) }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) }{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) } \leq  {\Lambda }^{ * }
\]

for every \( A > 1 \) . Hence, for each \( A > 1 \) , we can find a large integer \( m \) (depending on \( A \) ) such that \( {\tau }_{m} \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },{\tau }^{ * } + \frac{1}{{1000\eta }{\Lambda }^{ * }}}\right\rbrack \) and

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{g}\infty \left( 0\right) }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {{\tau }_{m}, A}\right) }{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }^{ * }.
\]

Using the pointwise derivative estimate in Step 1, we obtain

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },{\tau }^{ * } + \frac{1}{{1000\eta }{\Lambda }^{ * }}}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( 0\right) }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  4{\Lambda }^{ * }
\]

for every \( A > 1 \) . Since \( {\Lambda }^{ * } \) is independent of \( A \) , we conclude that

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },{\tau }^{ * } + \frac{1}{{1000\eta }{\Lambda }^{ * }}}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( t\right)  \leq  4{\Lambda }^{ * }.
\]

Therefore, the flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) , has bounded curvature. This contradicts the fact that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Thus, \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) .

To summarize, if we dilate the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) around the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) , then (after passing to a subsequence), the rescaled flows converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) , \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , satisfying \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. Here, \( \kappa \) depends only on the initial data. This contradicts statement (ii). This completes the proof of Theorem 7.2.

(i) Given \( w > 0, r > 0,\xi  > 0 \) , one can find \( T = T\left( {w, r,\xi ,\varepsilon }\right)  <  + \infty \) such that if the geodesic ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, r\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) at some time \( {t}_{0} \geq  T \) has volume at least \( w{r}^{3}{t}_{0}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and the sectional curvature at least \( - {r}^{-2}{t}_{0}^{-1} \) , then the curvature at \( {x}_{0} \) at time \( t = {t}_{0} \) satisfies

(7.6.5)

\[
\left| {{2t}{R}_{ij} + {g}_{ij}}\right|  < \xi
\]

(ii) Given in addition \( 1 \leq  A < \infty \) and allowing \( T \) to depend on \( A \) , we can ensure (7.6.5) for all points in \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) .

(iii) The same is true for all points in the forward parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}, A{r}^{2}{t}_{0}}\right)  \triangleq  \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{0} + A{r}^{2}{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\}  . \)

(7.6.10)

\[
{Rm} \geq   - {K}_{2}{\left( r\sqrt{{t}_{0}}\right) }^{-2}
\]

on \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{2Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) , where \( {K}_{2} = {K}_{2}\left( {w, r, A,\varepsilon }\right) \) is some positive constant depending only on \( w, r, A \) and \( \varepsilon \) . Thus by (7.6.9) and (7.6.10) we have

(7.6.11)

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {K}_{1}^{\prime }{\left( r\sqrt{{t}_{0}}\right) }^{-2},\text{ on }{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{2Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) ,
\]

for some positive constant \( {K}_{1}^{\prime } = {K}_{1}^{\prime }\left( {w, r, A,\varepsilon }\right) \) depending only on \( w, r, A \) and \( \varepsilon \) . This gives us the curvature estimate on \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{2Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) for all \( {t}_{0} \geq  T\left( {w, r, A,\varepsilon }\right) \) .

From the arguments in proving the above assertion (i), we have the estimates (7.6.6) and (7.6.7) and the solution is well-defined on the whole parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{{r}_{0}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}{4}, - \tau {\left( {r}_{0}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}\right) }^{2}}\right) \) for all \( {t}_{0} \geq  T\left( {w, r, A,\varepsilon }\right) \) . Clearly we may assume that \( {\left( {K}_{1}^{\prime }\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}r < \min \left\{  {\frac{{r}_{0}}{4},\sqrt{\tau }{r}_{0}}\right\} \) . Thus by combining with the curvature estimate (7.6.11), we can apply Theorem 7.5.1(i) to get the following volume control

(7.6.12)

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{\left( {K}_{1}^{\prime }\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}r\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {\left( {\left( {K}_{1}^{\prime }\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}r\sqrt{{t}_{0}}\right) }^{3}
\]

for any \( x \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) , where \( \kappa  = \kappa \left( {w, r, A,\varepsilon }\right) \) is some positive constant depending only on \( w, r, A \) and \( \varepsilon \) . So by using the assertion (i), we see that for \( {t}_{0} \geq  T \) with \( T = T\left( {w, r,\xi , A,\varepsilon }\right) \) large enough, the curvature estimate (7.6.5) holds for all points in \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) .

(iii) We next want to extend the curvature estimate (7.6.5) to all points in the forward parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}, A{r}^{2}{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Consider the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{0} + A{r}^{2}{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) in the parabolic neighborhood. In assertion (ii), we have obtained the desired estimate (7.6.5) at \( t = {t}_{0} \) . Suppose estimate (7.6.5) holds on a maximal time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) with \( {t}^{\prime } \leq  {t}_{0} + A{r}^{2}{t}_{0} \) . This says that we have

(7.6.13)

\[
\left| {{2t}{R}_{ij} + {g}_{ij}}\right|  < \xi
\]

on \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}},{t}^{\prime } - {t}_{0}}\right)  \triangleq  \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right\} \) so that either there exists a surgery in the ball \( {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) at \( t = {t}^{\prime } \) , or there holds \( \left| {{2t}{R}_{ij} + {g}_{ij}}\right|  = \; \xi \) somewhere in \( {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) at \( t = {t}^{\prime } \) . Since the Ricci curvature is near \( - \frac{1}{2{t}^{\prime }} \) in the geodesic ball, the surgeries cannot occur there. Thus we only need to consider the latter possibility.

Recall that the evolution of the length of a curve \( \gamma \) and the volume of a domain \( \Omega \) are given by

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{L}_{t}\left( \gamma \right)  =  - {\int }_{\gamma }\operatorname{Ric}\left( {\dot{\gamma },\dot{\gamma }}\right) d{s}_{t}
\]

\[
\text{ and }\;\frac{d}{dt}{\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( \Omega \right)  =  - {\int }_{\Omega }{Rd}{V}_{t}
\]

By substituting the curvature estimate (7.6.13) into the above two evolution equations and using the volume lower bound (7.6.6), it is not hard to see

(7.6.14)

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{0},\sqrt{{t}^{\prime }}}\right) }\right)  \geq  {\kappa }^{\prime }{\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }^{\frac{3}{2}}
\]

for some positive constant \( {\kappa }^{\prime } = {\kappa }^{\prime }\left( {w, r,\xi , A,\varepsilon }\right) \) depending only on \( w, r,\xi , A \) and \( \varepsilon \) . Then by the above assertion (ii), the combination of the curvature estimate (7.6.13) and the volume lower bound (7.6.14) implies that the curvature estimate (7.6.5) still holds for all points in \( {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) provided \( T = T\left( {w, r,\xi , A,\varepsilon }\right) \) is chosen large enough. This is a contradiction. Therefore we have proved assertion (iii).

We now state and prove the important Thick-thin decomposition theorem. A more general version (without the restriction on \( \varepsilon \) ) was implicitly claimed by Perelman in [103] and [104].

\[
{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},{\left( 2{C}_{1}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},2{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)
\]

and

\[
{\left( 2{C}_{2}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  2{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  B \) . Moreover, \( B \) is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck (in the sense of [35]) with center at \( {x}_{0} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap.
