We argue by contradiction. Suppose that the assertion is false. Then we can find a sequence of Ricci flows with surgery \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) and a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) in space-time with the following properties:

(i) The flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{j}}\right) \) and has surgery parameters \( \varepsilon ,{\widehat{r}}_{j},{h}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) , where \( {\widehat{r}}_{j} \leq  \frac{1}{j} \) and \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \leq  \min \left\{  {\widetilde{\widetilde{\delta }}\left( {\widehat{r}}_{j}\right) ,\frac{1}{j}}\right\} \) . Here, \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( \cdot \right) \) is the function introduced in Proposition 10.9.

(ii) \( {Q}_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2{\widehat{r}}_{j}\right) }^{-2} \) .

(iii) The point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) does not satisfy the conclusion of Theorem 10.10.

Condition (iii) means that at least one of the following statements is true:

- There does not exist a neighborhood \( B \) of \( {x}_{j} \) with the property that \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{\left( 2{C}_{1}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},2{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and \( {\left( 2{C}_{2}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \leq  \operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right)  \leq  2{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) for all \( x \in  B \) , and such that \( B \) is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck (in the sense of [35]) with center at \( {x}_{j} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap.

- \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  > {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

- \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  > {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

We will proceed in several steps:

Step 1: By Definition 10.1, we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq \; {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) for each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  4{Q}_{j} \) . Moreover, by Proposition 10.9, the flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than \( \varepsilon \) for some uniform constant \( \kappa \) that may depend on the initial data, but it is independent of \( j \) .

Step 2: Suppose that \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is a point in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \; + {Q}_{j} \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that scal \( \leq \; 8{r}_{0}^{-2} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{{r}_{0}}{100\eta }, - \frac{{r}_{0}^{2}}{100\eta }}\right) \) . Using Proposition 10.4, we conclude that \( \left| {{D}^{m}R}\right|  \leq  C\left( {n, m,\eta }\right) {r}_{0}^{-m - 2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Moreover, Proposition 10.9 implies \( {\operatorname{vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}_{0}^{n} \) for some uniform constant \( \kappa \) that is independent of \( j \) .

Step 3: We next prove a long-range curvature estimate. Given any \( \rho  > 0 \) , we put

\[
\mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right) .
\]

The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  \leq  {16} \) for \( 0 < \; \rho  < \frac{1}{100\eta }. \)

We claim that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) for all \( \rho  > 0 \) . Suppose this is false. Let

\[
{\rho }^{ * } = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 : \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \}  < \infty .
\]

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , we have an upper bound for the curvature in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Using the results in Step 2, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Moreover, the noncollapsing estimate in Step 2 gives a lower bound for the volume. We rescale around \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) and pass to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) . In the limit, we obtain an incomplete manifold \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) that is weakly PIC2 (cf. [31, Th. 5.6]).

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , there exists a sequence of points \( {y}_{j} \) such that

\[
{\rho }_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {Q}_{j}^{\frac{1}{2}}{d}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{y}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }^{ * }\;\text{ and }\;{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty .
\]

Let \( {\gamma }_{j} : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) be a unit-speed geodesic such that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( 0\right)  = {x}_{j} \) and \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  = {y}_{j} \) , and let \( {\gamma }_{\infty } : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }^{ * }}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) denote the limit of \( {\gamma }_{j} \) . Using the estimate \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) we obtain for \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) ,

\[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( s\right) }\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {s{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2\eta \left( {\rho }^{ * } - s\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  {100}.
\]

Let us consider a real number \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) such that \( {64}{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . We claim that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) lies at the center of a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ). Indeed, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption implies that the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. Furthermore, the Canonical Neighborhood is contained in a geodesic ball around \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) of radius \( 8{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , and the scalar curvature is at most \( 8{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) at each point in the Canonical Neighborhood. Since \( \mathbb{M}\left( \bar{s}\right)  < \infty \) , we obtain \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  = \infty \) ; consequently, \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {16}{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {y}_{j} \) . We next observe that \( {32}{C}_{1}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}{\left( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  {64}{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . This implies \( {16}{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {x}_{j} \) . If the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap, then the geodesic \( {\gamma }_{j} \) must enter and exit this \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap, but this is impossible since \( {\gamma }_{j} \) minimizes length. To summarize, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) . \)

Passing to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) , we conclude that \( \left| {D{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) . Integrating this estimate along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) gives \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) }\right)  \geq \; {\left( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \left( {\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-2} \) . Moreover, since \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies at the center of a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck for \( j \) sufficiently large, the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) must lie on a strong \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) .

As in \( \left\lbrack  {{33},§{12.1}}\right\rbrack \) , there is a sequence of rescalings that converges to a piece of a nonflat metric cone in the limit. Let us fix a point on this metric cone. In view of the preceding discussion, this point must lie on a strong \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck. This gives a locally defined solution to the Ricci flow that is weakly PIC2 and that, at the final time, is a piece of nonflat metric cone. This contradicts Proposition 6.5.

Step 4: We now dilate the manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) around the point \( {x}_{j} \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . By Step 3, we have uniform bounds for the curvature at bounded distance. Using the results in Step 2, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor at bounded distance. Using these estimates together with the noncollapsing estimate in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled manifolds converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete limit manifold \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) . Since \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature, the curvature tensor of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is weakly PIC2 and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC. Using the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption, we conclude that every point in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with scalar curvature greater than 4 has a neighborhood that is either a strong \( {8\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {8\varepsilon } \) -cap.

We claim that \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature. Indeed, if there is a sequence of points in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with curvature going to infinity, then \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) contains a sequence of necks with radii converging to 0 , contradicting Proposition 6.9. This shows that \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature.

Step 5: We now extend the limit \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time. By Step 4, the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is bounded from above by a constant \( \Lambda  > 4 \) . We claim that, given any \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right)
\]

is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large. To prove this, fix \( A > 1 \) and suppose that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery. Let \( {s}_{j} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }}\right\rbrack \) be the largest number such that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. The pointwise curvature derivative estimate gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\left. P\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\right) \right) }\operatorname{scal} \leq  {2\Lambda }{Q}_{j}
\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Since the scalar curvature is greater than \( \frac{1}{2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \) at each point modified by surgery, we deduce that \( \frac{1}{2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \leq  {2\Lambda }{Q}_{j} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. In particular, \( {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1} \leq  \frac{1}{10\eta }{h}_{j}^{2} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Since \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) ,

Proposition 10.5 implies that the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right)
\]

is, after dilating by the factor \( {h}_{j} \) , arbitrarily close to a piece of the standard solution when \( j \) is sufficiently large. Using Corollary 9.3, we conclude that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap when \( j \) is sufficiently large. If \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, then this neck is actually a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, since we are assuming that each \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) -neck on which we perform surgery has a large backward parabolic neighborhood that is free of surgeries (cf. Definition 10.1). Moreover, Corollary 9.3 implies that \( \left| {D\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Therefore, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10, and this contradicts statement (iii). Thus, given any \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large.

Let \( {\tau }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }}  - \frac{1}{200\eta \Lambda } \) . In view of the preceding discussion, we may extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  {2\Lambda } \) .

We now repeat this process. Suppose that we can extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack \) , and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{m} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } < \infty \) . Let \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) . We claim that we can extend the solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) backward to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m} \) .

Indeed, if this is not possible, then there exists a number \( A > 1 \) with the property that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery for \( j \) sufficiently large. Let \( {s}_{j} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right\rbrack \) be the largest number such that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. The pointwise curvature derivative estimate gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\left. P\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}\right) \right) }\operatorname{scal} \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m}{Q}_{j}
\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Let us choose \( {\alpha }_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{n - 1}{2}}\right) \) so that \( \frac{{\alpha }_{m}}{{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) } \geq \; 8{\Lambda }_{m}\left( {\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) \) . If \( \left( {{s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1} \geq  {\alpha }_{m}{h}_{j}^{2} \) for \( j \) sufficiently large, then Proposition 10.5 together with the lower bound for the scalar curvature on the standard solution (cf. Theorem 9.1) gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal} \geq  \frac{1}{2{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) }{h}_{j}^{-2}
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{{\alpha }_{m}}{2{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) }{\left( {s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}\right) }^{-1}{Q}_{j}
\]

\[
\geq  4{\Lambda }_{m}{Q}_{j}
\]

for \( j \) sufficiently large, which is impossible. Consequently, \( \left( {{s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1} \leq  {\alpha }_{m}{h}_{j}^{2} \) for \( j \) sufficiently large. Since \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) , Proposition 10.5 implies that the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is, after dilating by the factor \( {h}_{j} \) , arbitrarily close to a piece of the standard solution when \( j \) is sufficiently large. Using Corollary 9.3, we conclude that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap when \( j \) is sufficiently large. If \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, then this neck is actually a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, since we are assuming that each \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) -neck on which we perform surgery has a large backward parabolic neighborhood that is free of surgeries (cf. Definition 10.1). Moreover, Corollary 9.3 implies that \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Therefore, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10, and this contradicts statement (iii). Thus, we may extend the flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) backward to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack \) , where \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) , and we have \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m}. \)

Let \( {\tau }^{ * } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\tau }_{m} \leq   - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda } \) . Using a standard diagonal sequence argument, we obtain a complete, smooth limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined on the interval \( \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) and that has bounded curvature for each \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Step 6: We next show that \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . Indeed, if \( {\tau }^{ * } >  - \infty \) , it follows that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {\tau }_{m + 1}}\right)  = 0 \) , hence \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Arguing as in Step 6 in the proof of Theorem 7.2, we can show that the limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) has bounded curvature. This contradicts the fact that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Thus, \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . Hence, if we dilate the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) around the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) , then (after passing to a subsequence) the rescaled flows converge to an ancient solution that is complete, has bounded curvature, is weakly PIC2, and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. By Proposition 10.9, the limiting ancient solution is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) that depends only on the initial data. By Corollary 6.22, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck with center at \( {x}_{j} \) ; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap; or a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) ; or a quotient neck. Recall that we have discarded all connected components that are diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) (see Definition 10.1). Hence, the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) cannot be a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) . If the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a quotient neck, then Theorem A. 1 in [6] implies that the underlying manifold contains a nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space form, contrary to our assumption. Consequently, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck with center at \( {x}_{j} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap. Finally, Corollary 6.20 implies that \( \left| {D\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\mathrm{{scal}}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . In summary, we have shown that the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10. This contradicts statement (iii). This completes the proof of Theorem 10.10.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(Justification of the canonical neighborhood assumption). Given any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist decreasing sequences \( 0 < {\widetilde{r}}_{j} < \varepsilon ,{\kappa }_{j} > 0 \) , and \( 0 < {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} < {\varepsilon }^{2}, j = 1,2,\cdots \) , with the following property. Define the positive function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) on \( \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) by \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) . Suppose there is a surgically modified solution, defined on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( T <  + \infty \) , to the Ricci flow which satisfies the following:

(1) it starts on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric, and

(2) it has only a finite number of surgeries such that each surgery at a time \( t \in  \left( {0, T}\right) \) is a \( \delta \left( t\right) \) -cutoff surgery with

\[
0 < \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \min \{ \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) ,\bar{\delta }\left( t\right) \} .
\]

Then on each time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack  \bigcap \lbrack 0, T), j = 1,2,\cdots \) , the solution satisfies the \( {\kappa }_{j} \) -noncollapsing condition on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) and the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {\widetilde{r}}_{j} \) .

Here and in the following, we call a (three-dimensional) surgically modified solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t < T,\kappa \) -noncollapsed at \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) on the scales less than \( \rho \) (for some \( \kappa  > 0,\rho  > 0 \) ) if it satisfies the following property: whenever \( r < \rho \) and

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {r}^{-2}
\]

for all those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}, r, - {r}^{2}}\right)  = \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the solution is defined, we have

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}^{3}.
\]

The proof of the proposition is by induction: having constructed our sequences for \( 1 \leq  j \leq  m \) , we make one more step, defining \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) , \( {\kappa }_{m + 1},{\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) , and redefining \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) . In view of the previous lemma, we only need to define \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .

In Theorem 7.1.1 we have obtained the canonical neighborhood structure for smooth solutions. When adapting the arguments in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1 to the present surgical solutions, we will encounter the new difficulty of how to take a limit for the surgically modified solutions. The idea to overcome the difficulty consists of two parts. The first part, due to Perelman [104], is to choose \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) small enough to push the surgical regions to infinity in space. (This is the reason why we need to redefine \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .) The second part is to show that solutions are smooth on some small, but uniform, time intervals (on compact subsets) so that we can apply Hamilton's compactness theorem, since we only have curvature bounds; otherwise Shi's interior derivative estimate may not be applicable. In fact, the second part is more crucial. That is just concerned with the question of whether the surgery times accumulate or not. Our argument will use the canonical neighborhood characterization of the standard solution in Lemma 7.3.5.

We now start to prove the proposition by contradiction. Suppose for sequence of positive numbers \( {r}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) , satisfying \( {r}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) as \( \alpha  \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  \frac{1}{\alpha  \cdot  \beta }\left( { \rightarrow  0}\right) \) , there exist sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery, where each of them has only a finite number of cutoff surgeries and has a compact orientable normalized three-manifold as initial data, so that the following two assertions hold:

(i) each \( \delta \) -cutoff at a time \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) satisfies \( \delta  \leq  {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) ; and

(ii) the solutions satisfy the statement of the proposition on \( \left\lbrack  {0, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) , but violate the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) on \( \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

For each solution \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) , we choose \( \bar{t} \) (depending on \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) ) to be the nearly first time for which the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) is violated. More precisely, we choose \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) so that the canonical neighborhood assumption with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) and with accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon \) is violated at some \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , however the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) holds on \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . After passing to subsequences, we may assume each \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) is less than the \( \widetilde{\delta } \) in Lemma 7.4.2 with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) when \( \alpha \) is fixed. Then by Lemma 7.4.2 we have uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) on \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) with some \( \kappa  > 0 \) independent of \( \alpha ,\beta \) .

Slightly abusing notation, we will often drop the indices \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) .

Let \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions around \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with factors \( R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \left( { \geq  {r}^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty }\right) \) and shift the times \( \bar{t} \) to zero. We hope to take a limit of the rescaled solutions for subsequences of \( \alpha ,\beta  \rightarrow  \infty \) and show the limit is an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which will give the desired contradiction. We divide our arguments into the following six steps.

Step 1. Let \( \left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right) \) be a point on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right)  \leq  A \) (for some \( A \geq  1 \) ) and \( \widehat{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {-\left( {\bar{t} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) . Then we have estimate

(7.4.14)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10A}
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {y,\widehat{t},\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1}}\right)  \triangleq \; \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {y,\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {\widehat{t} - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1},\widehat{t}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the rescaled solution is defined.

Indeed, as in the first step of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1, this follows directly from the gradient estimates (7.3.4) in the canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) .

Step 2. In this step, we will prove three time extension results.

Assertion 1. For arbitrarily fixed \( \alpha ,0 < A <  + \infty ,1 \leq  C <  + \infty \) and \( 0 \leq  B < \frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{2}{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{C}^{-1} \) , there is a \( {\beta }_{0} = {\beta }_{0}\left( {\varepsilon , A, B, C}\right) \) (independent of \( \alpha \) ) such that if \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) and the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is defined on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack \) with \( 0 \leq  b \leq  B \) and the scalar curvature satisfies

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C,\;\text{ on }{\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack  ,
\]

then the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{C}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) .

Before giving the proof, we make a simple observation: once a space point in the Ricci flow with surgery is removed by surgery at some time, then it never appears for later time; if a space point at some time \( t \) cannot be defined before the time \( t \) , then either the point lies in a gluing cap of the surgery at time \( t \) or the time \( t \) is the initial time of the Ricci flow.

Proof of Assertion 1. Firstly we claim that there exists \( {\beta }_{0} = {\beta }_{0}\left( {\varepsilon , A, B, C}\right) \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) , the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) can be defined before the time \( - b \) (i.e., there are no surgeries interfering in \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b - {\epsilon }^{\prime }, - b}\right\rbrack \) for some \( \left. {{\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0}\right) \) .

We argue by contradiction. Suppose not, then there is some point \( \widetilde{x} \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) such that the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) at \( \widetilde{x} \) cannot be defined before the time \( - b \) . By the above observation, there is a surgery at the time \( - b \) such that the point \( \widetilde{x} \) lies in the instant gluing cap.

Let \( \widetilde{h}\left( { = R{\left( \bar{x},\bar{t}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}h}\right) \) be the cut-off radius at the time \( - b \) for the rescaled solution. Clearly, there is a universal constant \( D \) such that \( {D}^{-1}\widetilde{h} \leq  \widetilde{R}{\left( \widetilde{x}, - b\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  D\widetilde{h} \) .

By Lemma 7.3.4 and looking at the rescaled solution at the time \( - b \) , the gluing cap and the adjacent \( \delta \) -neck, of radius \( \widetilde{h} \) , constitute a \( {\left( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) -cap \( \mathcal{K} \) . For any fixed small positive constant \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) (much smaller than \( \varepsilon \) ), we see that

\[
{\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{R}{\left( \widetilde{x}, - b\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  \mathcal{K}
\]

when \( \beta \) large enough. We first verify the following

CLAIM 1. For any small constants \( 0 < \widetilde{\theta } < 1,{\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) , there exists a \( \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right)  > 0 \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right) \) , we have

(i) the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) over \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack \)

(ii) the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) in the \( {\left( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) -cap \( \mathcal{K} \) evolved by the Ricci flow on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) is, after scaling with factor \( {\widetilde{h}}^{-2} \) , \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) -close (in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  {\delta }^{\prime  - 1}\right\rbrack  } \) topology) to the corresponding subset of the standard solution.

This claim essentially follows from Lemma 7.3.6. Indeed, suppose there is a surgery at some time \( \widetilde{\widetilde{t}} \in  \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left( {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) which removes some point \( \widetilde{\widetilde{x}} \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) . for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},\rho }\right) \) . This is a contradiction as \( \rho  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} \) .

Since for each fixed \( 0 < \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) with \( \rho \) near \( {\rho }_{0} \) , the rescaled solutions are defined on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},\rho }\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) for all large \( k \) , by Step 1 and Shi’s derivative estimate, we know that the covariant derivatives and higher order derivatives of the curvatures on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},\rho  - \frac{\left( {\rho }_{0} - \rho \right) }{2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{32}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) are also uniformly bounded.

By the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}},\bar{x}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },\bar{x}}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( \gamma \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( \bar{x} \) .

Clearly, the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption. Consider a tubular neighborhood along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) defined by

\[
V = \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{{q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty }}}{B}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,
\]

where \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty } \) denotes the scalar curvature of the limit and

\[
{B}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)
\]

is the ball centered at \( {q}_{0} \in  {B}_{\infty } \) with the radius \( {4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . Let \( {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) denote the completion of \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) \) , and \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) the limit point of \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . Exactly as in the second step of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1, it follows from the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty } \) is cylindrical at any point \( {q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) which is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) and then the metric space \( \bar{V} = V \cup  \left\{  {y}_{\infty }\right\} \) by adding the point \( {y}_{\infty } \) has nonnegative curvature in the Alexandrov sense. Consequently we have a three-dimensional non-flat tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) at \( {y}_{\infty } \) which is a metric cone with aperture \( \leq  {20\varepsilon } \) .

On the other hand, note that by the canonical neighborhood assumption, the canonical \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck neighborhoods are strong. Thus at each point \( q \in  V \) near \( {y}_{\infty } \) , the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty } \) actually exists on the whole parabolic neighborhood

\[
V\bigcap P\left( {q,0,\frac{1}{3}{\eta }^{-1}{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( q\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( q\right) \right) }^{-1}}\right) ,
\]

and is a smooth solution of the Ricci flow there. Pick \( z \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) with distance one from the vertex \( {y}_{\infty } \) and it is nonflat around \( z \) . By definition the ball \( B\left( {z,\frac{1}{2}}\right)  \subset \; {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) is the Gromov-Hausdorff convergent limit of the scalings of a sequence of balls \( {B}_{\infty }\left( {{z}_{\ell },{\sigma }_{\ell }}\right) \left( { \subset  \left( {V,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) }\right) \) where \( {\sigma }_{\ell } \rightarrow  0 \) . Since the estimate (7.4.14) survives on \( \left( {V,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) \) for all \( A <  + \infty \) , and the tangent cone is three-dimensional and nonflat around \( z \) , we see that this convergence is actually in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology and over some ancient time interval. Since the limiting \( {B}_{\infty }\left( {z,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \left( { \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V}}\right) \) is a piece of nonnegatively curved nonflat metric cone, we get a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum principle (Theorem 2.2.1) as before. So we have proved \( {\rho }_{0} = \infty \) . This proves (i).

By the same proof of Assertion 1 in Step 2, we can further show that for any \( L \) , the rescaled solutions on the balls \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, L}\right) \) are defined at least on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( L\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) . This proves (ii).

Step 4. For any subsequence \( \left( {{\alpha }_{k},{\beta }_{k}}\right) \) of \( \left( {\alpha ,\beta }\right) \) with \( {r}^{{\alpha }_{k}} \rightarrow  0 \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \rightarrow  0 \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) , by Step 3, the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property and Hamilton’s compactness theorem, we can extract a \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) convergent subsequence of \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) over some space-time open subsets containing the slice \( \{ t = 0\} \) . We now want to show any such limit has bounded curvature at \( t = 0 \) . We prove by contradiction. Suppose not, then there is a sequence of points \( {z}_{\ell } \) divergent to infinity in the limiting metric at time zero with curvature divergent to infinity. Since the curvature at \( {z}_{\ell } \) is large (comparable to one), \( {z}_{\ell } \) has a canonical neighborhood which is a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap or strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck. Note that the boundary of \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap lies in some \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck. So we get a sequence of \( {2\varepsilon } \) -necks with radius going to zero. Note also that the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature. Without loss of generality, we may assume \( {2\varepsilon } < {\varepsilon }_{0} \) , where \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) is the positive constant in Proposition 6.1.1. Thus this arrives at a contradiction with Proposition 6.1.1.

Step 5. In this step, we will choose some subsequence \( \left( {{\alpha }_{k},{\beta }_{k}}\right) \) of \( \left( {\alpha ,\beta }\right) \) so that we can extract a complete smooth limit of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) to the Ricci flow with surgery on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some \( a > 0 \) .

Choose \( {\alpha }_{k},{\beta }_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) so that \( {r}^{{\alpha }_{k}} \rightarrow  0,{\widetilde{\delta }}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \rightarrow  0 \) , and Assertion 1,2,3 hold with \( \alpha  = {\alpha }_{k},\beta  = {\beta }_{k} \) for all \( A \in  \{ p/q \mid  p, q = 1,2,\ldots , k\} \) , and \( B, C \in  \{ 1,2,\ldots , k\} \) . By Step 3, we may assume the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) converge in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology at the time \( t = 0 \) . Since the curvature of the limit at \( t = 0 \) is bounded by Step 4, it follows from Assertion 1 in Step 2 and the choice of the sequence \( \left( {{\alpha }_{k},{\beta }_{k}}\right) \) that the limiting \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is defined at least on a backward time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some positive constant \( a \) and is a smooth solution to the Ricci flow there.

Step 6. We further want to extend the limit in Step 5 backwards in time to infinity to get an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Let \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) be the convergent sequence obtained in the above Step 5.

Denote by

\( {t}_{\max } = \sup \left\{  {{t}^{\prime } \mid  }\right. \) we can take a smooth limit on \( \left( {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) (with bounded curvature at each time slice) from a subsequence of

\[
\text{ the rescaled solutions }\left. {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\right\}  \text{ . }
\]

We first claim that there is a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) which converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) on the maximal time interval \( \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Indeed, let \( {t}_{\ell } \) be a sequence of positive numbers such that \( {t}_{\ell } \rightarrow  {t}_{\max } \) and there exist smooth limits \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\ell }^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) defined on \( \left( {-{t}_{\ell },0}\right\rbrack \) . For each \( \ell \) , the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature and has bounded curvature at each time slice. Moreover by the gradient estimate in canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) , the limit has bounded curvature on each subinterval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \subset  \left( {-{t}_{\ell },0}\right\rbrack \) . Denote by \( \widetilde{Q} \) the scalar curvature upper bound of the limit at time zero \( \left( {\widetilde{Q}\text{ is independent of }}\right. \ell ) \) . Then we can apply Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5) to get

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\ell }^{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{{t}_{\ell }}{t + {t}_{\ell }}\widetilde{Q}
\]

where \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\ell }^{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right) \) are the scalar curvatures of the limits \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\ell }^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) . Hence by the definition of convergence and the above curvature estimates, we can find a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) which converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) on the maximal time interval \( \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

We need to show \( - {t}_{\max } =  - \infty \) . Suppose \( - {t}_{\max } >  - \infty \) , there are only the following two possibilities: either

(1) The curvature of the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) becomes unbounded as \( t \searrow   - {t}_{\max } \) ; or

(2) For each small constant \( \theta  > 0 \) and each large integer \( {k}_{0} > 0 \) , there is some \( k \geq \; {k}_{0} \) such that the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) has a surgery time \( {T}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \theta ,0}\right\rbrack \) and a surgery point \( {x}_{k} \) lying in a gluing cap at the times \( {T}_{k} \) so that \( {d}_{{T}_{k}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},\bar{x}}\right) \) is uniformly bounded from above by a constant independent of \( \theta \) and \( {k}_{0} \) .

We next claim that the possibility (1) always occurs. Suppose not; then the curvature of the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is bounded on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) by some positive constant \( \widehat{C} \) . In particular, for any \( A > 0 \) , there is a sufficiently large integer \( {k}_{1} > 0 \) such that any rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) with \( k \geq  {k}_{1} \) on the geodesic ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and its scalar curvature is bounded by \( 2\widehat{C} \) there. (Here, without loss of generality, we may assume that the upper bound \( \widehat{C} \) is so large that \( - {t}_{\max } + \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1} < 0 \) .) By Assertion 1 in Step 2, for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) over \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) can be defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and has the scalar curvature \( \widetilde{R} \leq  {10}\widehat{C} \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . So we can extract a smooth limit from the sequence to get the limiting solution which is defined on a larger time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . This contradicts the definition of the maximal time \( - {t}_{\max } \) .

It remains to exclude the possibility (1).

By using Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5) again, we have

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{{t}_{\max }}{t + {t}_{\max }}\widetilde{Q}.
\]

So we only need to control the curvature near \( - {t}_{\max } \) . Exactly as in Step 4 in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1, it follows from Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality that

(7.4.16)

\[
{\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  + {30}{t}_{\max }\sqrt{\widetilde{Q}}
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Since the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time, we have some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and some time \( - {t}_{\max } < {t}_{\infty } <  - {t}_{\max } + \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1} \) such that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty }}\right)  < \; 5/4 \) . By (7.4.16), there is a constant \( {\widetilde{A}}_{0} > 0 \) such that \( {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{y}_{\infty }}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{A}}_{0}/2 \) for all \( t \in  \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Now we come back to the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) . Clearly, for arbitrarily given small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) , when \( k \) large enough, there is a point \( {y}_{k} \) in the underlying manifold of \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) at time 0 satisfying the following properties

(7.4.17)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{\infty }}\right)  < \frac{3}{2},\;{\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{A}}_{0}
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . By the definition of convergence, we know that for any fixed \( {A}_{0} \geq  2{\widetilde{A}}_{0} \) , for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solution over \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{A}_{0}}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{2{t}_{\max }}{t + {t}_{\max }}\widetilde{Q}
\]

on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{A}_{0}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) . Then by Assertion 2 of Step 2, we have proved that there is a sufficiently large integer \( {\bar{k}}_{0} \) such that when \( k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0} \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) at \( {y}_{k} \) can be defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and satisfy

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{y}_{k}, t}\right)  \leq  {15}
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) .

We now prove a statement analogous to Assertion 4 (i) of Step 3.

Assertion 5. For the above rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) and \( {\bar{k}}_{0} \) , we have that for any \( L > 0 \) , there is a positive constant \( \omega \left( L\right) \) such that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \omega \left( L\right)
\]

for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  L \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) , and for all \( k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0} \) .

Proof of Assertion 5. We slightly modify the argument in the proof of Assertion 4 (i). Let

\[
M\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  \rho }\right. \text{ and }t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
\text{ in the rescaled solutions }\left. {{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}, k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0}}\right\}
\]

and

\[
{\rho }_{0} = \sup \{ \rho  > 0 \mid  M\left( \rho \right)  <  + \infty \} .
\]

Note that the estimate (7.4.14) implies that \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) . We only need to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) .

We argue by contradiction. Suppose \( {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) . Then, after passing to a subsequence, there is a sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{y}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) in the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) with \( {t}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\widetilde{d}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\widetilde{y}}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) such that \( \widetilde{R}\left( {{\widetilde{y}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Denote by \( {\gamma }_{k} \) a minimizing geodesic segment from \( {y}_{k} \) to \( {\widetilde{y}}_{k} \) at the time \( {t}_{k} \) and denote by \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) the open geodesic ball centered at \( {y}_{k} \) of radius \( {\rho }_{0} \) on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

For any \( 0 < \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) with \( \rho \) near \( {\rho }_{0} \) , by applying Assertion 3 as before, we get that the rescaled solutions on the balls \( {B}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho }\right) \) are defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for all large \( k \) . By Step 1 and Shi’s derivative estimate, we further know that the covariant derivatives and higher order derivatives of the curvatures on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho  - \frac{\left( {\rho }_{0} - \rho \right) }{2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{32}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) are also uniformly bounded. Then by the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) ,{y}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {y}_{\infty } \) .

Clearly, the limit also has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption. Then by repeating the same argument as in the proof of Assertion 4 (i) in the rest, we derive a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum principle. This proves Assertion 5.

We then apply the second estimate of (7.4.17) and Assertion 5 to conclude that for any large constant \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) , there is a positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) such that for any small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

(7.4.18)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Then by applying Assertion 1 in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on the geodesic balls \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Furthermore, by the gradient estimates as in Step 1, we have

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right)
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) is arbitrarily small and the positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) is independent of \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) , we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfy

(7.4.19)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right) ,
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) .

Now, by taking convergent subsequences from the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) , we see that the limit solution is defined smoothly on a space-time open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times \; ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . By Step 4, we see that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , - {t}_{\max }}\right) \) at time \( - {t}_{\max } \) has bounded curvature. Then by combining with the canonical neighborhood assumption of accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) , we conclude that the curvature of the limit is uniformly bounded on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . So we have excluded the possibility (1).

Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Finally by combining with the canonical neighborhood theorem (Theorem 6.4.6), we see that \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) has a canonical neighborhood with parameter \( \varepsilon \) , which is a contradiction. Therefore we have completed the proof of the proposition. 0

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \( C < \infty \) the following holds. Suppose that \( X \) is a connected subset of a Riemannian three-manifold \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) . Suppose that every point of \( X \) is either the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck or is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. Then one of the following holds (see FIG. 4):

(1) \( X \) is contained in a component of \( M \) that is the union of two \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -caps and is diffeomorphic to one of \( {S}^{3},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(2) \( X \) is contained in a component of \( M \) that is a double \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube. This component is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(3) \( X \) is contained in a single \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap.

(4) \( X \) is contained in a \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube.

(5) \( X \) is contained in an \( \epsilon \) -tube.

(6) \( X \) is contained in a component of \( M \) that is an \( \epsilon \) -fibration, which itself is a union of \( \epsilon \) -necks.
