Fix any \( \varepsilon  \in  \left( {0,1}\right) \) and \( {h}_{0} \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) . Define the set \( F \) to be the intersection of all closed convex \( \mathrm{O}\left( n\right) \) -invariant subsets of \( {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right) \) satisfying properties (1) and (2) in the statement of Theorem 11.64. We want to show that \( F \) is the desired generalized pinching set. Since \( {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( \varepsilon \right) \) is such a set, \( F \) is a well-defined closed convex \( \mathrm{O}\left( n\right) \) -invariant subset contained in \( {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( \varepsilon \right) \) .

(I) Suppose \( {\mathbf{R}}_{0} \in  F \) and \( \mathbf{R}\left( t\right) \) is a solution of the ODE \( \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{R} = Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) with \( \mathbf{R}\left( 0\right)  = {\mathbf{R}}_{0} \) . Then for any closed convex \( \mathrm{O}\left( n\right) \) -invariant subset \( G \) of \( {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right) \) satisfying properties (1) and (2), \( {}^{29} \) we have \( \mathbf{R}\left( t\right)  \in  G \) . Hence, by definition, \( \mathbf{R}\left( t\right)  \in  F \) . Thus property (1) holds for \( F \) .

(II) It is also clear that property (2) holds for \( F \) , i.e.,

\[
{C}_{\text{ ♣ }}\left( \varepsilon \right)  \cap  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \leq  {h}_{0}}\right\}   \subset  F.
\]

(III) It remains to prove property (3). Suppose, with the goal of obtaining a contradiction, that property (3) is false for \( F \) for some \( s \in  \lbrack \varepsilon ,1) \) . Let \( {s}_{0} \in  \lbrack \varepsilon ,1) \) be the infimum of all \( s \in  \lbrack \varepsilon ,1) \) for which property (3) is false for \( F \) , i.e.,

\[
{s}_{0} \Doteq  \inf \{ s \in  \lbrack \varepsilon ,1) : F \smallsetminus  {C}_{ \clubsuit  }\left( s\right) \text{ is unbounded }\} .
\]

Then there exists a sequence \( {\left\{  {s}_{i}\right\}  }_{i \in  \mathbb{N}} \) with \( {s}_{i} \rightarrow  {s}_{0} \) such that \( F \smallsetminus  {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( {s}_{i}\right) \) is unbounded for all \( i \) . We shall obtain the contradiction from showing that \( F \smallsetminus  {C}_{4}\left( s\right) \) is bounded for any \( s \) sufficiently close to \( {s}_{0} \) .

For \( s \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) and \( \delta  > 0 \) define

\[
{C}_{\delta }\left( s\right)  \Doteq  \text{ the cone over the set }
\]

\[
\left\{  {\mathbf{R} \in  {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( s\right)  : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = 1,\operatorname{dist}\left( {\mathbf{R},\partial {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( s\right) }\right)  \geq  \delta }\right\}  ,
\]

which is a slightly smaller cone contained in \( {C}_{4}\left( s\right) \) (with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\delta  \rightarrow  0}}{C}_{\delta }\left( s\right)  = \; \left. {{C}_{4}\left( s\right) }\right) \) . For \( \delta , h > 0 \) define

\[
{T}_{h}{C}_{\delta }\left( s\right)  \Doteq  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \in  {C}_{\delta }\left( s\right) ,\operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \geq  h}\right\}  ,
\]

which is, as noted in [43], a 'truncated shifted cone'. We leave it to the reader to show that both \( {C}_{\delta }\left( s\right) \) and \( {T}_{h}{C}_{\delta }\left( s\right) \) are closed, convex, and \( \mathrm{O}\left( n\right) \) -invariant (convexity is the main issue). \( {}^{30} \)

(1) When \( \delta \) is sufficiently small, the cones \( {C}_{\delta }\left( s\right) \) are preserved by the ODE. For any \( s \in  \left( {0,1}\right) \) there exists \( {\delta }_{0} = {\delta }_{0}\left( s\right)  > 0 \) such that for all \( \delta  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{\delta }_{0}}\right\rbrack \) and \( \mathbf{R} \in  \partial {C}_{\delta }\left( s\right)  - \{ 0\} \) the vector \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone of \( {C}_{\delta }\left( s\right) \) .

This fact follows from

(i) \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\delta  \rightarrow  0}}\partial {C}_{\delta }\left( s\right)  = \partial {C}_{\Phi }\left( s\right) \) ,

(ii) the continuity of \( Q \) ,

(iii) our assumption that for \( \mathbf{R} \in  \partial {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( s\right)  \smallsetminus  \{ 0\} , Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the interior of tangent cone of \( {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( s\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} \) , and

(iv) the fact that \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is homogeneous of degree 2, i.e., \( Q\left( {c\mathbf{R}}\right)  = \; {c}^{2}Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) for all \( c \geq  0 \) (which addresses the issue of the noncompactness of the cones).

---

\( {}^{29} \) Note that we do not use property (2) here.

\( {}^{30} \) Note that the set \( \sum  \doteq  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} \in  {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( s\right)  : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = 1}\right\} \) is convex. To prove the convexity of \( {C}_{\delta }\left( s\right) \) , one just needs to show that

\[
\{ \mathbf{R} \in  \sum  : \operatorname{dist}\left( {\mathbf{R},\partial \sum }\right)  \geq  \delta \}
\]

is convex. The convexity of \( {T}_{h}{C}_{\delta }\left( s\right) \) also follows easily.

---

(2) Truncated shifted cones are preserved by the ODE. There exists \( \bar{h} \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) (in particular, for \( \bar{h} \) sufficiently large) such that the set

\[
{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right)  = \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \in  {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right\}   \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \geq  \bar{h}\}
\]

is preserved by the ODE \( \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{R} = Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) for all \( \delta  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{\delta }_{0}\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right\rbrack \) .

First note that

\[
\partial \left( {{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right)  \subset  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \in  \partial {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right\}   \cup  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\} .
\]

We have

\[
\operatorname{trace}Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = {\left| \operatorname{Rc}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \right| }^{2} \geq  \frac{4}{n}{\left( \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \right) }^{2} \geq  \frac{4}{n}{\bar{h}}^{2} > 0
\]

for \( \mathbf{R} \in  {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) (note that \( \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}\left( {\operatorname{Rc}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }\right) \) ).

Case (a). Hence for \( \mathbf{R} \) with \( \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h} \) the vector \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone of \( \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \geq  \bar{h}\} \) . This implies that for

\[
\mathbf{R} \in  \partial \left( {{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right)  \smallsetminus  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \in  \partial {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right\}   \subset  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\} ,
\]

the vector \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} \) , which is the half-space \( \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \geq  0\} \) .

Case (b). Now assume

\[
\mathbf{R} \in  \partial \left( {{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right)  \smallsetminus  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\}
\]

\[
\subset  \partial \left( {{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right)  \cap  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \in  \partial {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right\}
\]

so that in particular trace \( \left( \mathbf{R}\right)  > \bar{h} \) . In this case the tangent cone of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} \) is the same as the tangent cone of \( {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \) (after shifting the vertex by \( \mathbf{I} \) ).

Let \( {\eta }_{0} \) be the infimum of the distance from \( Q\left( {\mathbf{R}}^{\prime }\right) \) to the boundary of the tangent cone of \( {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) among \( {\mathbf{R}}^{\prime } \in  \partial {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) with \( \operatorname{trace}\left( {\mathbf{R}}^{\prime }\right)  = 1 \) . Since by part (1), \( {\eta }_{0} > 0 \) , we have that the distance from \( Q\left( {\mathbf{R}}^{\prime }\right) \) to the boundary of the tangent cone of \( {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) grows quadratically; in particular, it is at least

(11.128)

\[
{\eta }_{0}{\left( \operatorname{trace}\left( {\mathbf{R}}^{\prime }\right) \right) }^{2} \geq  c{\eta }_{0}{\left| {\mathbf{R}}^{\prime }\right| }^{2}
\]

for all \( {\mathbf{R}}^{\prime } \in  \partial {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) , where \( c > 0 \) . For \( \mathbf{R} \in  \partial \left( {{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right)  \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \in \; \left. {\partial {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right\} \)

(i) let \( {d}_{1}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) be the distance of \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) to the boundary of the tangent cone of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} \) and

(ii) let \( {d}_{2}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) be the distance of \( Q\left( {\mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I}}\right) \) to the boundary of the tangent cone of \( {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \) , so that by (11.128)

\[
{d}_{2}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \geq  c{\eta }_{0}{\left| \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I}\right| }^{2} \geq  \frac{1}{2}c{\eta }_{0}{\left| \mathbf{R}\right| }^{2}
\]

(with the last inequality holding for \( \bar{h} \) large enough). Next observe that

\[
\left| {Q\left( {\mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I}}\right)  - Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }\right|  = \left| {2\mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} + 2\mathbf{R}\# \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{I}\# \mathbf{I}}\right|
\]

\[
\leq  {A}_{1}\left| \mathbf{R}\right|
\]

for some constant \( {A}_{1} < \infty \) . Hence, by the triangle inequality and the above estimates,

\[
{d}_{1}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \geq  {d}_{2}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  - \left| {Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  - Q\left( {\mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I}}\right) }\right|
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{1}{2}c{\eta }_{0}{\left| \mathbf{R}\right| }^{2} - {A}_{1}\left| \mathbf{R}\right|
\]

so that \( {d}_{1}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  > 0 \) provided that \( \left| \mathbf{R}\right| \) is sufficiently large. Thus \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} \) .

Case (c). Finally, if

\[
\mathbf{R} \in  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \in  \partial {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right\}   \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\}  \subset  \partial \left( {{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right) ,
\]

then by the arguments in proving Cases (a) and (b), it follows that \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} \) .

By Cases (a),(b), and (c), we have shown that for all \( \mathbf{R} \in  \partial \left( {{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right) \) , the vector \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) .

(3) Given any \( \bar{h} \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) , there exists \( \delta  > 0 \) (in particular, for \( \delta \) sufficiently small) such that the set \( {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( {s}_{0}\right)  \cap  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}}\right\} \) is contained in the interior of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right)  \cap  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}}\right\} \) as subsets of the hyperplane \( \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}}\right\} \) . This is geometrically clear from considering the limit as \( \delta  \rightarrow  0 \) .

(4) By part (3), for \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small and for \( s \) close enough to \( {s}_{0} \) , \( {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( s\right)  \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\} \) is contained in the interior of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right)  \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \; \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\} \) . We claim that by the definition of \( {s}_{0} \) , for \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small there exists \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {\varepsilon ,{s}_{0}}\right) \) (except when \( {s}_{0} = \varepsilon \) , where we let \( \bar{s} = {s}_{0} \) ) and \( k \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) large enough such that

(11.129)

\( F \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = k\bar{h}\}  \subset  {C}_{\Phi }\left( \bar{s}\right)  \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = k\bar{h}\}  \subset  k \cdot  {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) , \) that is,

\[
\frac{1}{k}F \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\}  \subset  {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( \bar{s}\right)  \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\}  \subset  {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) .
\]

(a) If \( {s}_{0} = \varepsilon  = \bar{s} \) , then the claim is clear since \( F \subset  {C}_{\Phi }\left( \varepsilon \right) \) .

(b) If \( {s}_{0} > \varepsilon \) , then \( F \smallsetminus  {C}_{\Phi }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) is compact for all \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {\varepsilon ,{s}_{0}}\right) \) . Therefore, for each \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {\varepsilon ,{s}_{0}}\right) \) , there exists \( {k}_{0} \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) such that the first inclusion in (11.129) holds for all \( k \geq  {k}_{0} \) .

(5) By part (4), for \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small and \( k \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) large enough, the set

\[
{F}^{\prime } \Doteq  \left( {F \cap  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \leq  k\bar{h}}\right\}  }\right)  \cup  \left( {F \cap  k \cdot  {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right)
\]

is closed, convex, \( \mathrm{O}\left( n\right) \) -invariant, and preserved by the ODE \( \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{R} = Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) . In particular, the convexity of \( {F}^{\prime } \) follows from the inclusion (11.129). Now clearly \( {F}^{\prime } \subset  F \) . On the other hand, by the definition of \( F \) (in particular, its minimality), we have \( F \subset  {F}^{\prime } \) . Hence for \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small and \( k \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) large enough,

\[
F = {F}^{\prime }\text{ . }
\]

(6) Since the set \( k \cdot  {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right)  \smallsetminus  {C}_{\delta /2}\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) is bounded, we have that the set \( {F}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  {C}_{\delta /2}\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) is bounded. On the other hand, clearly

\[
{F}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( s\right)  \subset  {F}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  {C}_{\delta /2}\left( {s}_{0}\right)
\]

for any \( s \) close enough to \( {s}_{0} \) . Hence the set \( F \smallsetminus  {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( s\right)  = {F}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( s\right) \) is bounded for any \( s \) close enough to \( {s}_{0} \) . This contradicts the definition of \( {s}_{0} \) since there exists a sequence \( {\left\{  {s}_{i}\right\}  }_{i \in  \mathbb{N}} \) with \( {s}_{i} \rightarrow  {s}_{0} \) such that \( F \smallsetminus  {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( {s}_{i}\right) \) is not bounded for all \( i \) .

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(Justification of the canonical neighborhood assumption). Given any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist decreasing sequences \( 0 < {\widetilde{r}}_{j} < \varepsilon ,{\kappa }_{j} > 0 \) , and \( 0 < {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} < {\varepsilon }^{2}, j = 1,2,\cdots \) , with the following property. Define the positive function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) on \( \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) by \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) . Suppose there is a surgically modified solution, defined on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( T <  + \infty \) , to the Ricci flow which satisfies the following:

(1) it starts on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric, and

(2) it has only a finite number of surgeries such that each surgery at a time \( t \in  \left( {0, T}\right) \) is a \( \delta \left( t\right) \) -cutoff surgery with

\[
0 < \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \min \{ \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) ,\bar{\delta }\left( t\right) \} .
\]

Then on each time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack  \bigcap \lbrack 0, T), j = 1,2,\cdots \) , the solution satisfies the \( {\kappa }_{j} \) -noncollapsing condition on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) and the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {\widetilde{r}}_{j} \) .

Here and in the following, we call a (three-dimensional) surgically modified solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t < T,\kappa \) -noncollapsed at \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) on the scales less than \( \rho \) (for some \( \kappa  > 0,\rho  > 0 \) ) if it satisfies the following property: whenever \( r < \rho \) and

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {r}^{-2}
\]

for all those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}, r, - {r}^{2}}\right)  = \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the solution is defined, we have

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}^{3}.
\]

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
The proof of the proposition is by induction: having constructed our sequences for \( 1 \leq  j \leq  m \) , we make one more step, defining \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) , \( {\kappa }_{m + 1},{\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) , and redefining \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) . In view of the previous lemma, we only need to define \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .

In Theorem 7.1.1 we have obtained the canonical neighborhood structure for smooth solutions. When adapting the arguments in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1 to the present surgical solutions, we will encounter the new difficulty of how to take a limit for the surgically modified solutions. The idea to overcome the difficulty consists of two parts. The first part, due to Perelman [104], is to choose \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) small enough to push the surgical regions to infinity in space. (This is the reason why we need to redefine \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .) The second part is to show that solutions are smooth on some small, but uniform, time intervals (on compact subsets) so that we can apply Hamilton's compactness theorem, since we only have curvature bounds; otherwise Shi's interior derivative estimate may not be applicable. In fact, the second part is more crucial. That is just concerned with the question of whether the surgery times accumulate or not. Our argument will use the canonical neighborhood characterization of the standard solution in Lemma 7.3.5.

We now start to prove the proposition by contradiction. Suppose for sequence of positive numbers \( {r}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) , satisfying \( {r}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) as \( \alpha  \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  \frac{1}{\alpha  \cdot  \beta }\left( { \rightarrow  0}\right) \) , there exist sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery, where each of them has only a finite number of cutoff surgeries and has a compact orientable normalized three-manifold as initial data, so that the following two assertions hold:

(i) each \( \delta \) -cutoff at a time \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) satisfies \( \delta  \leq  {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) ; and

(ii) the solutions satisfy the statement of the proposition on \( \left\lbrack  {0, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) , but violate the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) on \( \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

For each solution \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) , we choose \( \bar{t} \) (depending on \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) ) to be the nearly first time for which the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) is violated. More precisely, we choose \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) so that the canonical neighborhood assumption with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) and with accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon \) is violated at some \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , however the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) holds on \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . After passing to subsequences, we may assume each \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) is less than the \( \widetilde{\delta } \) in Lemma 7.4.2 with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) when \( \alpha \) is fixed. Then by Lemma 7.4.2 we have uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) on \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) with some \( \kappa  > 0 \) independent of \( \alpha ,\beta \) .

Slightly abusing notation, we will often drop the indices \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) .

Let \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions around \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with factors \( R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \left( { \geq  {r}^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty }\right) \) and shift the times \( \bar{t} \) to zero. We hope to take a limit of the rescaled solutions for subsequences of \( \alpha ,\beta  \rightarrow  \infty \) and show the limit is an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which will give the desired contradiction. We divide our arguments into the following six steps.

Step 1. Let \( \left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right) \) be a point on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right)  \leq  A \) (for some \( A \geq  1 \) ) and \( \widehat{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {-\left( {\bar{t} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) . Then we have estimate

(7.4.14)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10A}
\]

For any \( 0 < \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) with \( \rho \) near \( {\rho }_{0} \) , by applying Assertion 3 as before, we get that the rescaled solutions on the balls \( {B}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho }\right) \) are defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for all large \( k \) . Then by the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) ,{y}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {y}_{\infty } \) .

Clearly, the limit also has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption. Then by repeating the same argument as in the proof of Assertion 4 (i) in the rest, we derive a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum principle. This proves Assertion 5.

We then apply the second estimate of (7.4.17) and Assertion 5 to conclude that for any large constant \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) , there is a positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) such that for any small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

(7.4.18)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Then by applying Assertion 1 in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on the geodesic balls \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Furthermore, by the gradient estimates as in Step 1, we have

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right)
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) is arbitrarily small and the positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) is independent of \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) , we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfy

(7.4.19)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right) ,
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) .

Now, by taking convergent subsequences from the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) , we see that the limit solution is defined smoothly on a space-time open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times \; ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . By Step 4, we see that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , - {t}_{\max }}\right) \) at time \( - {t}_{\max } \) has bounded curvature. Then by combining with the canonical neighborhood assumption of accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) , we conclude that the curvature of the limit is uniformly bounded on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . So we have excluded the possibility (1).

Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Finally by combining with the canonical neighborhood theorem (Theorem 6.4.6), we see that \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) has a canonical neighborhood with parameter \( \varepsilon \) , which is a contradiction. Therefore we have completed the proof of the proposition. 0

Moreover, suppose that \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is an arbitrary point in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2\widehat{r}\right) }^{-2} \) . \[
{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},{\left( 2{C}_{1}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},2{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)
\]

and

\[
{\left( 2{C}_{2}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  2{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  B \) . Moreover, \( B \) is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck (in the sense of [35]) with center at \( {x}_{0} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap. We argue by contradiction. Suppose that the assertion is false. Then we can find a sequence of Ricci flows with surgery \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) and a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) in space-time with the following properties:

(i) The flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{j}}\right) \) and has surgery parameters \( \varepsilon ,{\widehat{r}}_{j},{h}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) , where \( {\widehat{r}}_{j} \leq  \frac{1}{j} \) and \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \leq  \min \left\{  {\widetilde{\widetilde{\delta }}\left( {\widehat{r}}_{j}\right) ,\frac{1}{j}}\right\} \) . Here, \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( \cdot \right) \) is the function introduced in Proposition 10.9.

(ii) \( {Q}_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2{\widehat{r}}_{j}\right) }^{-2} \) .

(iii) The point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) does not satisfy the conclusion of Theorem 10.10.

Condition (iii) means that at least one of the following statements is true:

- There does not exist a neighborhood \( B \) of \( {x}_{j} \) with the property that \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{\left( 2{C}_{1}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},2{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and \( {\left( 2{C}_{2}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \leq  \operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right)  \leq  2{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) for all \( x \in  B \) , and such that \( B \) is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck (in the sense of [35]) with center at \( {x}_{j} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap.

- \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  > {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

- \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  > {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

We will proceed in several steps:

Step 1: By Definition 10.1, we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq \; {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) for each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  4{Q}_{j} \) . Moreover, by Proposition 10.9, the flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than \( \varepsilon \) for some uniform constant \( \kappa \) that may depend on the initial data, but it is independent of \( j \) .

Step 2: Suppose that \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is a point in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \; + {Q}_{j} \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that scal \( \leq \; 8{r}_{0}^{-2} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{{r}_{0}}{100\eta }, - \frac{{r}_{0}^{2}}{100\eta }}\right) \) . Using Proposition 10.4, we conclude that \( \left| {{D}^{m}R}\right|  \leq  C\left( {n, m,\eta }\right) {r}_{0}^{-m - 2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Moreover, Proposition 10.9 implies \( {\operatorname{vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}_{0}^{n} \) for some uniform constant \( \kappa \) that is independent of \( j \) .

Step 3: We next prove a long-range curvature estimate. Given any \( \rho  > 0 \) , we put

\[
\mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right) .

The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  \leq  {16} \) for \( 0 < \; \rho  < \frac{1}{100\eta }. \)

\[

As in \( \left\lbrack  {{33},§{12.1}}\right\rbrack \) , there is a sequence of rescalings that converges to a piece of a nonflat metric cone in the limit. Let us fix a point on this metric cone. Step 4: We now dilate the manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) around the point \( {x}_{j} \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . \[

\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. In particular, \( {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1} \leq  \frac{1}{10\eta }{h}_{j}^{2} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Since \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) ,

Proposition 10.5 implies that the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right)

is, after dilating by the factor \( {h}_{j} \) , arbitrarily close to a piece of the standard solution when \( j \) is sufficiently large. If \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, then this neck is actually a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, since we are assuming that each \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) -neck on which we perform surgery has a large backward parabolic neighborhood that is free of surgeries (cf. Definition 10.1). Moreover, Corollary 9.3 implies that \( \left| {D\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Therefore, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10, and this contradicts statement (iii). Thus, given any \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large.

Let \( {\tau }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }}  - \frac{1}{200\eta \Lambda } \) . In view of the preceding discussion, we may extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  {2\Lambda } \) .

We now repeat this process. Suppose that we can extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack \) , and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{m} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } < \infty \) . Let \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) . We claim that we can extend the solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) backward to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m} \) .

Indeed, if this is not possible, then there exists a number \( A > 1 \) with the property that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery for \( j \) sufficiently large. Let \( {s}_{j} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right\rbrack \) be the largest number such that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. The pointwise curvature derivative estimate gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\left. P\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}\right) \right) }\operatorname{scal} \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m}{Q}_{j}
\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Let us choose \( {\alpha }_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{n - 1}{2}}\right) \) so that \( \frac{{\alpha }_{m}}{{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) } \geq \; 8{\Lambda }_{m}\left( {\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) \) . If \( \left( {{s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1} \geq  {\alpha }_{m}{h}_{j}^{2} \) for \( j \) sufficiently large, then Proposition 10.5 together with the lower bound for the scalar curvature on the standard solution (cf. Theorem 9.1) gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal} \geq  \frac{1}{2{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) }{h}_{j}^{-2}
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{{\alpha }_{m}}{2{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) }{\left( {s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}\right) }^{-1}{Q}_{j}
\]

\[
\geq  4{\Lambda }_{m}{Q}_{j}
\]

for \( j \) sufficiently large, which is impossible. Consequently, \( \left( {{s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1} \leq  {\alpha }_{m}{h}_{j}^{2} \) for \( j \) sufficiently large. Since \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) , Proposition 10.5 implies that the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is, after dilating by the factor \( {h}_{j} \) , arbitrarily close to a piece of the standard solution when \( j \) is sufficiently large. Using Corollary 9.3, we conclude that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap when \( j \) is sufficiently large. If \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, then this neck is actually a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, since we are assuming that each \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) -neck on which we perform surgery has a large backward parabolic neighborhood that is free of surgeries (cf. Definition 10.1). Moreover, Corollary 9.3 implies that \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Therefore, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10, and this contradicts statement (iii). Thus, we may extend the flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) backward to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack \) , where \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) , and we have \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m}. \)

Let \( {\tau }^{ * } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\tau }_{m} \leq   - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda } \) . Using a standard diagonal sequence argument, we obtain a complete, smooth limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined on the interval \( \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) and that has bounded curvature for each \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Step 6: We next show that \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . Indeed, if \( {\tau }^{ * } >  - \infty \) , it follows that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {\tau }_{m + 1}}\right)  = 0 \) , hence \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Arguing as in Step 6 in the proof of Theorem 7.2, we can show that the limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) has bounded curvature. This contradicts the fact that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Thus, \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . Hence, if we dilate the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) around the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) , then (after passing to a subsequence) the rescaled flows converge to an ancient solution that is complete, has bounded curvature, is weakly PIC2, and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. By Proposition 10.9, the limiting ancient solution is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) that depends only on the initial data. By Corollary 6.22, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck with center at \( {x}_{j} \) ; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap; or a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) ; or a quotient neck. Recall that we have discarded all connected components that are diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) (see Definition 10.1). Hence, the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) cannot be a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) . If the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a quotient neck, then Theorem A. 1 in [6] implies that the underlying manifold contains a nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space form, contrary to our assumption. Consequently, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck with center at \( {x}_{j} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap. Finally, Corollary 6.20 implies that \( \left| {D\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\mathrm{{scal}}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . In summary, we have shown that the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10. This contradicts statement (iii). This completes the proof of Theorem 10.10.

Suppose the result does not hold. Then there are \( {A}^{\prime },{D}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } < \infty \) and we can pass to a subsequence (in \( a \) ) such that the hypotheses of the lemma hold for every \( a \) but no \( {x}_{a} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. The essential point of the argument is to show that in the units of the surgery scale the elapsed time between the surgery time and 0 is less than 1 and the distance from the point \( {z}_{a} \) to the tip of the surgery cap is bounded independent of \( a \) .

By Lemma 12.3, the fact that the scalar curvature at \( {z}_{a} \) is bounded by \( {D}^{\prime } \) implies that for all \( a \) sufficiently large the scale \( {\bar{h}}_{a} \) of the surgery at time \( - {t}_{a} \) satisfies

(17.2)

\[
{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \geq  {\left( 2{D}^{\prime }D\right) }^{-1}.
\]

(Recall that we are working in the rescaled flow \( \left( {{\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a},{\widetilde{G}}_{a}}\right) \) .)

Now we are ready to show that the elapsed time is bounded less than 1 in the surgery scale.

CLAIM 17.8. There is \( {\theta }_{1} < 1 \) , depending on \( {D}^{\prime } \) and \( {t}^{\prime } \) , such that for all a sufficiently large we have \( {t}_{a} < {\theta }_{1}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \) .

Proof. We consider two cases: either \( {t}_{a} \leq  {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2}/2 \) or \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2}/2 < {t}_{a} \) . In the first case, the claim is obviously true with \( {\theta }_{1} \) anything greater than \( 1/2 \) and less than 1. In the second case, the curvature everywhere along the flow line is at most \( {D}^{\prime } < \left( {2{t}_{a}{D}^{\prime }}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \leq  \left( {2{t}^{\prime }{D}^{\prime }}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) . Using Proposition 12.31 fix \( 1/2 < {\theta }_{1} < 1 \) so that every point of the standard solution \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( t \geq  \left( {2{\theta }_{1} - 1}\right) \) satisfies \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  6{t}^{\prime }{D}^{\prime } \) . Notice that \( {\theta }_{1} \) depends only on \( {D}^{\prime } \) and \( {t}^{\prime } \) . If \( {t}_{a} < {\theta }_{1}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \) , then the claim holds for this value of \( {\theta }_{1} < 1 \) . Suppose \( {t}_{a} \geq  {\theta }_{1}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \) , so that \( - {t}_{a} + \left( {2{\theta }_{1} - 1}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} < 0 \) . For all \( a \) sufficiently large we have \( {\delta }_{a} \leq  {\delta }_{0}^{\prime \prime }\left( {{A}_{0} + 5,{\theta }_{1},{\bar{\delta }}_{0}}\right) \) where \( {\bar{\delta }}_{0} \) is the constant from Definition 16.12 and \( {\delta }_{0}^{\prime \prime } \) is the constant from Proposition 16.5. This means that the scalar curvatures at corresponding points of the rescaled standard solution and the evolution of the surgery cap (up to time 0) in \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a} \) differ by at most a factor of two. Thus, for these \( a \) , we have \( R\left( {{y}_{a},\left( {-{t}_{a} + \left( {2{\theta }_{1} - 1}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2}}\right) }\right)  \geq  3\left( {{t}^{\prime }{D}^{\prime }}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) from the definition of \( {\bar{\delta }}_{0} \) and Proposition 16.5. But this is impossible since \( - {t}_{a}\left( {2{\theta }_{1} - 1}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} < 0 \) and \( 3{t}^{\prime }{D}^{\prime }/{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \geq  3{t}_{a}{D}^{\prime }/{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} > {D}^{\prime } \) as \( {t}_{a} > {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2}/2 \) . Hence, \( R\left( {{y}_{a},\left( {-{t}_{a} + \left( {2{\theta }_{1} - 1}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2}}\right) }\right)  \leq  2{t}_{a}{D}^{\prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \leq  2{t}^{\prime }{D}^{\prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) . This contradiction shows that if \( a \) is sufficiently large then \( {t}_{a} < {\theta }_{1}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \) .

We pass to a subsequence so that \( {t}_{a}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) converges to some \( \theta  \leq  {\theta }_{1} \) . We define \( \widetilde{C} \) to be the maximum of \( C \) and \( 3{\epsilon }^{-1}{\beta }^{-1} \) . Now, using part 5 of Theorem 12.5 we set \( {A}^{\prime \prime } \geq  \left( {9\widetilde{C} + 3{A}^{\prime }}\right) \sqrt{{2D}{D}^{\prime }} + 6\left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) \) sufficiently large so that in the standard flow \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0,{A}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \) contains \( B\left( {{p}_{0}, t,{A}^{\prime \prime }/2}\right) \) for any \( t \leq  \left( {{\theta }_{1} + 1}\right) /2 \) . This constant is chosen only to depend on \( {\theta }_{1},{A}^{\prime } \) , and \( C \) . As \( a \) tends to infinity, \( {\delta }_{a} \) tends to zero which means, by Proposition 16.5, that for all \( a \) sufficiently large there is an embedding

\[
{\rho }_{a} : B\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a},{A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{a},0}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a}
\]

compatible with time and the vector field such that (after translating by \( {t}_{a} \) to make the flow start at time 0 and scaling by \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) ) the restriction of \( {\widetilde{G}}_{a} \) to this image is close in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to the restriction of the standard flow to \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0,{A}^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right\rbrack \) . The image \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a}}\right) \) is the tip \( {p}_{a} \) of the surgery cap \( {\mathcal{C}}_{a} \) in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{a} \) . Thus, for all \( a \) sufficiently large the image \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a},{A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}}\right) \times \{ 0\} }\right) \) contains the \( {A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}/3 \) -neighborhood of the image \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {{p}_{0},0}\right) \) of the tip of the surgery cap under the flow forward to time 0. By our choice of \( {A}^{\prime \prime } \) , and Equation (17.2), this means that for all \( a \) sufficiently large \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a},{A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}}\right)  \times  \left\{  {-{t}_{a}}\right\}  }\right) \) contains the \( \left( {3\widetilde{C} + {A}^{\prime }}\right)  + 2\left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a} \) - neighborhood of \( {p}_{a} = {\rho }_{a}\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a}}\right) \) . Notice also that, since the standard solution has positive curvature and hence the distance between points is nonincreasing in time by Lemma 3.14, the distance at time 0 between \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {{p}_{0},0}\right) \) and \( {y}_{a} \) is less than \( 2\left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a} \) . By the triangle inequality, we conclude that for all \( a \) sufficiently large, \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a},{A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}}\right) \times \{ 0\} }\right) \) contains the \( 3\widetilde{C} \) - neighborhood of \( {x}_{a} \) . Since the family of metrics on

\[
{\rho }_{a}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a},{A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{a},0}\right\rbrack  }\right) \}
\]

(after time-shifting by \( {t}_{a} \) and rescaling by \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) ) are converging smoothly to the ball \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0,{A}^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,\theta }\right\rbrack \) in the standard flow, for all \( a \) sufficiently large, the flow from time \( - {t}_{a} \) to 0 on the \( 3\widetilde{C} \) -neighborhood of \( {x}_{a} \) is, after rescaling by \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) , very nearly isometric to the restriction of the standard flow from time 0 to \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a} \) on the \( 3\widetilde{C}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-1} \) -neighborhood of some point \( {q}_{a} \) in the standard flow. Of course, since the scalar curvature of \( {x}_{a} \) is \( 1, R\left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) in the standard flow is close to \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) . Hence, by Theorem 12.32 there is a neighborhood \( X \) of \( \left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) in the standard solution that either is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, or is an evolving \( {\beta \epsilon }/3 \) -neck centered at \( \left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) . In the latter case either the evolving neck is defined for backward time \( \left( {1 + {\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) \) or its initial time-slice is the zero time-slice and this initial time-slice lies at distance at least 1 from the surgery cap. Of course, \( X \) is contained in the \( {CR}{\left( {q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}\right) }^{-1/2} \) -neighborhood of \( \left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) in the standard solution. Since \( \widetilde{C} \geq  C \) and \( R\left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) is close to \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) , the neighborhood \( X \) is contained in the \( 2\widetilde{C}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-1} \) -neighborhood of \( \left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) in the standard solution. Hence, after rescaling, the corresponding neighborhood of \( {x}_{a} \) is contained in the \( 3\widetilde{C} \) -neighborhood of \( {x}_{a} \) . If either of the first two cases in Theorem 12.32 occurs for a subsequence of \( a \) tending to infinity, then by Lemma 9.79 and the fact that \( \widetilde{C} > \max \left( {C,{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) , we see that there is a subsequence of \( a \) for which \( {x}_{a} \) either is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap or is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck.

We must examine further the last case. We suppose that for every \( a \) this last case holds. Then for all \( a \) sufficiently large we have an \( {\beta \epsilon }/3 \) -neck \( {N}_{a} \) in the zero time-slice of \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a} \) centered at \( {x}_{a} \) . It is an evolving neck and there is an embedding \( \psi  : {N}_{a} \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{a},0}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a} \) compatible with time and the vector field so that the initial time-slice \( \psi \left( {{N}_{a} \times  \left\{  {-{t}_{a}}\right\}  }\right) \) is in the surgery time-slice \( {M}_{-{t}_{a}} \) and is disjoint from the surgery cap, so in fact it is contained in the continuing region at time \( - {t}_{a} \) . As we saw above, the image of the central 2-sphere \( \psi \left( {{S}_{a}^{2} \times  \left\{  {-{t}_{a}}\right\}  }\right) \) lies at distance at most \( {A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a} \) from the tip of the surgery cap \( {p}_{a} \) (where, recall, \( {A}^{\prime \prime } \) is a constant independent of \( a \) ). The 2-sphere, \( {\sum }_{a} \) , along which we do surgery, creating the surgery cap with \( {p}_{a} \) as its tip, is the central 2-sphere of a strong \( {\delta }_{b\left( a\right) } \) -neck. As \( a \) tends to infinity the surgery control parameter \( {\delta }_{b\left( a\right) } \) tends to zero. Thus, for \( a \) sufficiently large this strong \( {\delta }_{b\left( a\right) } \) -neck will contain a strong \( {\beta \epsilon }/2 \) - neck \( {N}^{\prime } \) centered at \( \psi \left( {{x}_{a}, - {t}_{a}}\right) \) . Since we know that the continuing region at time \( - {t}_{a} \) contains a \( {\beta \epsilon }/3 \) -neck centered at \( \left( {{x}_{a}, - {t}_{a}}\right) \) , it follows that \( {N}^{\prime } \) is also contained in \( {C}_{-{t}_{a}} \) . That is to say, \( {N}^{\prime } \) is contained in the negative half of the \( {\delta }_{b\left( a\right) } \) -neck centered at \( {\sum }_{a} \) . Now we are in the situation of Proposition 15.2. Applying this result tells us that \( {x}_{a} \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck.

This completes the proof that for all \( a \) sufficiently large, \( {x}_{a} \) has a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood in contradiction to our assumption. This contradiction completes the proof of Lemma 17.7.

(Perelman [104]). For any \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) and \( 1 \leq  A <  + \infty \) , one can find \( \kappa  = \kappa \left( {A,\varepsilon }\right)  > 0,{K}_{1} = {K}_{1}\left( {A,\varepsilon }\right)  <  + \infty ,{K}_{2} = {K}_{2}\left( {A,\varepsilon }\right)  <  + \infty \) and \( \bar{r} = \; \bar{r}\left( {A,\varepsilon }\right)  > 0 \) such that for any \( {t}_{0} <  + \infty \) there exists \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A} = {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) (depending also on \( \varepsilon \) ), nonincreasing in \( {t}_{0} \) , with the following property. Suppose we have a solution, constructed by Theorem 7.4.3 with the nonincreasing (continuous) positive functions \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) and \( \widetilde{r}\left( t\right) \) , to the Ricci flow with \( \delta \) -cutoff surgeries on time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) and with a compact orientable normalized three-manifold as initial data, where each \( \delta \) -cutoff at a time \( t \) satisfies \( \delta  = \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) on \( \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) and \( \delta  = \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  {\bar{\delta }}_{A} \) on \( \left\lbrack  {\frac{{t}_{0}}{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) ; assume that the solution is defined on the whole parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \triangleq \; \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\}  ,2{r}_{0}^{2} < {t}_{0} \) , and satisfies

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2}\;\text{ on }\;P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) ,
\]

\[
\text{ and }\;{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  {A}^{-1}{r}_{0}^{3}\text{ . }
\]

Then

(i) the solution is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales less than \( {r}_{0} \) in the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, A{r}_{0}}\right) \)

(ii) every point \( x \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, A{r}_{0}}\right) \) with \( R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {K}_{1}{r}_{0}^{-2} \) has a canonical neighborhood \( B \) , with \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,\sigma }\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{2\sigma }}\right) \) for some \( 0 < \sigma  < {C}_{1}\left( \varepsilon \right) {R}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) , which is either a strong \( \varepsilon \) -neck or an \( \varepsilon \) -cap;

(iii) if \( {r}_{0} \leq  \bar{r}\sqrt{{t}_{0}} \) then \( R \leq  {K}_{2}{r}_{0}^{-2} \) in \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, A{r}_{0}}\right) \) .

Here \( {C}_{1}\left( \varepsilon \right) \) is the positive constant in the canonical neighborhood assumption.

Without loss of generality, we may assume \( 0 < \varepsilon  \leq  {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) , where \( {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) is the sufficiently small (universal) positive constant in Lemma 7.4.2.

(i) This is analog of no local collapsing theorem II (Theorem 3.4.2). In comparison with the no local collapsing theorem II, this statement gives \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property no matter how big the time is and it also allows the solution to be modified by surgery.

Let \( \eta \left( { \geq  {10}}\right) \) be the universal constant in the definition of the canonical neighborhood assumption. Recall that we had removed every component which has positive sectional curvature in our surgery procedure. By the same argument as in the first part of the proof of Lemma 7.4.2, the canonical neighborhood assumption of the solution implies the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing on the scales less than \( \frac{1}{2\eta }\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) for some positive constant \( \kappa \) depending only on \( {C}_{1}\left( \varepsilon \right) \) and \( {C}_{2}\left( \varepsilon \right) \) (in the definition of the canonical neighborhood assumption). So we may assume \( \frac{1}{2\eta }\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \leq  {r}_{0} \leq  \sqrt{\frac{{t}_{0}}{2}} \) , and study the scales \( \rho ,\frac{1}{2\eta }\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \leq  \rho  \leq  {r}_{0} \) . Let \( x \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, A{r}_{0}}\right) \) and assume that the solution satisfies

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {\rho }^{-2}
\]

for those points in \( P\left( {x,{t}_{0},\rho , - {\rho }^{2}}\right)  \triangleq  \left\{  {\left( {y, t}\right)  \mid  y \in  {B}_{t}\left( {x,\rho }\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {\rho }^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) for which the solution is defined. We want to bound the ratio \( {\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,\rho }\right) }\right) /{\rho }^{3} \) from below.

Recall that a space-time curve is called admissible if it stays in the region unaffected by surgery, and a space-time curve on the boundary of the set of admissible curves is called a barely admissible curve. Consider any barely admissible curve \( \gamma \) , parametrized by \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\gamma },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  ,{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2} \leq  {t}_{\gamma } \leq  {t}_{0} \) , with \( \gamma \left( {t}_{0}\right)  = x \) . The same proof for the assertion (7.4.2) (in the proof of Lemma 7.4.2) shows that for arbitrarily large \( L > 0 \) (to be determined later), one can find a sufficiently small \( \bar{\delta }\left( {L,{t}_{0},\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right) ,\widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}}{2}\right) ,\varepsilon }\right)  > 0 \) such that when each \( \delta \) -cutoff in \( \left\lbrack  {\frac{{t}_{0}}{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) satisfies \( \delta  \leq  \bar{\delta }\left( {L,{t}_{0},\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right) ,\widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}}{2}\right) ,\varepsilon }\right) \) , there holds

(7.5.1)

\[
{\int }_{{t}_{\gamma }}^{{t}_{0}}\sqrt{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {{R}_{ + }\left( {\gamma \left( t\right) , t}\right)  + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( t\right) \right| }^{2}}\right) {dt} \geq  L{r}_{0}.
\]

From now on, we assume that each \( \delta \) -cutoff of the solution in the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\frac{{t}_{0}}{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) satisfies \( \delta  \leq  \bar{\delta }\left( {L,{t}_{0},\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right) ,\widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}}{2}\right) ,\varepsilon }\right) \) .

\[

\geq   - 4{\tau }^{2}

\[
\left( {\bar{L} + 2\sqrt{\tau }}\right) \nabla \phi  =  - \phi \nabla \bar{L},

and then by the computations and estimates in the proof of Theorem 3.4.2,

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \bigtriangleup }\right) h
\]

\[
\geq  \left( {{\phi }^{\prime }\left\lbrack  {\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \bigtriangleup }\right) {d}_{t} - {2A}}\right\rbrack   - {\phi }^{\prime \prime } + 2\frac{{\left( {\phi }^{\prime }\right) }^{2}}{\phi }}\right)  \cdot  \left( {\bar{L} + 2\sqrt{\tau }}\right)  - \left( {6 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}}\right) \phi
\]

\[

As before, denoting by \( {h}_{\min }\left( \tau \right)  = \mathop{\min }\limits_{z}h\left( {z,1 - \tau }\right) \) , we obtain

\[
\frac{d}{d\tau }\left( {\log \left( \frac{{h}_{\min }\left( \tau \right) }{\sqrt{\tau }}\right) }\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)  + \frac{6\sqrt{\tau } + 1}{{2\tau } - 4{\tau }^{2}\sqrt{\tau }} - \frac{1}{2\tau }
\]

\[

(7.5.6)

\[
\inf \left\{  {\bar{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right)  \mid  {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0}, y}\right)  \leq  A\left( {{2t} - 1}\right)  + \frac{1}{10}\text{ with }\tau  = 1 - t}\right\}
\]

\[
\leq  2\sqrt{\tau }\exp \left( {C\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) .
\]

By combining with (7.5.1), we know that any barely admissible curve \( \gamma \) , parametrized by \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\tau }\right\rbrack  ,0 \leq  \tau  \leq  \frac{1}{2} \) , with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = x \) , satisfies

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\tau }\sqrt{s}\left( {R + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {ds} \geq  \frac{7}{4}\exp \left( {C\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) ,
\]

by assuming \( L \geq  2\exp \left( {C\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) \) .

Since \( \left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {\rho }^{-2} \) on \( P\left( {x,{t}_{0},\rho , - {\rho }^{2}}\right) \) with \( \rho  \geq  \frac{1}{2\eta }\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) (and \( {t}_{0} = 1 \) ) and \( \bar{\delta }\left( {L,{t}_{0},\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right) ,\widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}}{2}\right) ,\varepsilon }\right)  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {x,1,\rho , - {\rho }^{2}}\right) \) around the point \( \left( {x,1}\right) \) is contained in the region unaffected by the surgery. \[
{\int }_{0}^{\tau }\sqrt{s}\left( {R + {\left| {\dot{\gamma }}_{\tau }\right| }^{2}}\right) {ds} \leq  \exp \left( {C\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) .
\]

\[
\min \left\{  {l\left( {y,{t}_{0} - \frac{1}{2}{r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \mid  y \in  {B}_{{t}_{0} - \frac{1}{2}{r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{10}{r}_{0}}\right) }\right\}   \leq  \exp \left( {C\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) ,

by noting the (parabolic) scaling invariance of the Li-Yau-Perelman distance.

\[
L = \max \{ {2L}\left( A\right) ,2\exp \left( {C\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) \} .
\]

(7.5.8)

\[
{\widetilde{V}}_{{r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  = {\int }_{{B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }{\left( 4\pi {r}_{0}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,{r}_{0}^{2}}\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( q\right)
\]

\[
\geq  c\left( A\right)
\]

for some positive constant \( c\left( A\right) \) depending only on \( A \) .

We can now argue as in the last part of the proof of Lemma 7.4.2 to get a lower bound estimate for the volume of the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,\rho }\right) \) . The union of all shortest \( \mathcal{L} \) - geodesics from \( \left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) to the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) , defined by

\[
C{B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right)  = \{ \left( {y, t}\right)  \mid  \left( {y, t}\right) \text{ lies in a shortest }\mathcal{L}\text{ -geodesic from }
\]

\[
\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \text{ to a point in }\left. {{B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right\}  \text{ , }
\]

forms a cone-like subset in space-time with vertex \( \left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Denote by \( B\left( t\right) \) the intersection of the cone-like subset \( C{B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) with the time-slice at \( t \) . Perelman’s reduced volume of the subset \( B\left( t\right) \) is given by

\[
{\widetilde{V}}_{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {B\left( t\right) }\right)  = {\int }_{B\left( t\right) }{\left( 4\pi \left( {t}_{0} - t\right) \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,{t}_{0} - t}\right) }\right) d{V}_{t}\left( q\right) .
\]

Since the cone-like subset \( C{B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) lies entirely in the region unaffected by surgery, we can apply Perelman's Jacobian comparison Theorem 3.2.7 and the estimate (7.5.8) to conclude that

(7.5.9)

\[
{\widetilde{V}}_{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {B\left( t\right) }\right)  \geq  {\widetilde{V}}_{{r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\geq  c\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) .

As before, denoting by \( \xi  = {\rho }^{-1}{\text{ Vol }}_{{t}_{0}}{\left( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( x,\rho \right) \right) }^{\frac{1}{3}} \) , we only need to get a positive lower bound for \( \xi \) . Since the curvature of the limit is bounded at \( t = 0 \) , it follows from the estimate (7.5.14) that the limit is a smooth solution to the Ricci flow defined at least on a backward time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some positive constant \( a \) . Let \( \left( {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal time interval over which we can extract a smooth limiting solution. It suffices to show \( {t}_{\infty } =  - \infty \) . If \( {t}_{\infty } >  - \infty \) , there are only two possibilities: either there exist surgeries in finite distance around the time \( {t}_{\infty } \) or the curvature of the limiting solution becomes unbounded as \( t \searrow  {t}_{\infty } \) .

Let \( c > 0 \) be a positive constant much smaller than \( \frac{1}{100}{\eta }^{-1} \) . Note again that the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time. Then we can find some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and some time \( t = {t}_{\infty } + \theta \) with \( 0 < \theta  < \frac{c}{3} \) such that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right)  \leq  2 \) .

Consider the (unrescaled) scalar curvature \( R \) of \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at the point \( \bar{x} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the scalar curvature \( {R}_{\infty } \) of the limit on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{3},0}\right\rbrack \) is uniformly bounded by some positive constant \( C \) , we have the curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {\bar{x}, t}\right)  \leq  {2C}\bar{Q}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) and all sufficiently large \( m \) . For each fixed \( m \) and \( {\alpha }_{m} \) , we may require the chosen \( {\beta }_{m} \) to satisfy

\[
{\left( {\bar{\delta }}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\right) }^{-2}{\left( \widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}}}{2}\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  m\widetilde{r}{\left( {t}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}}\right) }^{-2} \geq  m\bar{Q}.
\]

When \( m \) is large enough, we observe again that Lemma 3.4.1 (ii) is applicable for \( {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},\bar{x}}\right) \) with \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . Then by repeating the argument as in the derivation of (7.2.1),(7.2.2) and (7.2.3), we deduce that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) . \)

Let \( \left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) be a sequence of associated points and times in the (unrescaled) solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) so that after rescaling, the sequence converges to \( \left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right) \) in the limit. Clearly \( \frac{\theta }{2} \leq  {\theta }_{m} \leq  {2\theta } \) for all sufficiently large \( m \) . Then by the argument as in the derivation of (7.5.13), we know that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the solution \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at \( {y}_{m} \) is defined on the whole time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m} - }\right. }\right. \; \left. {\left. {\frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies the curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {{y}_{m}, t}\right)  \leq  8\bar{Q}
\]

there; moreover the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) with \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  4\bar{Q} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) .

We now consider the rescaled sequence \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) with the marked points replaced by \( {y}_{m} \) and the times replaced by \( {s}_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) . As before the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality implies the rescaling limit around \( \left( {{y}_{m},{s}_{m}}\right) \) agrees with the original one. Then the arguments in previous paragraphs imply the limit is well-defined and smooth on a space-time open neighborhood of the maximal time slice \( \left\{  {t = {t}_{\infty }}\right\} \) . Particularly this excludes the possibility of existing surgeries in finite distance around the time \( {t}_{\infty } \) . Moreover, the limit at \( t = {t}_{\infty } \) also has bounded curvature. By using the gradient estimates in the canonical neighborhood assumption on the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) , we see that the second possibility is also impossible. Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Therefore we have proved the canonical neighborhood statement (ii).

(iii) This is analogous to Theorem 7.2.1. We also argue by contradiction. Suppose for some \( A <  + \infty \) and sequences of positive numbers \( {K}_{2}^{\alpha } \rightarrow   + \infty ,{\bar{r}}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) there exists a sequence of times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) such that for any sequences \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } > 0 \) with \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \rightarrow  0 \) for fixed \( \alpha \) , we have sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery and sequences of points \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) , of positive constants \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\sqrt{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }} \) which satisfy the assumptions, but for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) there hold

(7.5.16)

\[
R\left( {{x}^{\alpha \beta },{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\right)  > {K}_{2}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2}\text{ , for some }{x}^{\alpha \beta } \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }, A{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) .
\]

We may assume that \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) , where \( {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) is chosen so that the statements (i) and (ii) hold on \( {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta },{4A}{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) \) . Let \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions of \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) around the origins \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with factor \( {\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \) and shift the times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) to zero. Then by applying the statement (ii), we know that the regions, where the scalar curvature of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) is at least \( {K}_{1}\left( { = {K}_{1}\left( {4A}\right) }\right) \) , are canonical neighborhood regions. Note that canonical \( \varepsilon \) -neck neighborhoods are strong. Also note that the pinching assumption and the assertion

\[
{t}_{0}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \geq  {\left( {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty ,\text{ as }\alpha  \rightarrow   + \infty ,
\]

imply that any subsequent limit of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) must have nonnegative sectional curvature. Thus by the above argument in the proof of the statement (ii) (or the argument in Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1), we conclude that there exist subsequences \( \alpha  = {\alpha }_{m},\beta  = {\beta }_{m} \) such that the curvatures of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) stay uniformly bounded at distances from the origins \( {x}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) not exceeding \( {2A} \) . This contradicts (7.5.16) for \( m \) sufficiently large. This proves the statements (iii).

Clearly for fixed \( A \) , after defining the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) for each \( {t}_{0} \) , one can adjust the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) so that it is nonincreasing in \( {t}_{0} \) .

Therefore we have completed the proof of the theorem.

From now on we redefine the function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) so that it is also less than \( {\bar{\delta }}_{2\left( {t + 1}\right) }\left( {2t}\right) \) and then the above theorem always holds for \( A \in  \left\lbrack  {1,2\left( {{t}_{0} + 1}\right) }\right\rbrack \) . Particularly, we still

have

\[
\widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  \leq  \bar{\delta }\left( t\right)  = \min \left\{  {\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}\log \left( {1 + t}\right) },{\delta }_{0}}\right\}  ,
\]

which tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) . We may also require that \( \widetilde{r}\left( t\right) \) tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) .
