\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {40}
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {\bar{x},0,\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}, - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}}\right)  \triangleq  \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {\bar{x},\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  }\right. \; \left. \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack  \right\} \) , for which the rescaled solution is defined. (Here \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) denotes the geodesic ball in the rescaled solution at time \( {t}^{\prime } \) ). Note again that \( R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{r}{\left( \bar{t}\right) }^{-2} \) and recall from our designed surgery procedure that if there is a cutoff surgery at a point \( x \) at a time \( t \) , the scalar curvature at \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is at least \( {\left( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2}\widetilde{r}{\left( t\right) }^{-2} \) . Then for each fixed sufficiently large \( \alpha \) , for \( \beta \) large enough, the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) is defined on the whole parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {\bar{x},0,\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}, - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}}\right) \) . More generally, for arbitrarily fixed \( 0 < \widetilde{K} <  + \infty \) , there is a positive integer \( {\alpha }_{0} \) so that for each \( \alpha  \geq  {\alpha }_{0} \) we can

find \( {\beta }_{0} > 0 \) (depending on \( \alpha \) ) such that if \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) and \( \left( {y,0}\right) \) is a point on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {y,0}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{K} \) and \( {\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {y,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{K} \) , we have estimate

(7.5.14)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {40}\widetilde{K}
\]

for \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {y,0,\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-1}}\right)  \triangleq  \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {y,}\right) }\right. \; \left. {\left. {\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\rbrack  ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) . In particular, the rescaled solution is defined on the whole parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {y,0,\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-1}}\right) \) .

Next, we want to show the curvature of the rescaled solutions at the new times zero (after shifting) stay uniformly bounded at bounded distances from \( \bar{x} \) for some subsequences of \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) . Let \( {\alpha }_{m},{\beta }_{m} \rightarrow   + \infty \) be chosen so that the estimate (7.5.14) holds with \( \widetilde{K} = m \) . For all \( \rho  \geq  0 \) , set

\[
M\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {\widetilde{R}\left( {x,0}\right)  \mid  m \geq  1,{d}_{0}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \rho \text{ in the rescaled solutions }{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}}\right\}
\]

and

\[
{\rho }_{0} = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 \mid  M\left( \rho \right)  <  + \infty \} .
\]

Clearly the estimate (7.5.14) yields \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) . As we consider the unshifted time \( \bar{t} \) , by combining with the assumption that \( {t}_{0} > 2{r}_{0}^{2} \) , we have

(7.5.15)

\[
\bar{t}R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \geq  \frac{{t}_{0}}{2}R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {r}_{0}^{2}\left( {{K}_{1}{r}_{0}^{-2}}\right)
\]

\[
= {K}_{1} \rightarrow   + \infty \text{ . }
\]

It then follows from the pinching assumption that we only need to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) . As before, we argue by contradiction. Suppose we have a sequence of points \( {y}_{m} \) in the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) with \( {\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{y}_{m}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) and \( \widetilde{R}\left( {{y}_{m},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Denote by \( {\gamma }_{m} \) a minimizing geodesic segment from \( \bar{x} \) to \( {y}_{m} \) and denote by \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) the open geodesic balls centered at \( \bar{x} \) of radius \( {\rho }_{0} \) of the rescaled solutions. By applying the assertion in statement (i), we have uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing at the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) . By combining with the local curvature estimate (7.5.14) and Hamilton's compactness theorem, we can assume that, after passing to a subsequence, the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}},\bar{x}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( {\gamma }_{m} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {x}_{\infty } \) . Moreover, by the pinching assumption and the estimate (7.5.15), the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature.

Then exactly as before, we consider the tubular neighborhood along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \)

\[
V = \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{{q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty }}}{B}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)
\]

and the completion \( {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) of \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) \) with \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) the limit point of \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . As before, by the choice of the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , we know that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty } \) is cylindrical at any point \( {q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) which is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) . Then by the same reason as before the metric space \( \bar{V} = V \cup  \left\{  {y}_{\infty }\right\} \) has nonnegative curvature in Alexandrov sense, and we have a three-dimensional nonflat tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) at \( {y}_{\infty } \) . Pick \( z \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) with distance one from the vertex and it is nonflat around \( z \) . By definition \( B\left( {z,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \left( { \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V}}\right) \) is the Gromov-Hausdoff convergent limit of the scalings of a sequence of balls \( {B}_{\infty }\left( {{z}_{k},{\sigma }_{k}}\right) \left( { \subset  \left( {V,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) }\right) \) with \( {\sigma }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) . Since the estimate (7.5.14) survives on \( \left( {V,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) \) for all \( \widetilde{K} <  + \infty \) , we know that this convergence is actually in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology and over some time interval. Since the limit \( B\left( {z,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \left( { \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V}}\right) \) is a piece of a nonnegatively curved nonflat metric cone, we get a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum Principle (Theorem 2.2.1) as before. Hence we have proved that a subsequence of the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) has uniformly bounded curvatures at bounded distance from \( \bar{x} \) at the new times zero.

Further, by the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing at the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) and the estimate (7.5.14) again, we can take a \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , defined on a space-time subset which contains the time slice \( \{ t = 0\} \) and is relatively open in \( {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , for the subsequence of the rescaled solutions. The limit is a smooth solution to the Ricci flow, and is complete at \( t = 0 \) , as well as has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption and the estimate (7.5.15). Thus by repeating the same argument as in the Step 4 of the proof Proposition 7.4.1, we conclude that the curvature of the limit at \( t = 0 \) is bounded.

Finally we try to extend the limit backwards in time to get an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Since the curvature of the limit is bounded at \( t = 0 \) , it follows from the estimate (7.5.14) that the limit is a smooth solution to the Ricci flow defined at least on a backward time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some positive constant \( a \) . Let \( \left( {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal time interval over which we can extract a smooth limiting solution. It suffices to show \( {t}_{\infty } =  - \infty \) . If \( {t}_{\infty } >  - \infty \) , there are only two possibilities: either there exist surgeries in finite distance around the time \( {t}_{\infty } \) or the curvature of the limiting solution becomes unbounded as \( t \searrow  {t}_{\infty } \) .

Let \( c > 0 \) be a positive constant much smaller than \( \frac{1}{100}{\eta }^{-1} \) . Note again that the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time. Then we can find some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and some time \( t = {t}_{\infty } + \theta \) with \( 0 < \theta  < \frac{c}{3} \) such that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right)  \leq  2 \) .

Consider the (unrescaled) scalar curvature \( R \) of \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at the point \( \bar{x} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the scalar curvature \( {R}_{\infty } \) of the limit on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{3},0}\right\rbrack \) is uniformly bounded by some positive constant \( C \) , we have the curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {\bar{x}, t}\right)  \leq  {2C}\bar{Q}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) and all sufficiently large \( m \) . For each fixed \( m \) and \( {\alpha }_{m} \) , we may require the chosen \( {\beta }_{m} \) to satisfy

\[
{\left( {\bar{\delta }}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\right) }^{-2}{\left( \widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}}}{2}\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  m\widetilde{r}{\left( {t}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}}\right) }^{-2} \geq  m\bar{Q}.
\]

When \( m \) is large enough, we observe again that Lemma 3.4.1 (ii) is applicable for \( {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},\bar{x}}\right) \) with \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . Then by repeating the argument as in the derivation of (7.2.1),(7.2.2) and (7.2.3), we deduce that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) . \)

Let \( \left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) be a sequence of associated points and times in the (unrescaled) solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) so that after rescaling, the sequence converges to \( \left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right) \) in the limit. Clearly \( \frac{\theta }{2} \leq  {\theta }_{m} \leq  {2\theta } \) for all sufficiently large \( m \) . Then by the argument as in the derivation of (7.5.13), we know that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the solution \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at \( {y}_{m} \) is defined on the whole time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m} - }\right. }\right. \; \left. {\left. {\frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies the curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {{y}_{m}, t}\right)  \leq  8\bar{Q}
\]

there; moreover the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) with \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  4\bar{Q} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) .

We now consider the rescaled sequence \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) with the marked points replaced by \( {y}_{m} \) and the times replaced by \( {s}_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) . As before the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality implies the rescaling limit around \( \left( {{y}_{m},{s}_{m}}\right) \) agrees with the original one. Then the arguments in previous paragraphs imply the limit is well-defined and smooth on a space-time open neighborhood of the maximal time slice \( \left\{  {t = {t}_{\infty }}\right\} \) . Particularly this excludes the possibility of existing surgeries in finite distance around the time \( {t}_{\infty } \) . Moreover, the limit at \( t = {t}_{\infty } \) also has bounded curvature. By using the gradient estimates in the canonical neighborhood assumption on the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) , we see that the second possibility is also impossible. Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Therefore we have proved the canonical neighborhood statement (ii).

(iii) This is analogous to Theorem 7.2.1. We also argue by contradiction. Suppose for some \( A <  + \infty \) and sequences of positive numbers \( {K}_{2}^{\alpha } \rightarrow   + \infty ,{\bar{r}}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) there exists a sequence of times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) such that for any sequences \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } > 0 \) with \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \rightarrow  0 \) for fixed \( \alpha \) , we have sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery and sequences of points \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) , of positive constants \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\sqrt{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }} \) which satisfy the assumptions, but for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) there hold

(7.5.16)

\[
R\left( {{x}^{\alpha \beta },{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\right)  > {K}_{2}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2}\text{ , for some }{x}^{\alpha \beta } \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }, A{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) .
\]

We may assume that \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) , where \( {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) is chosen so that the statements (i) and (ii) hold on \( {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta },{4A}{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) \) . Let \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions of \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) around the origins \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with factor \( {\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \) and shift the times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) to zero. Then by applying the statement (ii), we know that the regions, where the scalar curvature of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) is at least \( {K}_{1}\left( { = {K}_{1}\left( {4A}\right) }\right) \) , are canonical neighborhood regions. Note that canonical \( \varepsilon \) -neck neighborhoods are strong. Also note that the pinching assumption and the assertion

\[
{t}_{0}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \geq  {\left( {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty ,\text{ as }\alpha  \rightarrow   + \infty ,
\]

imply that any subsequent limit of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) must have nonnegative sectional curvature. Thus by the above argument in the proof of the statement (ii) (or the argument in Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1), we conclude that there exist subsequences \( \alpha  = {\alpha }_{m},\beta  = {\beta }_{m} \) such that the curvatures of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) stay uniformly bounded at distances from the origins \( {x}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) not exceeding \( {2A} \) . This contradicts (7.5.16) for \( m \) sufficiently large. This proves the statements (iii).

Clearly for fixed \( A \) , after defining the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) for each \( {t}_{0} \) , one can adjust the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) so that it is nonincreasing in \( {t}_{0} \) .

Therefore we have completed the proof of the theorem.

From now on we redefine the function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) so that it is also less than \( {\bar{\delta }}_{2\left( {t + 1}\right) }\left( {2t}\right) \) and then the above theorem always holds for \( A \in  \left\lbrack  {1,2\left( {{t}_{0} + 1}\right) }\right\rbrack \) . Particularly, we still

have

\[
\widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  \leq  \bar{\delta }\left( t\right)  = \min \left\{  {\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}\log \left( {1 + t}\right) },{\delta }_{0}}\right\}  ,
\]

which tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) . We may also require that \( \widetilde{r}\left( t\right) \) tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
By supposition, for each \( b \) there is a point \( x \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) at which the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption fails for the parameter \( {r}_{a} \) . We call points at which this condition fails counterexample points. Of course, since \( {r}_{a} \leq  {r}_{i} \) and since the restriction of \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{g}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) to \( {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{i}}\right) \right) \) satisfies the hypothesis of the proposition, we see that any counterexample point \( x \) has \( \mathbf{t}\left( x\right)  \geq  {T}_{i} \) . Take a sequence \( {x}_{n} = {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) of counterexample points with \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n + 1}\right)  \leq  \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) for all \( n \) that minimizes \( \mathbf{t} \) among all counterexample points in the sense that for any \( \xi  > 0 \) and for any counterexample point \( x \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) eventually \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right)  < \mathbf{t}\left( x\right)  + \xi \) . Let \( {t}^{\prime } = {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) . Clearly, \( {t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{T}_{i},{T}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) , and by construction the restriction of \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) to \( {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \right) \) satisfies the \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {r}_{a} \) . Since the surgery times are discrete, there is \( {t}^{\prime \prime } = {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime \prime } \) with \( {t}^{\prime } < {t}^{\prime \prime } \leq  {T}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) and a diffeomorphism \( \psi  = {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) } : {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \right) \) compatible with time and the vector field. We view \( {\psi }^{ * }{G}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) as a one-parameter family of metrics \( g\left( t\right)  = {g}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( t\right) \) on \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \) . By passing to a subsequence we can arrange that \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right)  \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \) for all \( n \) . Thus, for each \( n \) there are \( {y}_{n} = {y}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \in  {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) and \( {t}_{n} \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \) with \( \psi \left( {{y}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right)  = {x}_{n} \) . Since \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is a compact 3-manifold, by passing to a further subsequence we can assume that \( {y}_{n} \rightarrow  {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . Of course, \( {t}_{n} \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}{x}_{n} = {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b,\right) } \) .

We claim that, for all \( b \) sufficiently large, the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {r}_{a} \) fails at \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Notice that since \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is the limit of a sequence where the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -neighborhood assumption fails, the points in the sequence converging to \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) have scalar curvature at least \( {r}_{a}^{-2} \) . It follows that \( R\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right)  \geq  {r}_{a}^{-2} \) . Suppose that \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) satisfies the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {r}_{a} \) . This means that there is a neighborhood \( U = {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) of \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) which is a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood of \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . According to Definition 9.78 there are four possibilities. The first two we consider are that \( \left( {U, g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \) is an \( \epsilon \) -round component or a \( C \) -component. In either of these cases, since the defining inequalities given in Definition 9.76 and 9.75 are strong inequalities, all metrics on \( U \) sufficiently close to \( g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) - topology satisfy these same inequalities. But as \( n \) tends to \( \infty \) , the metrics \( {\left. g\left( {t}_{n}\right) \right| }_{U} \) converge in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to \( {\left. g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \right| }_{U} \) . Thus, in these two cases, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the metrics \( g\left( {t}_{n}\right) \) on \( U \) are \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood metrics of the same type as \( {\left. g\left( {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }\right) \right| }_{U} \) . Hence, in either of these cases, for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood of the same type as \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , contrary to our assumption about the sequence \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) .

Now suppose that there is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . This is to say that \( \left( {U, g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . By Proposition 9.79, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( \left( {U, g\left( {t}_{n}\right) }\right) \) is also a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap with the same core. This core contains \( {y}_{n} \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, showing that \( {x}_{n} \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap for all \( n \) sufficiently large.

Now let us consider the remaining case when \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. In this case we have an embedding

\[
{\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} : {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \left( {{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) ,{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) }

compatible with time and the vector field and a diffeomorphism \( {f}_{\left( a, b\right) } : {S}^{2} \times \; \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \rightarrow  {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) such that

\[
{\left( {f}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \mathrm{{Id}}\right) }^{ * }{\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }}^{ * }\left( {R\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) {G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right)

\[
{h}_{0}\left( t\right)  \times  d{s}^{2}, - 1 < t \leq  0,
\]

where \( {h}_{0}\left( t\right) \) is a round metric of scalar curvature \( 1/\left( {1 - t}\right) \) on \( {S}^{2} \) and \( d{s}^{2} \) is the Euclidean metric on the interval. Here, there are two subcases to consider.

(i) \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) extends backward past \( {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) .

Let us consider the first subcase. The embedding \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) extends forward in time because of the diffeomorphism \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) } : {M}_{{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime },{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) and, by assumption, \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) extends backward in time some amount. Thus, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, we can use these extensions of \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) to define an embedding \( {\psi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } : {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \left( {\mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right)  - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right) ,\mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right) \rbrack  \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right. \) compatible with time and the vector field. Under these identifications the points \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) correspond to points

\[
\left( {{p}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) },{s}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }}\right)  \in  {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)
\]

where \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}{s}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } = 0 \) . The last thing we do is to choose diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } : \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) that are the identity near both ends, such that \( {\varphi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) carries 0 to \( {s}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) and such that the \( {\varphi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) converge to the identity in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology for fixed \( \left( {a, b}\right) \) as \( n \) tends to infinity. \[

is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) . This shows that for any \( b \) for which the first subcase holds, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, there is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) .

Now suppose that the second subcase holds for all \( b \) . Here, unlike all previous cases, we shall have to let \( b \) vary and we shall prove the result only for \( b \) sufficiently large. We shall show that for all \( b \) sufficiently large, \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. This will establish the result by contradiction, for as we showed in the previous case, if \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, then the same is true for the \( {x}_{n} \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, contrary to our assumption.

For the moment fix \( b \) . Set \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}_{{G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}{\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) }^{-1} \) . (See FIG. 1.) We denote by \( {p}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) the tip of \( {\mathcal{C}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , and we denote by \( {\bar{h}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) the scale of the surgery at time \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) .

Since the statement that \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap is a scale invariant statement, we are free to replace \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) with \( \left( {{\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) , which has been rescaled to make \( {\bar{h}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = 1 \) and shifted in time so that \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = 0 \) . We denote the new time function by \( \widetilde{\mathbf{t}} \) . (Notice that this rescaling and time-shifting is different from what we usually do. Normally, when we have a base point like \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) we rescale to make its scalar curvature 1 and we shift time to make it be at time 0 . Here we have rescaled based on the scale of the surgery cap rather than \( R\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) .) We set \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = \; {R}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) and we set \( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } = \widetilde{\mathbf{t}}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) . Since the initial time of the strong \( \epsilon \) -neck is zero, \( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } = {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1} \) . We denote the flow line backward in time from \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) by \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( \widetilde{t}\right) ,0 \leq  \widetilde{t} \leq  {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } \) , so that \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }\right)  = {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Since \( {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck, by our choice of \( \epsilon \) , it follows from Lemma A. 2 and rescaling that \( R\left( {\psi \left( {{y}_{\left( a, b\right) },\widetilde{t}}\right) }\right) \) is within \( \left( {0.01}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) of \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }/\left( {1 + {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - \widetilde{t}}\right) }\right) \) for all \( t \in  \left( {0,{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) . By taking limits as \( t \) approaches 0, we see that \( {R}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) is within \( \left( {0.01}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) of \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }/2 \) . Let \( D \) be the universal constant given in Lemma 12.3, so that the scalar curvature at any point of the standard initial metric is at least \( {D}^{-1} \) and at most \( D \) . It follows from the third item in Theorem 13.2 that, since we have rescaled to make the surgery scale 1, for all \( b \) sufficiently large the scalar curvature on the surgery \( {\mathcal{C}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is at least \( {\left( 2D\right) }^{-1} \) and at most \( {2D} \) . \[
{\left( 2D\right) }^{-1} \leq  {R}_{\widetilde{G}\left( {a, b}\right) }\left( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right)  \leq  {2D}.
\]

Together with the above estimate relating \( {R}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) and \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , this gives

(17.1)

\[
{\left( 5D\right) }^{-1} \leq  {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \leq  {5D}.

Since the flow line from \( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) to \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) lies in the closure of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck of scale \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2} \) , the scalar curvature is less than \( {6D} \) at every point of this flow line. According to Proposition 12.31 there is \( {\theta }_{1} < 1 \) (depending only on \( D \) ) such that \( R\left( {q, t}\right)  \geq  {8D} \) for all \( \left( {q, t}\right) \) in the standard solution with \( t \geq  {\theta }_{1} \) .

\[
< \left( {1.1}\right) \sqrt{5D}{\epsilon }^{-1} + \left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) \text{ . }

\[

\[

\]

Since \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right) \) contains \( B\left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }, A/2}\right) \) , and since \( C > C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) \) , it follows from the definition of \( A \) , the above distance estimate, and the triangle inequality that for all \( b \) sufficiently large \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right)  \times  \left\{  {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }\right\} \) contains \( {Y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) .

Since \( C > C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right)  + 1 \) and since for \( b \) sufficiently large \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }^{ * }{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is arbitrarily close to the restriction of the standard solution metric, it follows from Theorem 12.32 and Proposition 9.79 that for all \( b \) sufficiently large, the image \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {Y}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . As we have already remarked, this contradicts the assumption that no \( {x}_{n} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood.

This completes the proof in the last case and establishes Lemma 17.2.

We argue by contradiction. Suppose that the assertion is false. Then we can find a sequence of Ricci flows with surgery \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) and a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) in space-time with the following properties:

(i) The flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{j}}\right) \) and has surgery parameters \( \varepsilon ,{\widehat{r}}_{j},{h}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) , where \( {\widehat{r}}_{j} \leq  \frac{1}{j} \) and \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \leq  \min \left\{  {\widetilde{\widetilde{\delta }}\left( {\widehat{r}}_{j}\right) ,\frac{1}{j}}\right\} \) . Here, \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( \cdot \right) \) is the function introduced in Proposition 10.9.

(ii) \( {Q}_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2{\widehat{r}}_{j}\right) }^{-2} \) .

(iii) The point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) does not satisfy the conclusion of Theorem 10.10.

Condition (iii) means that at least one of the following statements is true:

- There does not exist a neighborhood \( B \) of \( {x}_{j} \) with the property that \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{\left( 2{C}_{1}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},2{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and \( {\left( 2{C}_{2}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \leq  \operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right)  \leq  2{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) for all \( x \in  B \) , and such that \( B \) is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck (in the sense of [35]) with center at \( {x}_{j} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap.

- \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  > {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

- \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  > {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

We will proceed in several steps:

Step 1: By Definition 10.1, we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq \; {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) for each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  4{Q}_{j} \) . Moreover, by Proposition 10.9, the flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than \( \varepsilon \) for some uniform constant \( \kappa \) that may depend on the initial data, but it is independent of \( j \) .

Step 2: Suppose that \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is a point in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \; + {Q}_{j} \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that scal \( \leq \; 8{r}_{0}^{-2} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{{r}_{0}}{100\eta }, - \frac{{r}_{0}^{2}}{100\eta }}\right) \) . Using Proposition 10.4, we conclude that \( \left| {{D}^{m}R}\right|  \leq  C\left( {n, m,\eta }\right) {r}_{0}^{-m - 2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Moreover, Proposition 10.9 implies \( {\operatorname{vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}_{0}^{n} \) for some uniform constant \( \kappa \) that is independent of \( j \) .

Step 3: We next prove a long-range curvature estimate. Given any \( \rho  > 0 \) , we put

\[
\mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right) .
\]

The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  \leq  {16} \) for \( 0 < \; \rho  < \frac{1}{100\eta }. \)

We claim that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) for all \( \rho  > 0 \) . Suppose this is false. Let

\[
{\rho }^{ * } = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 : \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \}  < \infty .
\]

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , we have an upper bound for the curvature in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Using the results in Step 2, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Moreover, the noncollapsing estimate in Step 2 gives a lower bound for the volume. We rescale around \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) and pass to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) . In the limit, we obtain an incomplete manifold \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) that is weakly PIC2 (cf. [31, Th. 5.6]).

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , there exists a sequence of points \( {y}_{j} \) such that

\[
{\rho }_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {Q}_{j}^{\frac{1}{2}}{d}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{y}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }^{ * }\;\text{ and }\;{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty .
\]

Let \( {\gamma }_{j} : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) be a unit-speed geodesic such that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( 0\right)  = {x}_{j} \) and \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  = {y}_{j} \) , and let \( {\gamma }_{\infty } : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }^{ * }}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) denote the limit of \( {\gamma }_{j} \) . Using the estimate \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) we obtain for \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) ,

\[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( s\right) }\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {s{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2\eta \left( {\rho }^{ * } - s\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  {100}.
\]

Let us consider a real number \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) such that \( {64}{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . We claim that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) lies at the center of a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ). Indeed, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption implies that the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. Furthermore, the Canonical Neighborhood is contained in a geodesic ball around \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) of radius \( 8{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , and the scalar curvature is at most \( 8{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) at each point in the Canonical Neighborhood. Since \( \mathbb{M}\left( \bar{s}\right)  < \infty \) , we obtain \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  = \infty \) ; consequently, \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {16}{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {y}_{j} \) . We next observe that \( {32}{C}_{1}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}{\left( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  {64}{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . This implies \( {16}{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {x}_{j} \) . If the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap, then the geodesic \( {\gamma }_{j} \) must enter and exit this \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap, but this is impossible since \( {\gamma }_{j} \) minimizes length. To summarize, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) . \)

Passing to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) , we conclude that \( \left| {D{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) . Integrating this estimate along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) gives \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) }\right)  \geq \; {\left( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \left( {\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-2} \) . Moreover, since \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies at the center of a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck for \( j \) sufficiently large, the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) must lie on a strong \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) .

As in \( \left\lbrack  {{33},§{12.1}}\right\rbrack \) , there is a sequence of rescalings that converges to a piece of a nonflat metric cone in the limit. Let us fix a point on this metric cone. In view of the preceding discussion, this point must lie on a strong \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck. This gives a locally defined solution to the Ricci flow that is weakly PIC2 and that, at the final time, is a piece of nonflat metric cone. This contradicts Proposition 6.5.

Step 4: We now dilate the manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) around the point \( {x}_{j} \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . By Step 3, we have uniform bounds for the curvature at bounded distance. Using the results in Step 2, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor at bounded distance. Using these estimates together with the noncollapsing estimate in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled manifolds converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete limit manifold \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) . Since \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature, the curvature tensor of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is weakly PIC2 and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC. Using the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption, we conclude that every point in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with scalar curvature greater than 4 has a neighborhood that is either a strong \( {8\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {8\varepsilon } \) -cap.

We claim that \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature. Indeed, if there is a sequence of points in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with curvature going to infinity, then \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) contains a sequence of necks with radii converging to 0 , contradicting Proposition 6.9. This shows that \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature.

Step 5: We now extend the limit \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time. By Step 4, the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is bounded from above by a constant \( \Lambda  > 4 \) . We claim that, given any \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right)
\]

is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large. To prove this, fix \( A > 1 \) and suppose that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery. Let \( {s}_{j} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }}\right\rbrack \) be the largest number such that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. The pointwise curvature derivative estimate gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\left. P\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\right) \right) }\operatorname{scal} \leq  {2\Lambda }{Q}_{j}
\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Since the scalar curvature is greater than \( \frac{1}{2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \) at each point modified by surgery, we deduce that \( \frac{1}{2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \leq  {2\Lambda }{Q}_{j} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. In particular, \( {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1} \leq  \frac{1}{10\eta }{h}_{j}^{2} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Since \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) ,

Proposition 10.5 implies that the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right)
\]

is, after dilating by the factor \( {h}_{j} \) , arbitrarily close to a piece of the standard solution when \( j \) is sufficiently large. Using Corollary 9.3, we conclude that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap when \( j \) is sufficiently large. If \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, then this neck is actually a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, since we are assuming that each \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) -neck on which we perform surgery has a large backward parabolic neighborhood that is free of surgeries (cf. Definition 10.1). Moreover, Corollary 9.3 implies that \( \left| {D\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Therefore, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10, and this contradicts statement (iii). Thus, given any \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large.

Let \( {\tau }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }}  - \frac{1}{200\eta \Lambda } \) . In view of the preceding discussion, we may extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  {2\Lambda } \) .

We now repeat this process. Suppose that we can extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack \) , and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{m} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } < \infty \) . Let \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) . We claim that we can extend the solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) backward to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m} \) .

Indeed, if this is not possible, then there exists a number \( A > 1 \) with the property that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery for \( j \) sufficiently large. Let \( {s}_{j} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right\rbrack \) be the largest number such that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. The pointwise curvature derivative estimate gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\left. P\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}\right) \right) }\operatorname{scal} \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m}{Q}_{j}
\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Let us choose \( {\alpha }_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{n - 1}{2}}\right) \) so that \( \frac{{\alpha }_{m}}{{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) } \geq \; 8{\Lambda }_{m}\left( {\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) \) . If \( \left( {{s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1} \geq  {\alpha }_{m}{h}_{j}^{2} \) for \( j \) sufficiently large, then Proposition 10.5 together with the lower bound for the scalar curvature on the standard solution (cf. \[

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(Prolongation of Ricci flows with cutoff) Take the function \( \Phi \) to be the time-dependent pinching function associated to Definition B. 5 in Appendix B. Suppose that \( r \) and \( \delta \) are nonincreasing positive functions defined on \( \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack \) . Let \( \mathcal{M} \) be a Ricci flow with \( \left( {r,\delta }\right) \) -cutoff defined on an interval \( \left\lbrack  {a, c}\right\rbrack   \subset  \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack \) . Provided \( \sup \delta \) is sufficiently small, either

(1) \( \mathcal{M} \) can be prolonged to a Ricci flow with \( \left( {r,\delta }\right) \) -cutoff defined on \( \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack \) , or

(2) There is an extension of \( \mathcal{M} \) to a Ricci flow with surgery defined on an interval \( \left\lbrack  {a, T}\right\rbrack \) with \( T \in  (c, b\rbrack \) , where

a. The restriction of the flow to any subinterval \( \left\lbrack  {a,{T}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack  ,{T}^{\prime } < T \) , is a Ricci flow with \( \left( {r,\delta }\right) \) -cutoff, but

b. The \( r \) -canonical neighborhood assumption fails at some point \( \left( {x, T}\right)  \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{T}^{ - } \) .

In particular, the only obstacle to prolongation of Ricci flows with \( \left( {r,\delta }\right) \) -cutoff is the potential breakdown of the r-canonical neighborhood assumption.

Consider the time slice of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{c} = {\mathcal{M}}_{c}^{ - } \) at time \( c \) . If it is singular then we perform steps A-E of Definition 73.1 to produce \( {\mathcal{M}}_{c}^{ + } \) ; otherwise we set \( {\mathcal{M}}_{c}^{ + } = {\mathcal{M}}_{c}^{ - } \) . Since the surgery is done using Lemma 72.24, provided \( \delta  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, the forward time slice \( {\mathcal{M}}_{c}^{ + } \) will satisfy the \( \Phi \) -pinching assumption.

We claim that the \( r \) -canonical neighborhood assumption holds in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{c}^{ + } \) . More precisely, if a point \( \left( {x, c}\right)  \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{c}^{ + } \) lies within a distance of \( {10}{\epsilon }^{-1}h \) from the added part \( {\mathcal{M}}_{c}^{ + } - {\mathcal{M}}_{c}^{ - } \) then it lies in an \( \epsilon \) -cap, while if \( \left( {x, c}\right) \) lies at distance greater than \( {10}{\epsilon }^{-1}h \) from \( {\mathcal{M}}_{c}^{ + } - {\mathcal{M}}_{c}^{ - } \) and has scalar curvature greater than \( r{\left( c\right) }^{-2} \) then it lies in a canonical neighborhood that was present in the presurgery manifold \( {\mathcal{M}}_{c}^{ - } \) . (We are assuming that \( \epsilon  < \frac{1}{100} \) .) In view of Lemma 63.1, the only point to observe is that points at distance roughly \( {10}{\epsilon }^{-1}h \) lie in \( \epsilon \) -necks, as they are unaltered by the surgery and they were in \( \delta \) -necks before the surgery. This gives the \( \epsilon \) -neck needed to define an \( \epsilon \) -cap.

We now prolong \( \mathcal{M} \) by Ricci flow with initial condition \( {\mathcal{M}}_{c}^{ + } \) . If the flow extends smoothly up to time \( b \) then we are done because either the canonical neighborhood assumption holds up to time \( b \) yielding (a), or it fails at some time in the interval \( (c, b\rbrack \) , and we have (b). Otherwise, there is some time \( {t}_{\text{ sing }} \leq  b \) at which it goes singular. We add the singular limit \( \Omega \) at time \( {t}_{\text{ sing }} \) to obtain a Ricci flow with surgery defined on \( \left\lbrack  {a,{t}_{\text{ sing }}}\right\rbrack \) . From Lemma 72.24, \( \mathcal{M} \) satisfies the Hamilton-Ivey pinching condition of Definition B. 5 on \( \left\lbrack  {a,{t}_{\text{ sing }}}\right\rbrack \) . As the function \( r \) is nonincreasing in \( t \) , it follows from Definition 69.1 that the set of times \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {c,{t}_{\text{ sing }}}\right\rbrack \) for which the \( r \) -canonical neighborhood assumption holds is relatively open to the right (i.e. if the \( r \) -canonical neighborhood assumption holds at time \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {c,{t}_{\text{ sing }}}\right) \) then it also holds within some interval \( \left\lbrack  {t,{t}^{\prime })}\right\rbrack \) ). Thus the set of times \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {c,{t}_{\text{ sing }}}\right\rbrack \) for which the \( r \) -canonical neighborhood assumption holds is either an interval \( \lbrack c, T) \) , with \( T \leq  {t}_{\text{ sing }} \) , or \( \left\lbrack  {c,{t}_{\text{ sing }}}\right\rbrack \) . If the set of such times \( t \) is \( \left( {c, T}\right) \) for some \( T \leq  {t}_{\text{ sing }} \) then the lemma holds. Otherwise, the \( r \) -canonical neighborhood assumption holds at \( {t}_{\text{ sing }} \) . In this case we repeat the construction with \( c \) replaced by \( {t}_{\text{ sing }} \) , and iterate if necessary. Either we will reach time \( b \) after a finite number of iterations, or we will reach a time \( T \) satisfying (2), or we will hit an infinite number of singular times before time \( b \) . However, the last possibility cannot occur. A singular time corresponds to a component going extinct or to a surgery. The number of components going extinct before time \( b \) can be bounded in terms of the number of surgeries before time \( b \) , so it suffices to show that the latter is finite. Each surgery removes a volume of at least \( {h}^{3} \) , but the lower bound on the scalar curvature during the flow, coming from the maximum principle, gives a finite upper bound on the total volume growth during the complement of the singular times.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Proof. Clearly, for any \( {t}_{0} \) we have \( s\left( t\right)  = s\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) for \( t \geq  {t}_{0} \) sufficiently close to \( {t}_{0} \) . Also, if \( t \) is not a surgery time, then \( s\left( t\right)  = s\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) for all \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) and sufficiently close to \( t \) . According to Proposition 15.3, if \( t \) is a surgery time then for \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) but sufficiently close to it, the manifold \( {M}_{t} \) is obtained from \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) by doing surgery on a finite number of 2-spheres and removing certain components of the result. We divide the operations into three types: (i) surgery along homotopically trivial 2-spheres in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) ,(ii) surgery along homo-topically non-trivial 2-spheres in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) ,(iii) removal of components. Clearly, the first operation does not change the invariant \( s \) since it simply creates a manifold that is the disjoint union of a manifold homotopy equivalent to the original manifold with a collection of homotopy 3-spheres. Removal of components will not increase the invariant. The last operation to consider is surgery along a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere. Let \( {F}_{t} \) be a homotopi-cally essential family of disjointly embedded 2-spheres in \( {M}_{t} \) . This family of 2-spheres in \( {M}_{t} \) can be deformed to miss the 3-disks (the surgery caps) in \( {M}_{t} \) that we sewed in doing the surgery at time \( t \) along a homotopically nontrivial 2-sphere. After deforming the spheres in the family \( {F}_{t} \) away from the surgery caps, they produce a disjoint family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) of 2 -spheres in the manifold \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) , for \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) but \( {t}^{\prime } \) sufficiently close to \( t \) . Each 2-sphere in \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) is disjoint from the homotopically essential 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) along which we do surgery at time \( t \) . Let \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) be the family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \cup  \left\{  {S}_{0}\right\} \) . We claim that \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is a homotopically essential family in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) .

First, suppose that one of the spheres \( \sum \) in \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . Of course, we are in the case when the surgery 2-sphere is homotopically essential, so \( \sum \) is not \( {S}_{0} \) and hence is the image of one of the 2-spheres in \( {F}_{t} \) . Since \( \sum \) is homotopically trivial, it is the boundary of a homotopy 3-ball \( B \) in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . If \( B \) is disjoint from the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) , then it exists in \( {M}_{t} \) and hence \( \sum \) is homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{t} \) , which is not possible from the assumption about the family \( {F}_{t} \) . If \( B \) meets the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) , then since the spheres in the family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) are disjoint, it follows that \( B \) contains the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) . This is not possible since in this case \( {S}_{0} \) would be homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) , contrary to assumption.

We also claim that no distinct members of \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) are homotopic. For suppose that two of the members \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) are homotopic. It cannot be the case that one of \( \sum \) or \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) is the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) since, in that case, the other one would be homotopically trivial after surgery, i.e., in \( {M}_{t} \) . The 2- spheres \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) are the boundary components of a submanifold \( A \) in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) homotopy equivalent to \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) . If \( A \) is disjoint from the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) , then \( A \) exists in \( {M}_{t} \) and \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) are homotopic in \( {M}_{t} \) , contrary to assumption. Otherwise, the surgery sphere \( {S}_{0} \) must be contained in \( A \) . Every 2-sphere in \( A \) is either homotopically trivial in \( A \) or is homotopic in \( A \) to either boundary component. If \( {S}_{0} \) is homotopically trivial in \( A \) , then it would be homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) and this contradicts our assumption. If \( {S}_{0} \) is homotopic in \( A \) to each of \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) , then each of \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) is homo-topically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) , contrary to assumption. This shows that the family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is homotopically essential. It follows immediately that doing surgery on a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere strictly decreases the invariant \( s \) .

(Justification of the canonical neighborhood assumption). Given any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist decreasing sequences \( 0 < {\widetilde{r}}_{j} < \varepsilon ,{\kappa }_{j} > 0 \) , and \( 0 < {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} < {\varepsilon }^{2}, j = 1,2,\cdots \) , with the following property. Define the positive function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) on \( \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) by \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) . Suppose there is a surgically modified solution, defined on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( T <  + \infty \) , to the Ricci flow which satisfies the following:

(1) it starts on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric, and

(2) it has only a finite number of surgeries such that each surgery at a time \( t \in  \left( {0, T}\right) \) is a \( \delta \left( t\right) \) -cutoff surgery with

\[
0 < \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \min \{ \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) ,\bar{\delta }\left( t\right) \} .
\]

Then on each time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack  \bigcap \lbrack 0, T), j = 1,2,\cdots \) , the solution satisfies the \( {\kappa }_{j} \) -noncollapsing condition on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) and the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {\widetilde{r}}_{j} \) .

Here and in the following, we call a (three-dimensional) surgically modified solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t < T,\kappa \) -noncollapsed at \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) on the scales less than \( \rho \) (for some \( \kappa  > 0,\rho  > 0 \) ) if it satisfies the following property: whenever \( r < \rho \) and

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {r}^{-2}
\]

for all those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}, r, - {r}^{2}}\right)  = \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the solution is defined, we have

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}^{3}.
\]

The proof of the proposition is by induction: having constructed our sequences for \( 1 \leq  j \leq  m \) , we make one more step, defining \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) , \( {\kappa }_{m + 1},{\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) , and redefining \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) . In view of the previous lemma, we only need to define \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .

In Theorem 7.1.1 we have obtained the canonical neighborhood structure for smooth solutions. When adapting the arguments in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1 to the present surgical solutions, we will encounter the new difficulty of how to take a limit for the surgically modified solutions. The idea to overcome the difficulty consists of two parts. The first part, due to Perelman [104], is to choose \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) small enough to push the surgical regions to infinity in space. (This is the reason why we need to redefine \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .) The second part is to show that solutions are smooth on some small, but uniform, time intervals (on compact subsets) so that we can apply Hamilton's compactness theorem, since we only have curvature bounds; otherwise Shi's interior derivative estimate may not be applicable. In fact, the second part is more crucial. That is just concerned with the question of whether the surgery times accumulate or not. Our argument will use the canonical neighborhood characterization of the standard solution in Lemma 7.3.5.

We now start to prove the proposition by contradiction. Suppose for sequence of positive numbers \( {r}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) , satisfying \( {r}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) as \( \alpha  \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  \frac{1}{\alpha  \cdot  \beta }\left( { \rightarrow  0}\right) \) , there exist sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery, where each of them has only a finite number of cutoff surgeries and has a compact orientable normalized three-manifold as initial data, so that the following two assertions hold:

(i) each \( \delta \) -cutoff at a time \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) satisfies \( \delta  \leq  {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) ; and

(ii) the solutions satisfy the statement of the proposition on \( \left\lbrack  {0, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) , but violate the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) on \( \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

For each solution \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) , we choose \( \bar{t} \) (depending on \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) ) to be the nearly first time for which the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) is violated. More precisely, we choose \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) so that the canonical neighborhood assumption with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) and with accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon \) is violated at some \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , however the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) holds on \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . After passing to subsequences, we may assume each \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) is less than the \( \widetilde{\delta } \) in Lemma 7.4.2 with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) when \( \alpha \) is fixed. Then by Lemma 7.4.2 we have uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) on \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) with some \( \kappa  > 0 \) independent of \( \alpha ,\beta \) .

Slightly abusing notation, we will often drop the indices \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) .

Let \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions around \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with factors \( R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \left( { \geq  {r}^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty }\right) \) and shift the times \( \bar{t} \) to zero. We hope to take a limit of the rescaled solutions for subsequences of \( \alpha ,\beta  \rightarrow  \infty \) and show the limit is an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which will give the desired contradiction. We divide our arguments into the following six steps.

Step 1. Let \( \left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right) \) be a point on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right)  \leq  A \) (for some \( A \geq  1 \) ) and \( \widehat{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {-\left( {\bar{t} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) . Then we have estimate

(7.4.14)

\[

Then by the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) ,{y}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {y}_{\infty } \) .

Clearly, the limit also has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption. Then by repeating the same argument as in the proof of Assertion 4 (i) in the rest, we derive a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum principle. This proves Assertion 5.

We then apply the second estimate of (7.4.17) and Assertion 5 to conclude that for any large constant \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) , there is a positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) such that for any small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

(7.4.18)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Then by applying Assertion 1 in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on the geodesic balls \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Furthermore, by the gradient estimates as in Step 1, we have

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right)
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) is arbitrarily small and the positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) is independent of \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) , we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfy

(7.4.19)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right) ,
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) .

Now, by taking convergent subsequences from the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) , we see that the limit solution is defined smoothly on a space-time open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times \; ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . By Step 4, we see that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , - {t}_{\max }}\right) \) at time \( - {t}_{\max } \) has bounded curvature. Then by combining with the canonical neighborhood assumption of accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) , we conclude that the curvature of the limit is uniformly bounded on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . So we have excluded the possibility (1).

Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Finally by combining with the canonical neighborhood theorem (Theorem 6.4.6), we see that \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) has a canonical neighborhood with parameter \( \varepsilon \) , which is a contradiction. Therefore we have completed the proof of the proposition. 0
