In particular, the rescaled solution is defined on the whole parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {y,0,\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-1}}\right) \) .

Next, we want to show the curvature of the rescaled solutions at the new times zero (after shifting) stay uniformly bounded at bounded distances from \( \bar{x} \) for some subsequences of \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) . Let \( {\alpha }_{m},{\beta }_{m} \rightarrow   + \infty \) be chosen so that the estimate (7.5.14) holds with \( \widetilde{K} = m \) . For all \( \rho  \geq  0 \) , set

\[
M\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {\widetilde{R}\left( {x,0}\right)  \mid  m \geq  1,{d}_{0}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \rho \text{ in the rescaled solutions }{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}}\right\}
\]

and

\[
{\rho }_{0} = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 \mid  M\left( \rho \right)  <  + \infty \} .
\]

Clearly the estimate (7.5.14) yields \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) . As we consider the unshifted time \( \bar{t} \) , by combining with the assumption that \( {t}_{0} > 2{r}_{0}^{2} \) , we have

(7.5.15)

\[
\bar{t}R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \geq  \frac{{t}_{0}}{2}R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {r}_{0}^{2}\left( {{K}_{1}{r}_{0}^{-2}}\right)
\]

\[
= {K}_{1} \rightarrow   + \infty \text{ . }
\]

It then follows from the pinching assumption that we only need to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) . As before, we argue by contradiction. Suppose we have a sequence of points \( {y}_{m} \) in the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) with \( {\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{y}_{m}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) and \( \widetilde{R}\left( {{y}_{m},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Denote by \( {\gamma }_{m} \) a minimizing geodesic segment from \( \bar{x} \) to \( {y}_{m} \) and denote by \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) the open geodesic balls centered at \( \bar{x} \) of radius \( {\rho }_{0} \) of the rescaled solutions. By applying the assertion in statement (i), we have uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing at the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) . By combining with the local curvature estimate (7.5.14) and Hamilton's compactness theorem, we can assume that, after passing to a subsequence, the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}},\bar{x}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( {\gamma }_{m} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {x}_{\infty } \) . Moreover, by the pinching assumption and the estimate (7.5.15), the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature.

Then exactly as before, we consider the tubular neighborhood along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \)

\[
V = \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{{q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty }}}{B}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)
\]

and the completion \( {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) of \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) \) with \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) the limit point of \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . As before, by the choice of the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , we know that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty } \) is cylindrical at any point \( {q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) which is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) . Then by the same reason as before the metric space \( \bar{V} = V \cup  \left\{  {y}_{\infty }\right\} \) has nonnegative curvature in Alexandrov sense, and we have a three-dimensional nonflat tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) at \( {y}_{\infty } \) . Pick \( z \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) with distance one from the vertex and it is nonflat around \( z \) . By definition \( B\left( {z,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \left( { \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V}}\right) \) is the Gromov-Hausdoff convergent limit of the scalings of a sequence of balls \( {B}_{\infty }\left( {{z}_{k},{\sigma }_{k}}\right) \left( { \subset  \left( {V,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) }\right) \) with \( {\sigma }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) . Since the estimate (7.5.14) survives on \( \left( {V,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) \) for all \( \widetilde{K} <  + \infty \) , we know that this convergence is actually in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology and over some time interval. Since the limit \( B\left( {z,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \left( { \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V}}\right) \) is a piece of a nonnegatively curved nonflat metric cone, we get a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum Principle (Theorem 2.2.1) as before. Hence we have proved that a subsequence of the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) has uniformly bounded curvatures at bounded distance from \( \bar{x} \) at the new times zero.

Further, by the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing at the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) and the estimate (7.5.14) again, we can take a \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , defined on a space-time subset which contains the time slice \( \{ t = 0\} \) and is relatively open in \( {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , for the subsequence of the rescaled solutions. The limit is a smooth solution to the Ricci flow, and is complete at \( t = 0 \) , as well as has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption and the estimate (7.5.15). Thus by repeating the same argument as in the Step 4 of the proof Proposition 7.4.1, we conclude that the curvature of the limit at \( t = 0 \) is bounded.

Finally we try to extend the limit backwards in time to get an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Since the curvature of the limit is bounded at \( t = 0 \) , it follows from the estimate (7.5.14) that the limit is a smooth solution to the Ricci flow defined at least on a backward time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some positive constant \( a \) . Let \( \left( {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal time interval over which we can extract a smooth limiting solution. It suffices to show \( {t}_{\infty } =  - \infty \) . If \( {t}_{\infty } >  - \infty \) , there are only two possibilities: either there exist surgeries in finite distance around the time \( {t}_{\infty } \) or the curvature of the limiting solution becomes unbounded as \( t \searrow  {t}_{\infty } \) .

Let \( c > 0 \) be a positive constant much smaller than \( \frac{1}{100}{\eta }^{-1} \) . Note again that the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time. Then we can find some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and some time \( t = {t}_{\infty } + \theta \) with \( 0 < \theta  < \frac{c}{3} \) such that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right)  \leq  2 \) .

Consider the (unrescaled) scalar curvature \( R \) of \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at the point \( \bar{x} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the scalar curvature \( {R}_{\infty } \) of the limit on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{3},0}\right\rbrack \) is uniformly bounded by some positive constant \( C \) , we have the curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {\bar{x}, t}\right)  \leq  {2C}\bar{Q}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) and all sufficiently large \( m \) . For each fixed \( m \) and \( {\alpha }_{m} \) , we may require the chosen \( {\beta }_{m} \) to satisfy

\[
{\left( {\bar{\delta }}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\right) }^{-2}{\left( \widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}}}{2}\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  m\widetilde{r}{\left( {t}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}}\right) }^{-2} \geq  m\bar{Q}.
\]

When \( m \) is large enough, we observe again that Lemma 3.4.1 (ii) is applicable for \( {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},\bar{x}}\right) \) with \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . Then by repeating the argument as in the derivation of (7.2.1),(7.2.2) and (7.2.3), we deduce that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) . \)

Let \( \left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) be a sequence of associated points and times in the (unrescaled) solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) so that after rescaling, the sequence converges to \( \left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right) \) in the limit. Clearly \( \frac{\theta }{2} \leq  {\theta }_{m} \leq  {2\theta } \) for all sufficiently large \( m \) . Then by the argument as in the derivation of (7.5.13), we know that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the solution \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at \( {y}_{m} \) is defined on the whole time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m} - }\right. }\right. \; \left. {\left. {\frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies the curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {{y}_{m}, t}\right)  \leq  8\bar{Q}
\]

there; moreover the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) with \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  4\bar{Q} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) .

We now consider the rescaled sequence \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) with the marked points replaced by \( {y}_{m} \) and the times replaced by \( {s}_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) . As before the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality implies the rescaling limit around \( \left( {{y}_{m},{s}_{m}}\right) \) agrees with the original one. Then the arguments in previous paragraphs imply the limit is well-defined and smooth on a space-time open neighborhood of the maximal time slice \( \left\{  {t = {t}_{\infty }}\right\} \) . Particularly this excludes the possibility of existing surgeries in finite distance around the time \( {t}_{\infty } \) . Moreover, the limit at \( t = {t}_{\infty } \) also has bounded curvature. By using the gradient estimates in the canonical neighborhood assumption on the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) , we see that the second possibility is also impossible. Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Therefore we have proved the canonical neighborhood statement (ii).

(iii) This is analogous to Theorem 7.2.1. We also argue by contradiction. Suppose for some \( A <  + \infty \) and sequences of positive numbers \( {K}_{2}^{\alpha } \rightarrow   + \infty ,{\bar{r}}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) there exists a sequence of times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) such that for any sequences \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } > 0 \) with \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \rightarrow  0 \) for fixed \( \alpha \) , we have sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery and sequences of points \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) , of positive constants \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\sqrt{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }} \) which satisfy the assumptions, but for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) there hold

(7.5.16)

\[
R\left( {{x}^{\alpha \beta },{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\right)  > {K}_{2}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2}\text{ , for some }{x}^{\alpha \beta } \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }, A{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) .
\]

We may assume that \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) , where \( {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) is chosen so that the statements (i) and (ii) hold on \( {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta },{4A}{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) \) . Let \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions of \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) around the origins \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with factor \( {\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \) and shift the times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) to zero. Then by applying the statement (ii), we know that the regions, where the scalar curvature of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) is at least \( {K}_{1}\left( { = {K}_{1}\left( {4A}\right) }\right) \) , are canonical neighborhood regions. Note that canonical \( \varepsilon \) -neck neighborhoods are strong. Also note that the pinching assumption and the assertion

\[
{t}_{0}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \geq  {\left( {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty ,\text{ as }\alpha  \rightarrow   + \infty ,
\]

imply that any subsequent limit of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) must have nonnegative sectional curvature. Thus by the above argument in the proof of the statement (ii) (or the argument in Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1), we conclude that there exist subsequences \( \alpha  = {\alpha }_{m},\beta  = {\beta }_{m} \) such that the curvatures of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) stay uniformly bounded at distances from the origins \( {x}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) not exceeding \( {2A} \) . This contradicts (7.5.16) for \( m \) sufficiently large. This proves the statements (iii).

Clearly for fixed \( A \) , after defining the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) for each \( {t}_{0} \) , one can adjust the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) so that it is nonincreasing in \( {t}_{0} \) .

Therefore we have completed the proof of the theorem.

From now on we redefine the function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) so that it is also less than \( {\bar{\delta }}_{2\left( {t + 1}\right) }\left( {2t}\right) \) and then the above theorem always holds for \( A \in  \left\lbrack  {1,2\left( {{t}_{0} + 1}\right) }\right\rbrack \) . Particularly, we still

have

\[
\widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  \leq  \bar{\delta }\left( t\right)  = \min \left\{  {\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}\log \left( {1 + t}\right) },{\delta }_{0}}\right\}  ,
\]

which tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) . We may also require that \( \widetilde{r}\left( t\right) \) tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
In view of condition (iii), \( \widehat{R} \) lies in the interior of the PIC cone. Therefore, the assertion is true for \( \widehat{b} = 0 \) . Hence, it suffices to consider the case \( 0 < \widehat{b} \leq  \delta {e}^{-8\widehat{t}} \) . Let us define functions \( a\left( t\right) , b\left( t\right) \) by \( b\left( t\right)  = {e}^{8\left( {\widehat{t} - t}\right) }\widehat{b} \) and \( a\left( t\right)  = {2b}\left( t\right)  + \left( {n - 2}\right) b{\left( t\right) }^{2} \) . Moreover, let \( S\left( t\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\ell }_{a\left( t\right) , b\left( t\right) }^{-1}\left( {R\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Since condition (i) holds up to time \( \widehat{t} \) , we know that \( S\left( t\right)  \in \) PIC for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\widehat{t}}\right\rbrack \) . The evolution of \( S\left( t\right) \) is given by

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{dt}S\left( t\right) \right| }_{t = \widehat{t}} = Q\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + {D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  - {b}^{\prime }\left( \widehat{t}\right) U = Q\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + {D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + 8\widehat{b}U,
\]

where

\[
U = \frac{1}{1 + \left( {n - 2}\right) \widehat{b}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \oslash  \mathrm{{id}}
\]

\[
- \frac{1}{n}\left( {\frac{1}{1 + \left( {n - 2}\right) \widehat{b}} - \frac{1 + \left( {n - 2}\right) \widehat{b}}{1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) \widehat{a}}}\right) \operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \text{ id } \oslash  \text{ id. }
\]

We claim that \( {D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + 8\widehat{b}U \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone \( {T}_{\widehat{S}} \) PIC. To verify this, we distinguish two cases:

Case 1: Suppose first that \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \) is strictly two-positive. By Lemma A.2, \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \oslash  \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \) lies in the interior of the PIC cone. Since \( 2\widehat{a} = 2\widehat{b} + \left( {n - 2}\right) {\widehat{b}}^{2} \) , this implies that \( {D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \) lies in the interior of the PIC cone. Since \( U \in  {T}_{\widehat{S}} \) PIC by Lemma 2.5, it follows that \( {D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + 8\widehat{b}U \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone \( {T}_{\widehat{S}} \) PIC, as claimed.

Case 2: Suppose next that \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \) is not strictly two-positive. In this case, \( \operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \leq  C\left( n\right) \left| {\mathop{\operatorname{Ric}}\limits^{ \circ  }\left( \widehat{S}\right) }\right| \) . Since \( 2\widehat{a} = 2\widehat{b} + \left( {n - 2}\right) {\widehat{b}}^{2} \) , it follows that

\[
{D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  - 2\widehat{a}\operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \oslash  \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  - 2{\widehat{b}}^{\frac{17}{8}}\operatorname{scal}{\left( \widehat{S}\right) }^{2}\mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} \in  \mathrm{{PIC}}
\]

if \( \widehat{b} > 0 \) is sufficiently small. Condition (ii) implies \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + \left( {1 + {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{4}}\operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) }\right) \) id is weakly two-positive. Using Lemma A.2, we obtain

\[
2\widehat{a}\operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \oslash  \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)
\]

\[
+ 4\widehat{a}\left( {1 + {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{4}}\operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) }\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} + 4\widehat{a}\left( {1 + {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{2}}\operatorname{scal}{\left( \widehat{S}\right) }^{2}}\right) \mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}}
\]

\[
= 2\widehat{a}\left\lbrack  {\operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + \left( {1 + {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{4}}\operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) }\right) \mathrm{{id}}}\right\rbrack   \oslash  \left\lbrack  {\operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + \left( {1 + {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{4}}\operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) }\right) \mathrm{{id}}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
+ 2\widehat{a}{\left( 1 - {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{4}}\operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \right) }^{2}\mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} \in  \text{ PIC. }
\]

On the other hand, Lemma 2.6 gives

\[
8\widehat{b}U - 4\widehat{a}\operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} - 4\widehat{a}\mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} + {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{17}{8}}\operatorname{scal}{\left( \widehat{S}\right) }^{2}\mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} \in  {T}_{\widehat{S}}\mathrm{{PIC}}\text{ . }
\]

Moreover, if \( \widehat{b} > 0 \) is sufficiently small, then \( \widehat{a}{\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{4}} \) is much smaller than \( {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{17}{8}} \) . Since \( \left| {\operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right) }\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \) , it follows that

\[
{\widehat{b}}^{\frac{17}{8}}\operatorname{scal}{\left( S\right) }^{2}\mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} - 4\widehat{a}{\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{4}}\operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} - 4\widehat{a}{\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{2}}\operatorname{scal}{\left( \widehat{S}\right) }^{2}\mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}}
\]

lies in the interior of the PIC cone. Adding all four formulae, we conclude that \( {D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + 8\widehat{b}U \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone \( {T}_{\widehat{S}} \) PIC.

To summarize, we have shown that \( {D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + 8\widehat{b}U \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone \( {T}_{\widehat{S}} \) PIC. Since \( Q\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \in  {T}_{\widehat{S}} \) PIC by Proposition 7.5 in [5], we conclude that \( {\left. \frac{d}{dt}S\left( t\right) \right| }_{t = \widehat{t}} \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone \( {T}_{\widehat{S}} \) PIC. Hence, if \( \widehat{S} \) lies on the boundary of the PIC cone, then \( S\left( t\right) \) lies outside the PIC cone if \( t \in  \lbrack 0,\widehat{t}) \) is sufficiently close to \( \widehat{t} \) . This is a contradiction. This completes the proof of Lemma 2.7.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that there are \( {A}^{\prime },{D}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } < \infty \) such that the following holds for all a sufficiently large. There is a point \( {y}_{a} \in  {B}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{a}}\left( {{\widetilde{x}}_{a},0,{A}^{\prime }}\right) \) and a flow line of \( \chi \) beginning at \( {y}_{a} \) , defined for backward time and ending at a point \( {z}_{a} \) in a surgery cap \( {\mathcal{C}}_{a} \) at time \( - {t}_{a} \) for some \( {t}_{a} \leq  {t}^{\prime } \) . Suppose the result does not hold. Then there are \( {A}^{\prime },{D}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } < \infty \) and we can pass to a subsequence (in \( a \) ) such that the hypotheses of the lemma hold for every \( a \) but no \( {x}_{a} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. The essential point of the argument is to show that in the units of the surgery scale the elapsed time between the surgery time and 0 is less than 1 and the distance from the point \( {z}_{a} \) to the tip of the surgery cap is bounded independent of \( a \) .

By Lemma 12.3, the fact that the scalar curvature at \( {z}_{a} \) is bounded by \( {D}^{\prime } \) implies that for all \( a \) sufficiently large the scale \( {\bar{h}}_{a} \) of the surgery at time \( - {t}_{a} \) satisfies

(17.2)

\[
{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \geq  {\left( 2{D}^{\prime }D\right) }^{-1}.
\]

(Recall that we are working in the rescaled flow \( \left( {{\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a},{\widetilde{G}}_{a}}\right) \) .)

Now we are ready to show that the elapsed time is bounded less than 1 in the surgery scale.

CLAIM 17.8. There is \( {\theta }_{1} < 1 \) , depending on \( {D}^{\prime } \) and \( {t}^{\prime } \) , such that for all a sufficiently large we have \( {t}_{a} < {\theta }_{1}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \) .

Proof. We consider two cases: either \( {t}_{a} \leq  {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2}/2 \) or \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2}/2 < {t}_{a} \) . In the first case, the claim is obviously true with \( {\theta }_{1} \) anything greater than \( 1/2 \) and less than 1. In the second case, the curvature everywhere along the flow line is at most \( {D}^{\prime } < \left( {2{t}_{a}{D}^{\prime }}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \leq  \left( {2{t}^{\prime }{D}^{\prime }}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) . Using Proposition 12.31 fix \( 1/2 < {\theta }_{1} < 1 \) so that every point of the standard solution \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( t \geq  \left( {2{\theta }_{1} - 1}\right) \) satisfies \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  6{t}^{\prime }{D}^{\prime } \) . Notice that \( {\theta }_{1} \) depends only on \( {D}^{\prime } \) and \( {t}^{\prime } \) . If \( {t}_{a} < {\theta }_{1}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \) , then the claim holds for this value of \( {\theta }_{1} < 1 \) . Suppose \( {t}_{a} \geq  {\theta }_{1}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \) , so that \( - {t}_{a} + \left( {2{\theta }_{1} - 1}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} < 0 \) . For all \( a \) sufficiently large we have \( {\delta }_{a} \leq  {\delta }_{0}^{\prime \prime }\left( {{A}_{0} + 5,{\theta }_{1},{\bar{\delta }}_{0}}\right) \) where \( {\bar{\delta }}_{0} \) is the constant from Definition 16.12 and \( {\delta }_{0}^{\prime \prime } \) is the constant from Proposition 16.5. This means that the scalar curvatures at corresponding points of the rescaled standard solution and the evolution of the surgery cap (up to time 0) in \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a} \) differ by at most a factor of two. Thus, for these \( a \) , we have \( R\left( {{y}_{a},\left( {-{t}_{a} + \left( {2{\theta }_{1} - 1}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2}}\right) }\right)  \geq  3\left( {{t}^{\prime }{D}^{\prime }}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) from the definition of \( {\bar{\delta }}_{0} \) and Proposition 16.5. But this is impossible since \( - {t}_{a}\left( {2{\theta }_{1} - 1}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} < 0 \) and \( 3{t}^{\prime }{D}^{\prime }/{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \geq  3{t}_{a}{D}^{\prime }/{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} > {D}^{\prime } \) as \( {t}_{a} > {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2}/2 \) . Hence, \( R\left( {{y}_{a},\left( {-{t}_{a} + \left( {2{\theta }_{1} - 1}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2}}\right) }\right)  \leq  2{t}_{a}{D}^{\prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \leq  2{t}^{\prime }{D}^{\prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) . This contradiction shows that if \( a \) is sufficiently large then \( {t}_{a} < {\theta }_{1}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \) .

We pass to a subsequence so that \( {t}_{a}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) converges to some \( \theta  \leq  {\theta }_{1} \) . We define \( \widetilde{C} \) to be the maximum of \( C \) and \( 3{\epsilon }^{-1}{\beta }^{-1} \) . Now, using part 5 of Theorem 12.5 we set \( {A}^{\prime \prime } \geq  \left( {9\widetilde{C} + 3{A}^{\prime }}\right) \sqrt{{2D}{D}^{\prime }} + 6\left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) \) sufficiently large so that in the standard flow \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0,{A}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \) contains \( B\left( {{p}_{0}, t,{A}^{\prime \prime }/2}\right) \) for any \( t \leq  \left( {{\theta }_{1} + 1}\right) /2 \) . This constant is chosen only to depend on \( {\theta }_{1},{A}^{\prime } \) , and \( C \) . As \( a \) tends to infinity, \( {\delta }_{a} \) tends to zero which means, by Proposition 16.5, that for all \( a \) sufficiently large there is an embedding

\[
{\rho }_{a} : B\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a},{A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{a},0}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a}
\]

compatible with time and the vector field such that (after translating by \( {t}_{a} \) to make the flow start at time 0 and scaling by \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) ) the restriction of \( {\widetilde{G}}_{a} \) to this image is close in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to the restriction of the standard flow to \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0,{A}^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right\rbrack \) . The image \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a}}\right) \) is the tip \( {p}_{a} \) of the surgery cap \( {\mathcal{C}}_{a} \) in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{a} \) . Thus, for all \( a \) sufficiently large the image \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a},{A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}}\right) \times \{ 0\} }\right) \) contains the \( {A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}/3 \) -neighborhood of the image \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {{p}_{0},0}\right) \) of the tip of the surgery cap under the flow forward to time 0. By our choice of \( {A}^{\prime \prime } \) , and Equation (17.2), this means that for all \( a \) sufficiently large \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a},{A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}}\right)  \times  \left\{  {-{t}_{a}}\right\}  }\right) \) contains the \( \left( {3\widetilde{C} + {A}^{\prime }}\right)  + 2\left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a} \) - neighborhood of \( {p}_{a} = {\rho }_{a}\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a}}\right) \) . Notice also that, since the standard solution has positive curvature and hence the distance between points is nonincreasing in time by Lemma 3.14, the distance at time 0 between \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {{p}_{0},0}\right) \) and \( {y}_{a} \) is less than \( 2\left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a} \) . By the triangle inequality, we conclude that for all \( a \) sufficiently large, \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a},{A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}}\right) \times \{ 0\} }\right) \) contains the \( 3\widetilde{C} \) - neighborhood of \( {x}_{a} \) . Since the family of metrics on

\[
{\rho }_{a}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a},{A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{a},0}\right\rbrack  }\right) \}
\]

(after time-shifting by \( {t}_{a} \) and rescaling by \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) ) are converging smoothly to the ball \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0,{A}^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,\theta }\right\rbrack \) in the standard flow, for all \( a \) sufficiently large, the flow from time \( - {t}_{a} \) to 0 on the \( 3\widetilde{C} \) -neighborhood of \( {x}_{a} \) is, after rescaling by \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) , very nearly isometric to the restriction of the standard flow from time 0 to \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a} \) on the \( 3\widetilde{C}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-1} \) -neighborhood of some point \( {q}_{a} \) in the standard flow. Of course, since the scalar curvature of \( {x}_{a} \) is \( 1, R\left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) in the standard flow is close to \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) . Hence, by Theorem 12.32 there is a neighborhood \( X \) of \( \left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) in the standard solution that either is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, or is an evolving \( {\beta \epsilon }/3 \) -neck centered at \( \left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) . In the latter case either the evolving neck is defined for backward time \( \left( {1 + {\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) \) or its initial time-slice is the zero time-slice and this initial time-slice lies at distance at least 1 from the surgery cap. Of course, \( X \) is contained in the \( {CR}{\left( {q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}\right) }^{-1/2} \) -neighborhood of \( \left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) in the standard solution. Since \( \widetilde{C} \geq  C \) and \( R\left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) is close to \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) , the neighborhood \( X \) is contained in the \( 2\widetilde{C}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-1} \) -neighborhood of \( \left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) in the standard solution. Hence, after rescaling, the corresponding neighborhood of \( {x}_{a} \) is contained in the \( 3\widetilde{C} \) -neighborhood of \( {x}_{a} \) . If either of the first two cases in Theorem 12.32 occurs for a subsequence of \( a \) tending to infinity, then by Lemma 9.79 and the fact that \( \widetilde{C} > \max \left( {C,{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) , we see that there is a subsequence of \( a \) for which \( {x}_{a} \) either is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap or is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck.

We must examine further the last case. We suppose that for every \( a \) this last case holds. Then for all \( a \) sufficiently large we have an \( {\beta \epsilon }/3 \) -neck \( {N}_{a} \) in the zero time-slice of \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a} \) centered at \( {x}_{a} \) . It is an evolving neck and there is an embedding \( \psi  : {N}_{a} \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{a},0}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a} \) compatible with time and the vector field so that the initial time-slice \( \psi \left( {{N}_{a} \times  \left\{  {-{t}_{a}}\right\}  }\right) \) is in the surgery time-slice \( {M}_{-{t}_{a}} \) and is disjoint from the surgery cap, so in fact it is contained in the continuing region at time \( - {t}_{a} \) . As we saw above, the image of the central 2-sphere \( \psi \left( {{S}_{a}^{2} \times  \left\{  {-{t}_{a}}\right\}  }\right) \) lies at distance at most \( {A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a} \) from the tip of the surgery cap \( {p}_{a} \) (where, recall, \( {A}^{\prime \prime } \) is a constant independent of \( a \) ). The 2-sphere, \( {\sum }_{a} \) , along which we do surgery, creating the surgery cap with \( {p}_{a} \) as its tip, is the central 2-sphere of a strong \( {\delta }_{b\left( a\right) } \) -neck. As \( a \) tends to infinity the surgery control parameter \( {\delta }_{b\left( a\right) } \) tends to zero. Thus, for \( a \) sufficiently large this strong \( {\delta }_{b\left( a\right) } \) -neck will contain a strong \( {\beta \epsilon }/2 \) - neck \( {N}^{\prime } \) centered at \( \psi \left( {{x}_{a}, - {t}_{a}}\right) \) . Since we know that the continuing region at time \( - {t}_{a} \) contains a \( {\beta \epsilon }/3 \) -neck centered at \( \left( {{x}_{a}, - {t}_{a}}\right) \) , it follows that \( {N}^{\prime } \) is also contained in \( {C}_{-{t}_{a}} \) . That is to say, \( {N}^{\prime } \) is contained in the negative half of the \( {\delta }_{b\left( a\right) } \) -neck centered at \( {\sum }_{a} \) . Now we are in the situation of Proposition 15.2. Applying this result tells us that \( {x}_{a} \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck.

This completes the proof that for all \( a \) sufficiently large, \( {x}_{a} \) has a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood in contradiction to our assumption. This contradiction completes the proof of Lemma 17.7.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
The proof of the first statement is by contradiction. Fix \( \rho  > 0 \) and \( \delta  > 0 \) and suppose that there is no \( 0 < h \leq  \min \left( {\rho  \cdot  \delta ,\rho /{2C}}\right) \) as required. Then there is a sequence of generalized Ricci flows \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) defined for \( 0 \leq  t < {T}_{n} < \infty \) satisfying Assumptions 11.18 and points \( {x}_{n} \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) with \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right)  = {T}_{n} \) contained in \( {2\epsilon } \) -horns \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) in \( {\Omega }_{n} \) with boundary contained in \( {\left( {\Omega }_{n}\right) }_{\rho /{2C}} \) with \( {Q}_{n} = R\left( {x}_{n}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) but such that no \( {x}_{n} \) is the center of a strong \( \delta \) -neck in \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) . Form the maximal extensions, \( \left( {{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n},{\widehat{G}}_{n}}\right) \) , to time \( T \) of the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) .

CLAIM 11.32. The sequence \( \left( {{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n},{\widehat{G}}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) satisfies the five hypotheses of Theorem 11.1.

Proof. By our assumptions, hypotheses (1) and (3) of Theorem 11.1 hold for this sequence. Also, we are assuming that any point \( y \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Since \( R\left( {x}_{n}\right)  = \; {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) this means that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, any point \( y \in  {\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  \geq  R\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. This establishes hypothesis (2) in the statement of Theorem 11.1.

Next, we have:

CLAIM 11.33. For any \( A < \infty \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the ball \( B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) is contained in the \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) and has compact closure in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) .

Proof. Any point \( z \in  \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) has scalar curvature at most \( {16}{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) and there is a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( z \) . This means that for all \( y \) with \( {d}_{{G}_{n}}\left( {z, y}\right)  < {\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) we have \( R\left( y\right)  \leq  {32}{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) . Hence, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {d}_{{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, z}\right)  > {\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) , and thus \( {d}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, z}\right)  > {Q}_{n}^{1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) . This implies that, given \( A < \infty \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( z \notin  {B}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right) \) . Since this is true for all \( z \in  \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) , it follows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {B}_{{Q}_{n},{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right)  \subset  {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) . Next, we must show that, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, this ball has compact closure. That is to say, we must show that for every \( A \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large the distance from \( {x}_{n} \) to the end of the horn \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) is greater than \( A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2} \) . If not, then since the curvature at the end of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) goes to infinity for each \( n \) , this sequence would violate Theorem 10.2.

Because \( B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) is contained in a \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn, it is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on scales \( \leq  r \) for a universal \( \kappa  > 0 \) and \( r > 0 \) . Also, because every point in the horn is the center of a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck, for every \( n \) sufficiently large and every \( y \in  B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) the flow is defined on an interval through \( y \) defined for backward time \( R{\left( y\right) }^{-1} \) .

This completes the proof that all the hypotheses of Theorem 11.1 hold and establishes Claim 11.32.

We form a new sequence of generalized Ricci flows from the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) by translating by \( - {T}_{n} \) , so that the final time-slice is at \( {\mathbf{t}}_{n} = 0 \) , where \( {\mathbf{t}}_{n} \) is the time function for \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) .

Theorem 11.1 implies that, after passing to a subsequence, there is a limit flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) }\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack  ) \) defined for some \( {t}_{0} > 0 \) for the sequence \( \left( {{Q}_{n}{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n},{Q}_{n}{\widehat{G}}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) . Because of the curvature pinching toward positive assumption, by Theorem 5.33, the limit Ricci flow has non-negative sectional curvature. Of course, \( R\left( {x}_{\infty }\right)  = 1 \) so that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is non-flat.

CLAIM 11.34. \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is isometric to the product \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h}\right)  \times  \left( {\mathbb{R}, d{s}^{2}}\right) \) , where \( h \) is a metric of non-negative curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) and \( d{s}^{2} \) is the usual Euclidean metric on the real line.

Proof. Because of the fact that the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) have curvature pinched toward positive, and since \( {Q}_{n} \) tend to \( \infty \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, it follows that the geometric limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has non-negative curvature. In \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) take a minimizing geodesic ray \( {\alpha }_{n} \) from \( {x}_{n} \) to the end of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) and a minimizing geodesic \( {\beta }_{n} \) from \( {x}_{n} \) to \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) . As we have seen, the lengths of both \( {\alpha }_{n} \) and \( {\beta }_{n} \) tend to \( \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) . By passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the \( {\alpha }_{n} \) converge to a minimizing geodesic ray \( \alpha \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) and that the \( {\beta }_{n} \) converge to a minimizing geodesic ray \( \beta \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) . Since, for all \( n \) , the union of \( {\alpha }_{n} \) and \( {\beta }_{n} \) forms a piecewise smooth ray in \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) meeting the central 2-sphere of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n} \) in a single point and at this point crossing from one side of this 2-sphere to the other, the union of \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) forms a proper, piecewise smooth map of \( \mathbb{R} \) to \( {M}_{\infty } \) that meets the central 2-sphere of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{\infty } \) in a single point and crosses from one side to the other at the point. This means that \( {M}_{\infty } \) has at least two ends. Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has non-negative curvature, according to Theorem 2.13, this implies that \( {M}_{\infty } \) is a product of a surface with \( \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( M \) has nonnegative curvature, the surface has non-negative curvature. Since \( M \) has positive curvature at least at one point, the surface is diffeomorphic to the 2-sphere.

According to Theorem 11.1, after passing to a subsequence there is a limit flow defined on some interval of the form \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) for \( {t}_{0} > 0 \) . Suppose that, after passing to a subsequence there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) for some \( 0 < T < \infty \) . It follows that for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) , the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is of non-negative curvature and has two ends. Again by Theorem 2.13, this implies that for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a Riemannian product of a metric of non-negative curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) with \( \mathbb{R} \) . Thus, by Corollary 4.19 the Ricci flow is a product of a Ricci flow \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h\left( t\right) }\right) \) with the trivial flow on \( \left( {\mathbb{R}, d{s}^{2}}\right) \) . It now follows from Corollary 4.14 that for every \( t \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) the curvature of \( {g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) on \( {S}^{2} \) is positive.

Let \( {M}_{n} \) be the zero time-slice of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is the geometric limit of the \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{n}}\right) \) , there is an exhaustive sequence \( {x}_{\infty } \in \; {V}_{1} \subset  {V}_{2} \subset  \cdots \) of open subsets of \( {M}_{\infty } \) with compact closure and embeddings \( {\varphi }_{n} : {V}_{n} \rightarrow  {M}_{n} \) sending \( {x}_{\infty } \) to \( {x}_{n} \) such that \( {\varphi }_{n}^{ * }\left( {{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) converges in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology, uniformly on compact sets, to \( {g}_{\infty } \) .

CLAIM 11.35. For any \( z \in  {M}_{\infty } \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( z \in  {V}_{n} \) , so that \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) \) is defined. Furthermore, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, there is a backward flow line through \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) \) in the generalized Ricci flow \( \left( {{Q}_{n}{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\right) \) defined on the interval \( \left( {-T - \left( {{R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) /2}\right) ,0}\right) \) . The scalar curvature is bounded above on this entire flow line by \( R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) \) .

Proof. Of course, for any compact subset \( K \subset  {M}_{\infty } \) and any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( K \subset  {V}_{n} \) , and there is an embedding \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack   \subset \; {Q}_{n}{\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) compatible with time and the vector field. The map \( {\varphi }_{n} \) defines a map \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n} : K \times  \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since the scalar curvature of the limit is positive, and hence bounded away from zero on the compact set \( K \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) and since \( {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, the following is true: For any compact subset \( K \subset  M \) and any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the scalar curvature of \( {G}_{n} \) on the image \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) is greater than \( {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , and hence for all \( n \) sufficiently large, every point in \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times \; \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since having a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood is invariant under rescaling, it follows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, every point of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood.

Next we claim that, for all \( n \) sufficiently large and for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. We have already seen that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Of course, since \( {M}_{\infty } \) is non-compact, for \( n \) sufficiently large, the canonical neighborhood of \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) must either be a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap or a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. We shall rule out the possibility of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, at least for all \( n \) sufficiently large.

To do this, take \( K \) to be a neighborhood of \( \left( {z,0}\right) \) in the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) with the topology of \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) and with the metric being the product of a positively curved metric on \( {S}^{2} \) with the Euclidean metric on \( I \) . We take \( K \) to be sufficiently large to contain the \( {2C} \) -ball centered at \( \left( {z,0}\right) \) . Because the limit flow is the product of a positively curved flow on \( {S}^{2} \) with the trivial flow on \( \mathbb{R} \) , the flow is distance decreasing. Thus, for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) the subman-ifold \( K \times  \{ t\} \) contains the ball in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) centered at \( \left( {z, t}\right) \) of radius \( {2C} \) . For every \( n \) sufficiently large, consider the submanifolds \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) of \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Since the metrics \( {\varphi }_{n}^{ * }{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) \) are converging uniformly for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) to the product flow on \( K \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large and any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , this submanifold contains the \( C \) -ball centered at \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) in \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Furthermore, the maximal curvature two-plane at any point of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) is almost tangent to the \( {S}^{2} \) -direction of \( K \) . Hence, by Lemma A. 2 the central 2-sphere of any \( \epsilon \) -neck contained \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) is almost parallel to the \( {S}^{2} \) -factors in the product structure on \( K \) at every point. This implies that the central 2-sphere of any such \( \epsilon \) -neck is isotopic to the \( {S}^{2} \) -factor of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) . Suppose that \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( \mathcal{C} \) . Then \( \mathcal{C} \) is contained in \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) . Consider the \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N \subset  \mathcal{C} \) that is the complement of the core of \( \mathcal{C} \) . Its central 2-sphere, \( \sum \) , is isotopic in \( K \) to the 2-sphere factor of \( K \) , but this is absurd since \( \sum \) bounds a 3-ball in the \( \mathcal{C} \) . This contradiction shows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , it is not possible for \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) to be contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. The only other possibility is that for all \( n \) sufficiently large and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) .

Fix \( n \) sufficiently large. Since, for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck, it follows from Definition 9.78 that for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) we have \( R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right)  \leq  R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) \) (this follows from the fact that the partial derivative in the time-direction of the scalar curvature of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck of scale one is positive and bounded away from 0 \( ) \) . It also follows from Definition 9.78 that the flow near \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , - {t}^{\prime }}\right) \) extends backwards to time

\[
- {t}^{\prime } - {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( {z,{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  <  - {t}^{\prime } - {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( {z,0}\right) }\right) ,
\]

with the same inequality for scalar curvature holding for all \( t \) in this extended interval. Applying this for \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) but sufficiently close to \( T \) establishes the last statement in the claim, and completes the proof of the claim.

Let \( {Q}_{0} \) be the upper bound of the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . By the previous claim, \( {Q}_{0} \) is also an upper bound for the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right) \) for any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) . Applying Theorem 11.1 to the flows

\[
\left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) , - {t}^{\prime } - {Q}_{0}^{-1}/2 < t \leq   - {t}^{\prime },
\]

we conclude that there is \( {t}_{0} \) depending only on the bound of the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right) \) , and hence depending only on \( {Q}_{0} \) , such that, after passing to a subsequence the limit flow exists for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime } - {t}_{0}, - {t}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) . Since the limit flow already exists on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , we conclude that, for this further subsequence, the limit flow exists on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime } - {t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Now apply this with \( {t}^{\prime } = T - {t}_{0}/2 \) . This proves that if, after passing to a subsequence, there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) , then, after passing to a further subsequence there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T - {t}_{0}/2,0}\right\rbrack \) where \( {t}_{0} \) depends only on \( {Q}_{0} \) , and in particular, is independent of \( T \) . Repeating this argument with \( T + \left( {{t}_{0}/2}\right) \) replacing \( T \) , we pass to a further subsequence so that the limit flow is defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T - {t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Repeating this inductively, we can find a sequence of subsequences so that for the \( n \) subsequence the limit flow is defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T - n{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Taking a diagonal subsequence produces a subsequence for which the limit is defined on \( ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) .

The limit flow is the product of a flow on \( {S}^{2} \) of positive curvature defined for \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) and the trivial flow on \( \mathbb{R} \) . Now, invoking Hamilton’s result (Corollary 9.50), we see that the ancient solution of positive curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) must be a shrinking round \( {S}^{2} \) . This means that the limit flow is the product of the shrinking round \( {S}^{2} \) with \( \mathbb{R} \) , and implies that for all \( n \) sufficiently large there is a strong \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n} \) . This contradiction proves the existence of \( h \) as required.

Now let us establish the last statement in Theorem 11.31. The subset of \( \mathcal{H} \) consisting of all \( z \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( z\right)  \leq  {\rho }^{-2} \) is compact (since \( R \) is a proper function), and disjoint from any \( \delta \) -neck of scale \( h \) since \( h < \rho /{2C} \) . On the other hand, for any point \( z \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( z\right)  \leq  {\rho }^{-2} \) take a minimal geodesic from \( z \) to the end of \( \mathcal{H} \) . There must be a point \( y \) on this geodesic with \( R\left( y\right)  = {h}^{-2} \) . The \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( y \) is disjoint from \( z \) (since \( h < \rho /{2C} \) ) and hence this neck separates \( z \) from the end of \( \mathcal{H} \) . It now follows easily that there is a point \( y \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  = {h}^{-2} \) and such that the central 2-sphere of the \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( y \) divides \( \mathcal{H} \) into two pieces with the non-compact piece disjoint from \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) .

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compactness of Long-Time Blow-Up Sequences
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that \( {\left\{  \left( {\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n},{x}_{n}\right) \right\}  }_{n = 1}^{\infty } \) is a sequence of generalized 3-dimensional Ricci flows satisfying the hypotheses of Theorem 11.1. Suppose in addition that there is \( {T}_{0} \) with \( 0 < {T}_{0} \leq  \infty \) such that the following holds. For any \( T < {T}_{0} \) , for each \( A < \infty \) , and all \( n \) sufficiently large, there is an embedding \( B\left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right)  \times  \left( {{t}_{n} - T{Q}_{n}^{-1},{t}_{n}}\right\rbrack \) into \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) compatible with time and with the vector field and at every point of the image the generalized flow is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on scales \( \leq  r \) . Then, after shifting the times of the generalized flows so that \( {t}_{n} = 0 \) for all \( n \) and passing to a subsequence there is a geometric limit Ricci flow

\[
\left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) , - {T}_{0} < t \leq  0,
\]

for the rescaled generalized flows \( \left( {{Q}_{n}{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) . This limit flow is complete and of non-negative curvature. Furthermore, the curvature is locally bounded in time. If in addition \( {T}_{0} = \infty \) , then it is a \( \kappa \) -solution.

(2) \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) has a strong canonical \( \left( {C\left( \epsilon \right) ,\epsilon }\right) \) -neighborhood. If this canonical neighborhood is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , then the strong neck extends to an evolving neck defined for backward rescaled time \( \left( {1 + \epsilon }\right) \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Take an increasing sequence of times \( {t}_{n}^{\prime } \) converging to \( T \) . Since the curvature of \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is locally bounded in time, for each \( n \) , there is a bound on the scalar curvature on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{n}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) . Hence, there is a finite upper bound \( {R}_{n} \) on \( R\left( {x, t}\right) \) for all points \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( t \leq  {t}_{n}^{\prime } \) for which the conclusion of the theorem does not hold. (There clearly are such points since the conclusion of the theorem fails for all \( \left( {x,0}\right) \) .) Pick \( \left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{n} \leq  {t}_{n}^{\prime } \) , with \( R\left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right)  \geq  {R}_{n}/2 \) and such that the conclusion of the theorem does not hold for \( \left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right) \) . To prove the theorem we must show that \( {\overline{\lim }}_{n \rightarrow  \infty }R\left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right)  < \infty \) . Suppose the contrary. By passing to a subsequence we can suppose that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}R\left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right)  = \infty \) . We set \( {Q}_{n} = R\left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right) \) . We claim that all the hypotheses of Theorem 11.8 apply to the sequence \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( t\right) ,\left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right) }\right) \) . First, we show that all the hypotheses of Theorem 11.1 (except the last) hold. Since \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has non-negative curvature all these flows have curvature pinched toward positive. By Proposition 12.13 there are \( r > 0 \) and \( \kappa  > 0 \) so that all these flows are \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on scales \( \leq  r \) . By construction if \( t \leq  {t}_{n} \) and \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  > 2{Q}_{n} \geq  {R}_{n} \) then the point \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) has a strong canonical \( \left( {C\left( \epsilon \right) ,\epsilon }\right) \) -neighborhood. We are assuming that \( {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) in order to achieve the contradiction. Since all time-slices are complete, all balls of finite radius have compact closure.

Lastly, we need to show that the extra hypothesis of Theorem 11.8 (which includes the last hypothesis of Theorem 11.1) is satisfied. This is clear since \( {t}_{n} \rightarrow  T \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) . Applying Theorem 11.8 we conclude that after passing to a subsequence there is a limiting flow which is a \( \kappa \) -solution. Clearly, this and Corollary 9.95 imply that for all sufficiently large \( n \) (in the subsequence) the neighborhood as required by the theorem exists. This contradicts our assumption that none of the points \( \left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right) \) have these neighborhoods. This contradiction proves the result.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
We evolve the initial metric \( {g}_{0} \) by smooth Ricci flow until the flow becomes singular for the first time. It follows from Theorem 10.10 and a standard continuity argument that the flow satisfies the Canonical Neighborhood Property with accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) on all scales less than \( 2\widehat{r} \) , up until the first singular time. At the first singular time, we perform finitely many surgeries on \( \widehat{\delta } \) -necks that have curvature level \( {h}^{-2} \) . The existence of such necks is ensured by Proposition 11.1. After performing surgery, we restart the flow and continue until the second singular time. Using Theorem 10.10 and a standard continuity argument, we conclude that the flow with surgery satisfies the Canonical Neighborhood Property with accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) on all scales less than \( 2\widehat{r} \) , up until the second singular time. Consequently, Proposition 11.1 ensures that, at the second singular time, we can again find \( \widehat{\delta } \) -necks on which to perform surgery. After performing surgery, we continue the flow until the third singular time. Again, Theorem 10.10 guarantees that the flow with surgery satisfies the Canonical Neighborhood Property with accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) on all scales less than \( 2\widehat{r} \) , up until the third singular time. We can now perform surgery again and repeat the process.

Since each surgery reduces the volume by at least \( c\left( n\right) {h}^{n} \) , we have an upper bound for the number of surgeries. By Proposition 10.2, the flow with surgery must become extinct by time \( \frac{n}{2\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \in  M}}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,0}\right) } \) at the latest. This completes the proof of Theorem 11.2.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given any \( 0 < \varepsilon  \leq  {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) (for some sufficiently small universal constant \( {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) ), suppose we have constructed the sequences satisfying the proposition for \( 1 \leq  j \leq  m \) (for some positive integer \( m \) ). Then there exists \( \kappa  > 0 \) , such that for any \( r,0 < r < \varepsilon \) , one can find \( \widetilde{\delta } = \widetilde{\delta }\left( {r,\varepsilon }\right) ,0 < \widetilde{\delta } < {\varepsilon }^{2} \) , which may also depend on the already constructed sequences, with the following property. Suppose we have a solution with a compact orientable normalized three-manifold as initial data, to the Ricci flow with finite number of surgeries on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{T}}\right\rbrack \) with \( m{\varepsilon }^{2} \leq  \bar{T} < \left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} \) , satisfying the assumptions and the conclusions of Proposition 7.4.1 on \( \left\lbrack  {0, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) , and the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r \) on \( \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{T}}\right\rbrack \) , as well as \( 0 < \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \min \{ \widetilde{\delta },\bar{\delta }\left( t\right) \} \) for any \( \delta \) -cutoff surgery with \( \delta  = \delta \left( t\right) \) at a time \( t \in \; \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{T}}\right\rbrack \) . Then the solution is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{T}}\right\rbrack \) for all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) .
