knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Consider a parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \triangleq  \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\}
\]

with \( m{\varepsilon }^{2} \leq  {t}_{0} \leq  \bar{T} \) and \( 0 < {r}_{0} < \varepsilon \) , where the solution satisfies \( \left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , whenever it is defined. We will use an argument analogous to the proof of Theorem 3.3.2 (no local collapsing theorem I) to prove

(7.4.1)

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}_{0}^{3}\text{ . }
\]

Let \( \eta \) be the universal positive constant in the definition of the canonical neighborhood assumption. Without loss of generality, we always assume \( \eta  \geq  {10} \) . Firstly, we want to show that one may assume \( {r}_{0} \geq  \frac{1}{2\eta }r \) .

Obviously, the curvature satisfies the estimate

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {20}{r}_{0}^{-2},
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{1}{2\eta }{r}_{0}, - \frac{1}{8\eta }{r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  = \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{2\eta }{r}_{0}}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \frac{1}{8\eta }{r}_{0}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the solution is defined. When \( {r}_{0} < \frac{1}{2\eta }r \) , we can enlarge \( {r}_{0} \) to some \( {r}_{0}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{r}_{0}, r}\right\rbrack \) so that

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {20}{r}_{0}^{\prime  - 2}
\]

on \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{1}{2\eta }{r}_{0}^{\prime }, - \frac{1}{8\eta }{r}_{0}^{\prime 2}}\right) \) (whenever it is defined), and either the equality holds somewhere in \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{1}{2\eta }{r}_{0}^{\prime }, - \left( {\frac{1}{8\eta }{r}_{0}^{\prime 2} + {\epsilon }^{\prime }}\right) }\right) \) for any arbitrarily small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) or \( {r}_{0}^{\prime } = r \) .

In the case that the equality holds somewhere, it follows from the pinching assumption that we have

\[
R > {10}{r}_{0}^{\prime  - 2}
\]

somewhere in \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{1}{2\eta }{r}_{0}^{\prime }, - \left( {\frac{1}{8\eta }{r}_{0}^{\prime }{}^{2} + {\epsilon }^{\prime }}\right) }\right) \) for any arbitrarily small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) . Here, without loss of generality, we have assumed \( r \) is suitably small. Then by the gradient estimates in the definition of the canonical neighborhood assumption, we know

\[
R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  > {r}_{0}^{\prime  - 2} \geq  {r}^{-2}.
\]

Hence the desired noncollapsing estimate (7.4.1) in this case follows directly from the canonical neighborhood assumption. (Recall that we have excluded every compact component which has positive sectional curvature in the surgery procedure and then we have excluded them from the list of canonical neighborhoods. Here we also used the standard volume comparison when the canonical neighborhood is an \( \varepsilon \) -cap.)

While in the case that \( {r}_{0}^{\prime } = r \) , we have the curvature bound

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {\left( \frac{1}{2\eta }r\right) }^{-2},
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{1}{2\eta }r, - {\left( \frac{1}{2\eta }r\right) }^{2}}\right)  = \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right) \left| {\;x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{2\eta }r}\right) }\right. , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - }\right. }\right. \; \left. \left. {{\left( \frac{1}{2\eta }r\right) }^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  \right\} \) , for which the solution is defined. It follows from the standard volume comparison that we only need to verify the noncollapsing estimate (7.4.1) for \( {r}_{0} = \frac{1}{2\eta }r \) . Thus we have reduced the proof to the case \( {r}_{0} \geq  \frac{1}{2\eta }r \) .

Recall from Theorem 3.3.2 that if a solution is smooth everywhere, we can get a lower bound for the volume of the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) as follows: define \( \tau \left( t\right)  = {t}_{0} - t \) and consider Perelman's reduced volume function and the Li-Yau-Perelman distance associated to the point \( {x}_{0} \) ; take a point \( \bar{x} \) at the time \( t = {\varepsilon }^{2} \) so that the Li-Yau-Perelman distance \( l \) attains its minimum \( {l}_{\min }\left( \tau \right)  = l\left( {\bar{x},\tau }\right)  \leq  \frac{3}{2} \) for \( \tau  = {t}_{0} - {\varepsilon }^{2} \) ; use it to obtain an upper bound for the Li-Yau-Perelman distance from \( {x}_{0} \) to each point of \( {B}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},1}\right) \) , thus getting a lower bound for Perelman’s reduced volume at \( \tau  = {t}_{0} \) ; apply the monotonicity of Perelman's reduced volume to deduce a lower bound for Perelman’s reduced volume at \( \tau \) near 0, and then get the desired estimate for the volume of the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) . Now since our solution has undergone surgeries, we need to localize this argument to the region which is unaffected by surgery.

We call a space-time curve in the solution track admissible if it stays in the spacetime region unaffected by surgery, and we call a space-time curve in the solution track a barely admissible curve if it is on the boundary of the set of admissible curves.

First of all, we want to estimate the \( \mathcal{L} \) -length of a barely admissible curve.

CLAIM. For any \( L < \infty \) one can find \( \bar{\delta } = \bar{\delta }\left( {L, r,{\widetilde{r}}_{m},\varepsilon }\right)  > 0 \) with the following property. Suppose that we have a curve \( \gamma \) , parametrized by \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{T}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  ,\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} \leq \; {T}_{0} < {t}_{0} \) , such that \( \gamma \left( {t}_{0}\right)  = {x}_{0},{T}_{0} \) is a surgery time, and \( \gamma \left( {T}_{0}\right) \) lies in the gluing cap. Suppose also each \( \delta \) -cutoff surgery at a time in \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{T}}\right\rbrack \) has \( \delta  \leq  \bar{\delta } \) . Then we have an estimate

(7.4.2)

\[
{\int }_{{T}_{0}}^{{t}_{0}}\sqrt{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {{R}_{ + }\left( {\gamma \left( t\right) , t}\right)  + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( t\right) \right| }^{2}}\right) {dt} \geq  L
\]

where \( {R}_{ + } = \max \{ R,0\} \) .

Since \( {r}_{0} \geq  \frac{1}{2\eta }r \) and \( \left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) on \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) (whenever it is defined), we can require \( \bar{\delta } > 0 \) , depending on \( r \) and \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m} \) , to be so small that \( \gamma \left( {T}_{0}\right) \) does not lie in the region \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) . Let \( {\Delta t} \) be the maximal number such that \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  {t}_{0} - \Delta t,{t}_{0}\right\rbrack  } \subset \; P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {\Delta t}}\right) \) (i.e., \( {t}_{0} - {\Delta t} \) is the first time when \( \gamma \) escapes the parabolic region \( \left. {P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) }\right) \) . Obviously we only need to consider the case:

\[
{\int }_{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}^{{t}_{0}}\sqrt{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {{R}_{ + }\left( {\gamma \left( t\right) , t}\right)  + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( t\right) \right| }^{2}}\right) {dt} < L.
\]

We observe that \( {\Delta t} \) can be bounded from below in terms of \( L \) and \( {r}_{0} \) . Indeed, if \( {\Delta t} \geq  {r}_{0}^{2} \) , there is nothing to prove. Thus we may assume \( {\Delta t} < {r}_{0}^{2} \) . By the curvature bound \( \left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) on \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) and the Ricci flow equation we see

\[
{\int }_{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}^{{t}_{0}}\left| {\dot{\gamma }\left( t\right) }\right| {dt} \geq  c{r}_{0}
\]

for some universal positive constant \( c \) . On the other hand, by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have

\[
{\int }_{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}^{{t}_{0}}\left| {\dot{\gamma }\left( t\right) }\right| {dt} \leq  {\left( {\int }_{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}^{{t}_{0}}\sqrt{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {R}_{ + } + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}\right) dt\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot  {\left( {\int }_{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}^{{t}_{0}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}_{0} - t}}dt\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}
\]

\[
\leq  {\left( 2L\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}{\left( \Delta t\right) }^{\frac{1}{4}}
\]

which implies

(7.4.3)

\[
{\left( \Delta t\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \geq  \frac{{c}^{2}{r}_{0}^{2}}{2L}.
\]

Thus

\[
{\int }_{{T}_{0}}^{{t}_{0}}\sqrt{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {{R}_{ + } + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {dt} \geq  {\int }_{{T}_{0}}^{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}\sqrt{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {{R}_{ + } + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {dt}
\]

\[
\geq  {\left( \Delta t\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}{\int }_{{T}_{0}}^{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}\left( {{R}_{ + } + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {dt}
\]

\[
\left. { \geq  \left( {\min \left\{  {\frac{{c}^{2}{r}_{0}^{2}}{2L},{r}_{0}}\right\}  }\right) {\int }_{{T}_{0}}^{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}\left( {{R}_{ + } + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {dt}}\right)
\]

while by Corollary 7.3.7, we can find \( \bar{\delta } = \bar{\delta }\left( {L, r,{\widetilde{r}}_{m},\varepsilon }\right)  > 0 \) so small that

\[
{\int }_{{T}_{0}}^{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}\left( {{R}_{ + } + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {dt} \geq  L{\left( \min \left\{  \frac{{c}^{2}{r}_{0}^{2}}{2L},{r}_{0}\right\}  \right) }^{-1}.
\]

Then we have proved the desired assertion (7.4.2).

Recall that for a curve \( \gamma \) , parametrized by \( \tau  = {t}_{0} - t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{\tau }}\right\rbrack \) , with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = {x}_{0} \) and \( \bar{\tau } \leq  {t}_{0} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} \) , we have \( L\left( \gamma \right)  = {\int }_{0}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }\left( {R + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {d\tau } \) . We can also define \( {L}_{ + }\left( \gamma \right) \) by replacing \( R \) with \( {R}_{ + } \) in the previous formula. Recall that \( R \geq   - 1 \) at the initial time \( t = 0 \) for the normalized initial manifold. Recall that the surgeries occur at the parts where the scalar curvatures are very large. Thus we can apply the maximum principle to conclude that the solution with surgery still satisfies \( R \geq   - 1 \) everywhere in space-time. This implies

(7.4.4)

\[
{L}_{ + }\left( \gamma \right)  \leq  L\left( \gamma \right)  + {\left( 2{\varepsilon }^{2}\right) }^{\frac{3}{2}}.
\]

By applying the assertion (7.4.2), we now choose \( \widetilde{\delta } > 0 \) (depending on \( r,\varepsilon \) and \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m} \) ) such that as each \( \delta \) -cutoff surgery at the time interval \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, T}\right\rbrack \) has \( \delta  \leq  \widetilde{\delta } \) , every barely admissible curve \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) to a point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) (with \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},{t}_{0}}\right) \) ) has

\[
{L}_{ + }\left( \gamma \right)  \geq  {22}\sqrt{2}.
\]

Thus if the Li-Yau-Perelman distance from \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) to a point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) (with \( t \in  \lbrack (m - \; 1){\varepsilon }^{2},{t}_{0})) \) is achieved by a space-time curve which is not admissible, then its Li-Yau-Perelman distance has

(7.4.5)

\[
l \geq  \frac{{L}_{ + } - {\left( 2{\varepsilon }^{2}\right) }^{\frac{3}{2}}}{2\sqrt{2}\varepsilon } > {10}{\varepsilon }^{-1}.
\]

We also observe that the absolute value of \( l\left( {{x}_{0},\tau }\right) \) is very small as \( \tau \) closes to zere. Thus the maximum principle argument in Corollary 3.2.6 still works for our solutions with surgery because barely admissible curves do not attain the minimum. So we conclude that

\[
{l}_{\min }\left( \bar{\tau }\right)  = \min \{ l\left( {x,\bar{\tau }}\right)  \mid  x\text{ lies in the solution manifold at }{t}_{0} - \bar{\tau }\}  \leq  \frac{3}{2}
\]

for \( \bar{\tau } \in  \left( {0,{t}_{0} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) . In particular, there exists a minimizing curve \( \gamma \) of \( {l}_{\min }\left( {{t}_{0} - }\right. \; \left. {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) , defined on \( \tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = {x}_{0} \) , such that

(7.4.6)

\[
{L}_{ + }\left( \gamma \right)  \leq  \frac{3}{2} \cdot  2\sqrt{2}\varepsilon  + 2\sqrt{2}{\varepsilon }^{3}
\]

\[
\leq  {5\varepsilon }
\]

since \( 0 < \varepsilon  \leq  {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) with \( {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) sufficiently small (to be further determined). Consequently, there exists a point \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) on the minimizing curve \( \gamma \) with \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} + \frac{1}{4}{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m - }\right. }\right. \) 1) \( {\varepsilon }^{2} + \frac{3}{4}{\varepsilon }^{2}\rbrack \) (i.e., \( \tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} - \frac{3}{4}{\varepsilon }^{2},{t}_{0} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} - \frac{1}{4}{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) ) such that

(7.4.7)

\[
R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \leq  {25}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{-2}.
\]

Otherwise, we have

\[
{L}_{ + }\left( \gamma \right)  \geq  {\int }_{{t}_{0} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} - \frac{1}{4}{\varepsilon }^{2}}^{{t}_{0} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} - \frac{1}{4}{\varepsilon }^{2}}\sqrt{\tau }R\left( {\gamma \left( \tau \right) ,{t}_{0} - \tau }\right) {d\tau }
\]

\[
> {25}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{-2}\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}{\varepsilon }^{2}}\left( {\frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right)
\]

\[
> {5\varepsilon }
\]

since \( 0 < {\widetilde{r}}_{m} < \varepsilon \) . This contradicts (7.4.6).

Next we want to get a lower bound for Perelman's reduced volume of a ball around \( \bar{x} \) of radius about \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m} \) at some time slightly before \( \bar{t} \) .

Denote by \( {\theta }_{1} = \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1} \) and \( {\theta }_{2} = \frac{1}{64}{\eta }^{-1} \) , where \( \eta \) is the universal positive constant in the gradient estimates (7.3.4). Since the solution satisfies the canonical neighborhood assumption on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) , it follows from the gradient estimates (7.3.4) that

(7.4.8)

\[
R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {400}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{-2}
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}, - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\right)  \triangleq  \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the solution is defined. And since the scalar curvature at the points where the \( \delta \) -cutoff surgeries occur in the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) is at least \( {\left( \widetilde{\delta }\right) }^{-2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{-2} \) , the solution is well-defined on the whole parabolic region \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}, - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\right) \) (i.e., this parabolic region is unaffected by surgery). Thus by combining (7.4.6) and (7.4.8), we know that the Li-Yau-Perelman distance from \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) to each point of the ball \( {B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) is uniformly bounded by some universal constant. Let us define Perelman’s reduced volume of the ball \( {B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) , by

\[
{\widetilde{V}}_{{t}_{0} - \bar{t} + {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {{B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= {\int }_{{B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) }{\left( 4\pi \left( {t}_{0} - \bar{t} + {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}
\]

\[
\cdot  \exp \left( {-l\left( {q,{t}_{0} - \bar{t} + {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\right) }\right) d{V}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( q\right) ,
\]

where \( l\left( {q,\tau }\right) \) is the Li-Yau-Perelman distance from \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Hence by the \( {\kappa }_{{m}^{ - }} \) noncollapsing assumption on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) , we conclude that Perelman’s reduced volume of the ball \( {B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) is bounded from below by a positive constant depending only on \( {\kappa }_{m} \) and \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m} \) .

Finally we want to apply a local version of the monotonicity of Perelman's reduced volume to get a lower bound estimate for the volume of the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) .

We have seen that the Li-Yau-Perelman distance from \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) to each point of the ball \( {B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) is uniformly bounded by some universal constant. Now we can choose a sufficiently small (universal) positive constant \( {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) such that when \( 0 < \varepsilon  \leq  {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) , by (7.4.5), all the points in the ball \( {B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) can be connected to \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) by shortest \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesics, and all of these \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesics are admissible (i.e., they stay in the region unaffected by surgery). The union of all shortest \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesics from \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) to the ball \( {B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) defined by \( C{B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right)  = \{ \left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  \left( {x, t}\right) \) lies in a shortest \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic from \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) to a point in \( \left. {{B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) }\right\} \) , forms a conelike subset in space-time with the vertex \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Denote \( B\left( t\right) \) by the intersection of the cone-like subset \( C{B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) with the time-slice at \( t \) . Perelman’s reduced volume of the subset \( B\left( t\right) \) is given by

\[
{\widetilde{V}}_{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {B\left( t\right) }\right)  = {\int }_{B\left( t\right) }{\left( 4\pi \left( {t}_{0} - t\right) \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,{t}_{0} - t}\right) }\right) d{V}_{t}\left( q\right) .
\]

Since the cone-like subset \( C{B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) lies entirely in the region unaffected by surgery, we can apply Perelman's Jacobian comparison theorem (Theorem 3.2.7) to conclude that

(7.4.9)

\[
{\widetilde{V}}_{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {B\left( t\right) }\right)  \geq  {\widetilde{V}}_{{t}_{0} - \bar{t} + {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {{B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\geq  c\left( {{\kappa }_{m},{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right)
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be a Ricci flow with surgery and for each \( t \) set \( s\left( t\right)  = s\left( {M}_{t}\right) \) . If \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) then \( s\left( {t}^{\prime }\right)  \geq  s\left( t\right) \) . If we do surgery at time \( t \) along at least one homotopically essential 2-sphere, then \( s\left( t\right)  < s\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) for any \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) .

Proof. Clearly, for any \( {t}_{0} \) we have \( s\left( t\right)  = s\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) for \( t \geq  {t}_{0} \) sufficiently close to \( {t}_{0} \) . Also, if \( t \) is not a surgery time, then \( s\left( t\right)  = s\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) for all \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) and sufficiently close to \( t \) . According to Proposition 15.3, if \( t \) is a surgery time then for \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) but sufficiently close to it, the manifold \( {M}_{t} \) is obtained from \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) by doing surgery on a finite number of 2-spheres and removing certain components of the result. We divide the operations into three types: (i) surgery along homotopically trivial 2-spheres in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) ,(ii) surgery along homo-topically non-trivial 2-spheres in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) ,(iii) removal of components. Clearly, the first operation does not change the invariant \( s \) since it simply creates a manifold that is the disjoint union of a manifold homotopy equivalent to the original manifold with a collection of homotopy 3-spheres. Removal of components will not increase the invariant. The last operation to consider is surgery along a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere. Let \( {F}_{t} \) be a homotopi-cally essential family of disjointly embedded 2-spheres in \( {M}_{t} \) . This family of 2-spheres in \( {M}_{t} \) can be deformed to miss the 3-disks (the surgery caps) in \( {M}_{t} \) that we sewed in doing the surgery at time \( t \) along a homotopically nontrivial 2-sphere. After deforming the spheres in the family \( {F}_{t} \) away from the surgery caps, they produce a disjoint family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) of 2 -spheres in the manifold \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) , for \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) but \( {t}^{\prime } \) sufficiently close to \( t \) . Each 2-sphere in \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) is disjoint from the homotopically essential 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) along which we do surgery at time \( t \) . Let \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) be the family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \cup  \left\{  {S}_{0}\right\} \) . We claim that \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is a homotopically essential family in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) .

First, suppose that one of the spheres \( \sum \) in \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . Of course, we are in the case when the surgery 2-sphere is homotopically essential, so \( \sum \) is not \( {S}_{0} \) and hence is the image of one of the 2-spheres in \( {F}_{t} \) . Since \( \sum \) is homotopically trivial, it is the boundary of a homotopy 3-ball \( B \) in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . If \( B \) is disjoint from the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) , then it exists in \( {M}_{t} \) and hence \( \sum \) is homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{t} \) , which is not possible from the assumption about the family \( {F}_{t} \) . If \( B \) meets the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) , then since the spheres in the family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) are disjoint, it follows that \( B \) contains the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) . This is not possible since in this case \( {S}_{0} \) would be homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) , contrary to assumption.

We also claim that no distinct members of \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) are homotopic. For suppose that two of the members \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) are homotopic. It cannot be the case that one of \( \sum \) or \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) is the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) since, in that case, the other one would be homotopically trivial after surgery, i.e., in \( {M}_{t} \) . The 2- spheres \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) are the boundary components of a submanifold \( A \) in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) homotopy equivalent to \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) . If \( A \) is disjoint from the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) , then \( A \) exists in \( {M}_{t} \) and \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) are homotopic in \( {M}_{t} \) , contrary to assumption. Otherwise, the surgery sphere \( {S}_{0} \) must be contained in \( A \) . Every 2-sphere in \( A \) is either homotopically trivial in \( A \) or is homotopic in \( A \) to either boundary component. If \( {S}_{0} \) is homotopically trivial in \( A \) , then it would be homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) and this contradicts our assumption. If \( {S}_{0} \) is homotopic in \( A \) to each of \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) , then each of \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) is homo-topically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) , contrary to assumption. This shows that the family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is homotopically essential. It follows immediately that doing surgery on a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere strictly decreases the invariant \( s \) .

\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {30}\bar{Q},
\]

for all \( x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\widetilde{t} - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) (or \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) ) and all sufficiently large \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) . Observe that Lemma 3.4.1 (ii) is applicable for \( {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},\bar{x}}\right) \) with \( t \in \; \left\lbrack  {\widetilde{t} - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) (or \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) ) since any minimal geodesic, with respect to the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) , connecting \( {x}_{0} \) and \( \bar{x} \) lies in the region unaffected by surgery; otherwise the geodesic is not minimal. After having obtained the above curvature estimate, we can argue as deriving (7.2.2) and (7.2.3) in the proof of Theorem 7.2.1 to conclude that any point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) , with \( \widetilde{t} - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) (or \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) ) and \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , satisfies

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {d}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  + \frac{1}{2}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},
\]

for all sufficiently large \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) . Then by combining with the choice of the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , we prove \( {t}^{\prime } = \bar{t} - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1} \) (i.e., the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any point \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) with \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  4\bar{Q} \) ) for all sufficiently large \( \alpha \) and then sufficiently large \( \beta \) .

Now it follows from the gradient estimates in the canonical neighborhood assumption that the scalar curvatures of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) satisfy

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {40}
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {\bar{x},0,\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}, - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}}\right)  \triangleq  \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {\bar{x},\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  }\right. \; \left. \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack  \right\} \) , for which the rescaled solution is defined. (Here \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) denotes the geodesic ball in the rescaled solution at time \( {t}^{\prime } \) ). Note again that \( R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{r}{\left( \bar{t}\right) }^{-2} \) and recall from our designed surgery procedure that if there is a cutoff surgery at a point \( x \) at a time \( t \) , the scalar curvature at \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is at least \( {\left( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2}\widetilde{r}{\left( t\right) }^{-2} \) . Then for each fixed sufficiently large \( \alpha \) , for \( \beta \) large enough, the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) is defined on the whole parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {\bar{x},0,\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}, - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}}\right) \) . More generally, for arbitrarily fixed \( 0 < \widetilde{K} <  + \infty \) , there is a positive integer \( {\alpha }_{0} \) so that for each \( \alpha  \geq  {\alpha }_{0} \) we can

find \( {\beta }_{0} > 0 \) (depending on \( \alpha \) ) such that if \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) and \( \left( {y,0}\right) \) is a point on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {y,0}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{K} \) and \( {\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {y,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{K} \) , we have estimate

(7.5.14)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {40}\widetilde{K}
\]

for \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {y,0,\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-1}}\right)  \triangleq  \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {y,}\right) }\right. \; \left. {\left. {\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\rbrack  ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) . In particular, the rescaled solution is defined on the whole parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {y,0,\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-1}}\right) \) .

Next, we want to show the curvature of the rescaled solutions at the new times zero (after shifting) stay uniformly bounded at bounded distances from \( \bar{x} \) for some subsequences of \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) . Let \( {\alpha }_{m},{\beta }_{m} \rightarrow   + \infty \) be chosen so that the estimate (7.5.14) holds with \( \widetilde{K} = m \) . For all \( \rho  \geq  0 \) , set

\[
M\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {\widetilde{R}\left( {x,0}\right)  \mid  m \geq  1,{d}_{0}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \rho \text{ in the rescaled solutions }{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}}\right\}
\]

and

\[
{\rho }_{0} = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 \mid  M\left( \rho \right)  <  + \infty \} .
\]

Clearly the estimate (7.5.14) yields \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) . As we consider the unshifted time \( \bar{t} \) , by combining with the assumption that \( {t}_{0} > 2{r}_{0}^{2} \) , we have

(7.5.15)

\[
\bar{t}R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \geq  \frac{{t}_{0}}{2}R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {r}_{0}^{2}\left( {{K}_{1}{r}_{0}^{-2}}\right)
\]

\[
= {K}_{1} \rightarrow   + \infty \text{ . }
\]

It then follows from the pinching assumption that we only need to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) . As before, we argue by contradiction. Suppose we have a sequence of points \( {y}_{m} \) in the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) with \( {\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{y}_{m}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) and \( \widetilde{R}\left( {{y}_{m},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Denote by \( {\gamma }_{m} \) a minimizing geodesic segment from \( \bar{x} \) to \( {y}_{m} \) and denote by \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) the open geodesic balls centered at \( \bar{x} \) of radius \( {\rho }_{0} \) of the rescaled solutions. By applying the assertion in statement (i), we have uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing at the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) . By combining with the local curvature estimate (7.5.14) and Hamilton's compactness theorem, we can assume that, after passing to a subsequence, the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}},\bar{x}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( {\gamma }_{m} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {x}_{\infty } \) . Moreover, by the pinching assumption and the estimate (7.5.15), the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature.

Then exactly as before, we consider the tubular neighborhood along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \)

\[
V = \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{{q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty }}}{B}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)
\]

and the completion \( {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) of \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) \) with \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) the limit point of \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . As before, by the choice of the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , we know that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty } \) is cylindrical at any point \( {q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) which is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) . Then by the same reason as before the metric space \( \bar{V} = V \cup  \left\{  {y}_{\infty }\right\} \) has nonnegative curvature in Alexandrov sense, and we have a three-dimensional nonflat tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) at \( {y}_{\infty } \) . Pick \( z \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) with distance one from the vertex and it is nonflat around \( z \) . By definition \( B\left( {z,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \left( { \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V}}\right) \) is the Gromov-Hausdoff convergent limit of the scalings of a sequence of balls \( {B}_{\infty }\left( {{z}_{k},{\sigma }_{k}}\right) \left( { \subset  \left( {V,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) }\right) \) with \( {\sigma }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) . Since the estimate (7.5.14) survives on \( \left( {V,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) \) for all \( \widetilde{K} <  + \infty \) , we know that this convergence is actually in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology and over some time interval. Since the limit \( B\left( {z,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \left( { \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V}}\right) \) is a piece of a nonnegatively curved nonflat metric cone, we get a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum Principle (Theorem 2.2.1) as before. Hence we have proved that a subsequence of the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) has uniformly bounded curvatures at bounded distance from \( \bar{x} \) at the new times zero.

Further, by the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing at the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) and the estimate (7.5.14) again, we can take a \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , defined on a space-time subset which contains the time slice \( \{ t = 0\} \) and is relatively open in \( {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , for the subsequence of the rescaled solutions. The limit is a smooth solution to the Ricci flow, and is complete at \( t = 0 \) , as well as has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption and the estimate (7.5.15). Thus by repeating the same argument as in the Step 4 of the proof Proposition 7.4.1, we conclude that the curvature of the limit at \( t = 0 \) is bounded.

Finally we try to extend the limit backwards in time to get an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Since the curvature of the limit is bounded at \( t = 0 \) , it follows from the estimate (7.5.14) that the limit is a smooth solution to the Ricci flow defined at least on a backward time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some positive constant \( a \) . Let \( \left( {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal time interval over which we can extract a smooth limiting solution. It suffices to show \( {t}_{\infty } =  - \infty \) . If \( {t}_{\infty } >  - \infty \) , there are only two possibilities: either there exist surgeries in finite distance around the time \( {t}_{\infty } \) or the curvature of the limiting solution becomes unbounded as \( t \searrow  {t}_{\infty } \) .

Let \( c > 0 \) be a positive constant much smaller than \( \frac{1}{100}{\eta }^{-1} \) . Note again that the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time. Then we can find some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and some time \( t = {t}_{\infty } + \theta \) with \( 0 < \theta  < \frac{c}{3} \) such that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right)  \leq  2 \) .

Consider the (unrescaled) scalar curvature \( R \) of \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at the point \( \bar{x} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the scalar curvature \( {R}_{\infty } \) of the limit on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{3},0}\right\rbrack \) is uniformly bounded by some positive constant \( C \) , we have the curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {\bar{x}, t}\right)  \leq  {2C}\bar{Q}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) and all sufficiently large \( m \) . For each fixed \( m \) and \( {\alpha }_{m} \) , we may require the chosen \( {\beta }_{m} \) to satisfy

\[
{\left( {\bar{\delta }}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\right) }^{-2}{\left( \widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}}}{2}\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  m\widetilde{r}{\left( {t}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}}\right) }^{-2} \geq  m\bar{Q}.
\]

When \( m \) is large enough, we observe again that Lemma 3.4.1 (ii) is applicable for \( {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},\bar{x}}\right) \) with \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . Then by repeating the argument as in the derivation of (7.2.1),(7.2.2) and (7.2.3), we deduce that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) . \)

Let \( \left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) be a sequence of associated points and times in the (unrescaled) solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) so that after rescaling, the sequence converges to \( \left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right) \) in the limit. Clearly \( \frac{\theta }{2} \leq  {\theta }_{m} \leq  {2\theta } \) for all sufficiently large \( m \) . Then by the argument as in the derivation of (7.5.13), we know that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the solution \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at \( {y}_{m} \) is defined on the whole time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m} - }\right. }\right. \; \left. {\left. {\frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies the curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {{y}_{m}, t}\right)  \leq  8\bar{Q}
\]

there; moreover the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) with \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  4\bar{Q} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) .

We now consider the rescaled sequence \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) with the marked points replaced by \( {y}_{m} \) and the times replaced by \( {s}_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) . As before the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality implies the rescaling limit around \( \left( {{y}_{m},{s}_{m}}\right) \) agrees with the original one. Then the arguments in previous paragraphs imply the limit is well-defined and smooth on a space-time open neighborhood of the maximal time slice \( \left\{  {t = {t}_{\infty }}\right\} \) . Particularly this excludes the possibility of existing surgeries in finite distance around the time \( {t}_{\infty } \) . Moreover, the limit at \( t = {t}_{\infty } \) also has bounded curvature. By using the gradient estimates in the canonical neighborhood assumption on the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) , we see that the second possibility is also impossible. Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Therefore we have proved the canonical neighborhood statement (ii).

(iii) This is analogous to Theorem 7.2.1. We also argue by contradiction. Suppose for some \( A <  + \infty \) and sequences of positive numbers \( {K}_{2}^{\alpha } \rightarrow   + \infty ,{\bar{r}}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) there exists a sequence of times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) such that for any sequences \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } > 0 \) with \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \rightarrow  0 \) for fixed \( \alpha \) , we have sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery and sequences of points \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) , of positive constants \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\sqrt{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }} \) which satisfy the assumptions, but for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) there hold

(7.5.16)

\[
R\left( {{x}^{\alpha \beta },{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\right)  > {K}_{2}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2}\text{ , for some }{x}^{\alpha \beta } \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }, A{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) .
\]

We may assume that \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) , where \( {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) is chosen so that the statements (i) and (ii) hold on \( {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta },{4A}{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) \) . Let \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions of \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) around the origins \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with factor \( {\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \) and shift the times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) to zero. Then by applying the statement (ii), we know that the regions, where the scalar curvature of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) is at least \( {K}_{1}\left( { = {K}_{1}\left( {4A}\right) }\right) \) , are canonical neighborhood regions. Note that canonical \( \varepsilon \) -neck neighborhoods are strong. Also note that the pinching assumption and the assertion

\[
{t}_{0}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \geq  {\left( {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty ,\text{ as }\alpha  \rightarrow   + \infty ,
\]

imply that any subsequent limit of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) must have nonnegative sectional curvature. Thus by the above argument in the proof of the statement (ii) (or the argument in Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1), we conclude that there exist subsequences \( \alpha  = {\alpha }_{m},\beta  = {\beta }_{m} \) such that the curvatures of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) stay uniformly bounded at distances from the origins \( {x}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) not exceeding \( {2A} \) . This contradicts (7.5.16) for \( m \) sufficiently large. This proves the statements (iii).

Clearly for fixed \( A \) , after defining the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) for each \( {t}_{0} \) , one can adjust the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) so that it is nonincreasing in \( {t}_{0} \) .

Therefore we have completed the proof of the theorem.

From now on we redefine the function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) so that it is also less than \( {\bar{\delta }}_{2\left( {t + 1}\right) }\left( {2t}\right) \) and then the above theorem always holds for \( A \in  \left\lbrack  {1,2\left( {{t}_{0} + 1}\right) }\right\rbrack \) . Particularly, we still

have

\[
\widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  \leq  \bar{\delta }\left( t\right)  = \min \left\{  {\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}\log \left( {1 + t}\right) },{\delta }_{0}}\right\}  ,
\]

which tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) . We may also require that \( \widetilde{r}\left( t\right) \) tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(Justification of the canonical neighborhood assumption). Given any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist decreasing sequences \( 0 < {\widetilde{r}}_{j} < \varepsilon ,{\kappa }_{j} > 0 \) , and \( 0 < {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} < {\varepsilon }^{2}, j = 1,2,\cdots \) , with the following property. Define the positive function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) on \( \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) by \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) . Suppose there is a surgically modified solution, defined on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( T <  + \infty \) , to the Ricci flow which satisfies the following:

(1) it starts on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric, and

(2) it has only a finite number of surgeries such that each surgery at a time \( t \in  \left( {0, T}\right) \) is a \( \delta \left( t\right) \) -cutoff surgery with

\[
0 < \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \min \{ \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) ,\bar{\delta }\left( t\right) \} .
\]

Then on each time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack  \bigcap \lbrack 0, T), j = 1,2,\cdots \) , the solution satisfies the \( {\kappa }_{j} \) -noncollapsing condition on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) and the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {\widetilde{r}}_{j} \) .

Here and in the following, we call a (three-dimensional) surgically modified solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t < T,\kappa \) -noncollapsed at \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) on the scales less than \( \rho \) (for some \( \kappa  > 0,\rho  > 0 \) ) if it satisfies the following property: whenever \( r < \rho \) and

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {r}^{-2}
\]

for all those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}, r, - {r}^{2}}\right)  = \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the solution is defined, we have

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}^{3}.
\]

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
The proof of the proposition is by induction: having constructed our sequences for \( 1 \leq  j \leq  m \) , we make one more step, defining \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) , \( {\kappa }_{m + 1},{\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) , and redefining \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) . In view of the previous lemma, we only need to define \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .

In Theorem 7.1.1 we have obtained the canonical neighborhood structure for smooth solutions. When adapting the arguments in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1 to the present surgical solutions, we will encounter the new difficulty of how to take a limit for the surgically modified solutions. The idea to overcome the difficulty consists of two parts. The first part, due to Perelman [104], is to choose \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) small enough to push the surgical regions to infinity in space. (This is the reason why we need to redefine \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .) The second part is to show that solutions are smooth on some small, but uniform, time intervals (on compact subsets) so that we can apply Hamilton's compactness theorem, since we only have curvature bounds; otherwise Shi's interior derivative estimate may not be applicable. In fact, the second part is more crucial. That is just concerned with the question of whether the surgery times accumulate or not. Our argument will use the canonical neighborhood characterization of the standard solution in Lemma 7.3.5.

We now start to prove the proposition by contradiction. Suppose for sequence of positive numbers \( {r}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) , satisfying \( {r}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) as \( \alpha  \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  \frac{1}{\alpha  \cdot  \beta }\left( { \rightarrow  0}\right) \) , there exist sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery, where each of them has only a finite number of cutoff surgeries and has a compact orientable normalized three-manifold as initial data, so that the following two assertions hold:

(i) each \( \delta \) -cutoff at a time \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) satisfies \( \delta  \leq  {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) ; and

(ii) the solutions satisfy the statement of the proposition on \( \left\lbrack  {0, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) , but violate the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) on \( \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

For each solution \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) , we choose \( \bar{t} \) (depending on \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) ) to be the nearly first time for which the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) is violated. More precisely, we choose \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) so that the canonical neighborhood assumption with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) and with accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon \) is violated at some \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , however the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) holds on \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . After passing to subsequences, we may assume each \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) is less than the \( \widetilde{\delta } \) in Lemma 7.4.2 with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) when \( \alpha \) is fixed. Then by Lemma 7.4.2 we have uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) on \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) with some \( \kappa  > 0 \) independent of \( \alpha ,\beta \) .

Slightly abusing notation, we will often drop the indices \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) .

Let \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions around \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with factors \( R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \left( { \geq  {r}^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty }\right) \) and shift the times \( \bar{t} \) to zero. We hope to take a limit of the rescaled solutions for subsequences of \( \alpha ,\beta  \rightarrow  \infty \) and show the limit is an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which will give the desired contradiction. We divide our arguments into the following six steps.

Step 1. Let \( \left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right) \) be a point on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right)  \leq  A \) (for some \( A \geq  1 \) ) and \( \widehat{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {-\left( {\bar{t} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) . Then we have estimate

(7.4.14)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10A}
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {y,\widehat{t},\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1}}\right)  \triangleq \; \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {y,\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {\widehat{t} - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1},\widehat{t}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the rescaled solution is defined.

Step 2. In this step, we will prove three time extension results.

Assertion 1. For arbitrarily fixed \( \alpha ,0 < A <  + \infty ,1 \leq  C <  + \infty \) and \( 0 \leq  B < \frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{2}{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{C}^{-1} \) , there is a \( {\beta }_{0} = {\beta }_{0}\left( {\varepsilon , A, B, C}\right) \) (independent of \( \alpha \) ) such that if \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) and the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is defined on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack \) with \( 0 \leq  b \leq  B \) and the scalar curvature satisfies

\[

then the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{C}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) .

Before giving the proof, we make a simple observation: once a space point in the Ricci flow with surgery is removed by surgery at some time, then it never appears for later time; if a space point at some time \( t \) cannot be defined before the time \( t \) , then either the point lies in a gluing cap of the surgery at time \( t \) or the time \( t \) is the initial time of the Ricci flow.

Proof of Assertion 1. Firstly we claim that there exists \( {\beta }_{0} = {\beta }_{0}\left( {\varepsilon , A, B, C}\right) \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) , the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) can be defined before the time \( - b \) (i.e., there are no surgeries interfering in \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b - {\epsilon }^{\prime }, - b}\right\rbrack \) for some \( \left. {{\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0}\right) \) .

We argue by contradiction. By the above observation, there is a surgery at the time \( - b \) such that the point \( \widetilde{x} \) lies in the instant gluing cap.

Let \( \widetilde{h}\left( { = R{\left( \bar{x},\bar{t}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}h}\right) \) be the cut-off radius at the time \( - b \) for the rescaled solution. Clearly, there is a universal constant \( D \) such that \( {D}^{-1}\widetilde{h} \leq  \widetilde{R}{\left( \widetilde{x}, - b\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  D\widetilde{h} \) .

By Lemma 7.3.4 and looking at the rescaled solution at the time \( - b \) , the gluing cap and the adjacent \( \delta \) -neck, of radius \( \widetilde{h} \) , constitute a \( {\left( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) -cap \( \mathcal{K} \) . For any fixed small positive constant \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) (much smaller than \( \varepsilon \) ), we see that

\[
{\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{R}{\left( \widetilde{x}, - b\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  \mathcal{K}
\]

when \( \beta \) large enough. We first verify the following

CLAIM 1. For any small constants \( 0 < \widetilde{\theta } < 1,{\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) , there exists a \( \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right)  > 0 \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right) \) , we have

\[

Let \( {\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) be much smaller than \( \varepsilon \) and \( \min \left\{  {{A}^{-1}, A}\right\} \) . \[

\[

\[
\left| {\widetilde{\widetilde{t}} + b}\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}

\[

\]

on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{A}_{0}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) . Then by Assertion 2 of Step 2, we have proved that there is a sufficiently large integer \( {\bar{k}}_{0} \) such that when \( k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0} \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) at \( {y}_{k} \) can be defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and satisfy

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{y}_{k}, t}\right)  \leq  {15}
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) .

We now prove a statement analogous to Assertion 4 (i) of Step 3.

Assertion 5. For the above rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) and \( {\bar{k}}_{0} \) , we have that for any \( L > 0 \) , there is a positive constant \( \omega \left( L\right) \) such that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \omega \left( L\right)
\]

for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  L \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) , and for all \( k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0} \) .

Proof of Assertion 5. We slightly modify the argument in the proof of Assertion 4 (i). Let

\[
M\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  \rho }\right. \text{ and }t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
\text{ in the rescaled solutions }\left. {{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}, k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0}}\right\}
\]

and

\[
{\rho }_{0} = \sup \{ \rho  > 0 \mid  M\left( \rho \right)  <  + \infty \} .
\]

Note that the estimate (7.4.14) implies that \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) . We only need to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) .

We argue by contradiction. Suppose \( {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) . Then, after passing to a subsequence, there is a sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{y}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) in the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) with \( {t}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\widetilde{d}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\widetilde{y}}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) such that \( \widetilde{R}\left( {{\widetilde{y}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Denote by \( {\gamma }_{k} \) a minimizing geodesic segment from \( {y}_{k} \) to \( {\widetilde{y}}_{k} \) at the time \( {t}_{k} \) and denote by \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) the open geodesic ball centered at \( {y}_{k} \) of radius \( {\rho }_{0} \) on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

For any \( 0 < \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) with \( \rho \) near \( {\rho }_{0} \) , by applying Assertion 3 as before, we get that the rescaled solutions on the balls \( {B}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho }\right) \) are defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for all large \( k \) . By Step 1 and Shi’s derivative estimate, we further know that the covariant derivatives and higher order derivatives of the curvatures on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho  - \frac{\left( {\rho }_{0} - \rho \right) }{2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{32}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) are also uniformly bounded. Then by the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) ,{y}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {y}_{\infty } \) .

Clearly, the limit also has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption. Then by repeating the same argument as in the proof of Assertion 4 (i) in the rest, we derive a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum principle. This proves Assertion 5.

We then apply the second estimate of (7.4.17) and Assertion 5 to conclude that for any large constant \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) , there is a positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) such that for any small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

(7.4.18)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Then by applying Assertion 1 in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on the geodesic balls \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Furthermore, by the gradient estimates as in Step 1, we have

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right)
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) is arbitrarily small and the positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) is independent of \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) , we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfy

(7.4.19)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right) ,
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) .

Now, by taking convergent subsequences from the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) , we see that the limit solution is defined smoothly on a space-time open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times \; ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . By Step 4, we see that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , - {t}_{\max }}\right) \) at time \( - {t}_{\max } \) has bounded curvature. Then by combining with the canonical neighborhood assumption of accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) , we conclude that the curvature of the limit is uniformly bounded on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . So we have excluded the possibility (1).

Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Finally by combining with the canonical neighborhood theorem (Theorem 6.4.6), we see that \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) has a canonical neighborhood with parameter \( \varepsilon \) , which is a contradiction. Therefore we have completed the proof of the proposition. 0

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a Ricci flow with surgery \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) defined on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( T \leq  {T}_{i + 1} \) with surgery control parameter \( \bar{\delta } \) a non-increasing positive function defined on \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{i + 1}}\right\rbrack \) satisfying the hypotheses of Theorem 15.9 on its entire time-domain of definition, there is a constant \( N \) depending only on the volume of \( \left( {{M}_{0}, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , on \( {T}_{i + 1} \) , on \( {r}_{i + 1} \) , and on \( \bar{\delta }\left( {T}_{i + 1}\right) \) such that this Ricci flow with surgery defined on the interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) has at most \( N \) surgery times.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Let \( \left( {{M}_{t}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) be the \( t \) time-slice of \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) . If \( {t}_{0} \) is not a surgery time, then \( \operatorname{Vol}\left( t\right)  = \operatorname{Vol}\left( {{M}_{t}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a smooth function of \( t \) near \( {t}_{0} \) and

\[
\frac{d\operatorname{Vol}}{dt}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  =  - {\int }_{{M}_{{t}_{0}}}{Rd}\operatorname{vol},
\]

so that, because of the curvature pinching toward positive hypothesis, we have \( \frac{d\mathrm{{Vol}}}{dt}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \leq  6\mathrm{{Vol}}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) . If \( {t}_{0} \) is a surgery time, then either \( {M}_{{t}_{0}} \) has fewer connected components than \( {M}_{{t}_{0}^{ - }} \) or we do a surgery in an \( \epsilon \) -horn of \( {M}_{{t}_{0}^{ - }} \) . In the latter case we remove the end of the \( \epsilon \) -horn, which contains the positive half of a \( \bar{\delta }\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) -neck of scale \( h\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) . We then sew in a ball with volume at most \( \left( {1 + \epsilon }\right) K{h}^{3}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) , where \( K < \infty \) is the universal constant given in Lemma 12.3. Since \( h\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \leq  {\bar{\delta }}^{2}\left( {t}_{0}\right) r\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \leq  {\delta }_{0}^{2}r\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) and since we have chosen \( \bar{\delta }\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \leq  {\delta }_{0} < \; {K}^{-1} \) , it follows that this operation lowers volume by at least \( {\delta }^{-1}{h}^{2}\left( {t}_{0}\right) /2 \) . Since \( \bar{\delta }\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \geq  \bar{\delta }\left( {T}_{i + 1}\right)  > 0 \) and the canonical neighborhood parameter \( r \) at time \( {t}_{0} \) is at least \( {r}_{i + 1} > 0 \) , it follows that \( h\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \geq  h\left( {T}_{i + 1}\right)  > 0 \) . Thus, each surgery at time \( {t}_{0} \leq  {T}_{i + 1} \) along a 2-sphere removes at least a fixed amount of volume depending on \( \bar{\delta }\left( {T}_{i + 1}\right) \) and \( {r}_{i + 1} \) . Since under Ricci flow the volume grows at most exponentially, we see that there is a bound depending only on \( \bar{\delta }\left( {T}_{i + 1}\right) ,{T}_{i + 1},{r}_{i + 1} \) and \( \operatorname{Vol}\left( {{M}_{0}, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) on the number of 2-sphere surgeries that we can do in this time interval. On the other hand, the number of components at any time \( t \) is at most \( {N}_{0} + S\left( t\right)  - D\left( t\right) \) where \( {N}_{0} \) is the number of connected components of \( {M}_{0}, S\left( t\right) \) is the number of 2-sphere surgeries performed in the time interval \( \lbrack 0, t) \) and \( D\left( t\right) \) is the number of connected components removed by surgeries at times in the interval \( \lbrack 0, t) \) . Hence, there is a bound on the number of components in terms of \( {N}_{0} \) and \( S\left( T\right) \) that can be removed by surgery in the interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) . Since the initial conditions are normalized, \( {N}_{0} \) is bounded by the volume of \( \left( {{M}_{0}, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . This completes the proof of the result.
